# How Java Runs

## [When Some Values are More Equal than Others](memory/where-things-are.html)

Student: Professor, my Java is broken.

Prof: What makes you say that?

Student: Well, the same thing sometimes returns `true` and sometimes returns `false`:

```java
String tp1 = "trash panda";
String trash = "trash";
String tp2 = trash + " panda";
String tp3 = tp2;
boolean same1and2 = tp1 == tp2;
boolean same1and3 = tp1 == tp3;
boolean same2and3 = tp2 == tp3;
```

Output:

```text
tp1 = trash panda
trash = trash
tp2 = trash panda
tp3 = trash panda
same1and2 = false
same1and3 = false
same2and3 = true
```

Prof: Fascinating! That’s a cool example you came up with to test. And I think you’re frustrated because the behavior is different than for numbers?

Student: Right. If I do `6 + 7 == 13` that’s clearly `true`. So why isn’t `trash + " panda" == "trash panda"`? And I don’t think it’s fascinating I think it’s annoying! The same thing happens with arrays, look:

```java
int[] nums1 = { 6, 7 };
int[] nums2 = { 6, 7 };
int[] nums3 = nums2;
boolean same1and2 = nums1 == nums2;
boolean same1and3 = nums1 == nums3;
boolean same2and3 = nums2 == nums3;
```

Output:

```text
nums1 = [6, 7]
nums2 = [6, 7]
nums3 = [6, 7]
same1and2 = false
same1and3 = false
same2and3 = true
```

Prof: Indeed. Alright, it’s time to unpack one of the things I told you to wait on. We need to talk about reference types vs primitive types and also introduce the idea of different parts of memory.

Student: Yes, please, make it make sense!

Prof: I often find it’s best to describe memory with a picture. I’ll focus on the array picture program. Here’s how I like to draw it:

```
Names (the stack)
  top level
    nums1 = @1001
    nums2 = @1002
    nums3 = @1002
    same1and2 = false
    same1and3 = false
    same2and3 = true
Heap
  @1001: [6, 7]
  @1002: [6, 7]
```

Hover over an address like `@1001` to draw an arrow to its object on the heap; click or tap it to keep the arrow showing.

Prof: OK, so stepping way back – our computers store data in memory. You can think of memory in Java as being split into two parts:

- The stack which holds all the definitions at the top level, all method arguments, and all definitions of variables inside methods
- The heap which holds all created objects. The objects we’ve seen so far are record instances like `Point[...]` or `Student[...]`, arrays, and as it turns out, `String`s. When an object is created, like with `new` or with `{"array", "initialization"}`, Java makes space for it on the heap and returns a reference to it. Only the reference actually gets stored in variables, fields, or array elements.

This picture makes that explicit. See the things that look like `@1001` and `@1002`? Those are the references. So we can see that the value stored in `nums2` and the value stored in `nums3` are **the same reference**. In contrast, `nums1` holds a separate reference to **a different array with the same contents**.

The last piece we need to understand this is that `==` compares **references**, not **contents**, of objects. So `same1and2` is calculating `@1001` `==` `@1002`, which is `false`, while `same2and3` is calculating `@1002` `==` `@1002`, which is `true`.

Whew, that was a lot. What do you think?

Student: It’s helping a little bit. Can we see what’s going on with the first example?

Prof: It looks like this in memory:

```
Names (the stack)
  top level
    tp1 = @1001
    trash = @1002
    tp2 = @1003
    tp3 = @1003
    same1and2 = false
    same1and3 = false
    same2and3 = true
Heap
  @1001: "trash panda"
  @1002: "trash"
  @1003: "trash panda"
```

Prof: Same shape, more or less, but the heap contents are the characters in the strings as opposed to arrays. Just like arrays, using `==` on strings compares the **references**, not the **contents**, which explains the output.

Student: OK, this seems really complicated, but I guess it **does** explain what I was seeing.

#### Practice

Exercise:

Java hands out references in the order objects are created, starting at `@1001`. Fill in the memory picture for this code:

```java
int[] a = { 3, 4 };
int[] b = { 3, 4 };
int[] c = b;
int[] d = a;
boolean ab = a == b;
boolean bc = b == c;
boolean ad = a == d;
```

```java
Names
a  = [@1002 / @1001]
b  = [@1002 / @1001]
c  = [@1002 / @1001]
d  = [@1002 / @1001]
ab = [false / true]
bc = [false / true]
ad = [false / true]

Heap
@1001: [3, 4]
@1002: [3, 4]
```

Exercise:

Same rules, starting again at `@1001`. This time one of the objects holds references of its own:

```java
String word = "hi";
String loud = word + word;
String same = loud;
String[] pair = { word, loud };
boolean match = pair[1] == same;
```

```java
Names
word  = [@1001 / @1003 / @1002]
loud  = [@1001 / @1003 / @1002]
same  = [@1001 / @1003 / @1002]
pair  = [@1001 / @1003 / @1002]
match = [false / true]

Heap
@1001: "hi"
@1002: "hihi"
@1003: [[@1001 / @1003 / @1002], [@1001 / @1003 / @1002]]
```

## [Checking Contents vs Checking Identity](memory/checking-contents.html)

Student: OK, so can we ever compare the contents of strings or arrays?

Prof: Absolutely! Many objects have a method called `equals` that helps with this. So for strings, just use `s1.equals(s2)` instead of `s1 == s2`. That’s actually what’s happening with records and strings in `assertEquals`:

```java
record Point(int x, int y) { }
void main() {
  Point p1 = new Point(4, 5);
  Point p2 = new Point(4, 5);
  System.out.println("p1 == p2? " + (p1 == p2));
  System.out.println("p1.equals(p2)? " + p1.equals(p2));
  assertEquals(p1, p2); // succeeds!

  String tp1 = "trash panda";
  String trash = "trash";
  String tp2 = trash + " panda";
  System.out.println("tp1 == tp2? " + (tp1 == tp2));
  System.out.println("tp1.equals(tp2)? " + tp1.equals(tp2));
  assertEquals(tp1, tp2); // succeeds!
}
```

Output:

```text
p1 == p2? false
p1.equals(p2)? true
tp1 == tp2? false
tp1.equals(tp2)? true
```

Student: Oh, OK. So I should always use `.equals()`?

Prof: Well, we may see some cases where we want reference equality. We don’t have any right now. So it’s true, we mostly care about the `.equals()` kind, which is called structural equality (it inspects the structure). But we can’t get rid of `==` entirely because we need it for comparing, say, `int` values. Those are called primitive types, as opposed to objects which are reference types, and they compare the numbers themselves with `==`.

Student: Hmm I see. OK so we need `==` for numbers. What about arrays? You didn’t give an example of structural equality for those.

Prof: It’s a little trickier there. Arrays’ `equals` method checks reference equality, not structural. So there’s actually a separate helper for arrays called `Arrays.equals`; it takes two array arguments and compares them structurally. And JUnit has a separate `assertArrayEquals`.

```java
import java.util.Arrays;
void main() {
  int[] nums1 = { 6, 7 };
  int[] nums2 = { 6, 7 };
  System.out.println("nums1 == nums2? " + (nums1 == nums2));
  System.out.println("nums1.equals(nums2)? " + nums1.equals(nums2) + ", surprise!");
  System.out.println("Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? " + Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2));
  assertArrayEquals(nums1, nums2); // succeeds!
  assertEquals(nums1, nums2);      // fails!
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
nums1 == nums2? false
nums1.equals(nums2)? false, surprise!
Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? true
Exception in thread "Thread-0" org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: expected: <[I@85a> but was: <[I@85b>
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals(Unknown Source)
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

Student: But why?

Prof: Well, part of the issue is that because arrays can **change**, two arrays could have the same contents at one point in the program, but differ later.

Student: Huh?

Prof: Because of array update, which we saw in the last section. Here, I’ll show you:

```java
import java.util.Arrays;
void main() {
  int[] nums1 = { 6, 7 };
  int[] nums2 = { 6, 7 };
  System.out.println("nums1 == nums2? " + (nums1 == nums2));
  System.out.println("nums1.equals(nums2)? " + nums1.equals(nums2) + ", surprise!");
  
  System.out.println("Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? " + Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2));
  assertArrayEquals(nums1, nums2); // succeeds!
  
  nums2[0] = 999;
  System.out.println("Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? " + Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2));
  assertArrayEquals(nums1, nums2); // fails
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
nums1 == nums2? false
nums1.equals(nums2)? false, surprise!
Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? true
Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? false
Exception in thread "Thread-0" org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: array contents differ at index [0], expected: <6> but was: <999>
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failArrays(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.arraysEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertArrayEquals(Unknown Source)
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

Prof: So one way I think about it is that Java makes sure that `.equals()` between arrays only returns true if they are the same reference, because that’s the only way to guarantee that they will **always** be the same now and in the future. If they are different references, it could change. So you have to use `Arrays.equals` to “opt-in”, and acknowledge that you know you mean “equal right now”. The final memory diagram at the point the assertion fails looks like this:

```
Names (the stack)
  main()
    nums1 = @1001
    nums2 = @1002
  top level
Heap
  @1001: [6, 7]
  @1002: [999, 7]
```

Student: Hmm, that seems like a lot to remember.

Prof: It is. The main thing to think through is what you’re asking in an equality check. If it involves objects (which includes `String`), reach for `.equals()`. If it involves arrays, there may be more to check.

Student: I’ll have to sit with that a little bit.

#### Practice

Exercise:

Each pair below holds the same contents, built separately. Pick the check that gives `true` for each pair:

```java
record Point(int x, int y) { }
int a = 6 + 7;
int b = 13;
String trash = "trash";
String s1 = "trash panda";
String s2 = trash + " panda";
Point p1 = new Point(4, 5);
Point p2 = new Point(4, 5);
int[] n1 = { 6, 7 };
int[] n2 = { 6, 7 };
```

```java
boolean sameInts    = [a.equals(b) / Arrays.equals(a, b) / a == b];
boolean sameStrings = [s1 == s2 / Arrays.equals(s1, s2) / s1.equals(s2)];
boolean samePoints  = [p1.equals(p2) / p1 == p2 / Arrays.equals(p1, p2)];
boolean sameArrays  = [Arrays.equals(n1, n2) / n1 == n2 / n1.equals(n2)];
```

## [Methods and Memory](memory/stack-frames.html)

Student: Wait a minute. Show me that last memory diagram again?

Prof: This one?

```java
import java.util.Arrays;
void main() {
  int[] nums1 = { 6, 7 };
  int[] nums2 = { 6, 7 };
  System.out.println("nums1 == nums2? " + (nums1 == nums2));
  System.out.println("nums1.equals(nums2)? " + nums1.equals(nums2) + ", surprise!");
  
  System.out.println("Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? " + Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2));
  assertArrayEquals(nums1, nums2); // succeeds!
  
  nums2[0] = 999;
  System.out.println("Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? " + Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2));
  assertArrayEquals(nums1, nums2); // fails
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
nums1 == nums2? false
nums1.equals(nums2)? false, surprise!
Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? true
Arrays.equals(nums1, nums2)? false
Exception in thread "Thread-0" org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: array contents differ at index [0], expected: <6> but was: <999>
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failArrays(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.arraysEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertArrayEquals(Unknown Source)
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

```
Names (the stack)
  main()
    nums1 = @1001
    nums2 = @1002
  top level
Heap
  @1001: [6, 7]
  @1002: [999, 7]
```

Student: Yeah. What’s going on with the stack there?

Prof: Oh sharp eye! Right, so this is a program with a `main` method. That method is called to start the program. In this case, we didn’t have any definitions of values at the top level, so that’s empty. All the action is happening in `main`’s stack frame.

Student: Stack frame?

Prof: Every time a method is called, Java sets aside space for its parameters and its variables (the definitions in the method body) in what’s called a stack frame. So here we’re seeing that the two arrays were created inside `main`, which was called from the top level.

Student: Huh. OK. So that happens for all methods? Or is this just a `main` thing?

Prof: For all methods. It’s true even if we call some methods from the top level. For example if we have a builder pattern, there are some interesting aspects to the memory diagram:

```java
record Menu(int[] pricesCents) {
  int[] discounted() {
    int[] result = new int[pricesCents.length];
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      result[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
    return result;
  }
}
int[] regular = { 2000, 1000, 500, 800 };
Menu menu = new Menu(regular);
int[] sale = menu.discounted();
```

Output:

```text
regular = [2000, 1000, 500, 800]
menu = Menu[pricesCents=[I@880]
sale = [1800, 900, 450, 720]
```

Prof: So here we could talk about the memory diagram **in the middle of running the builder loop**. As in, what does memory look like when we are about to process the 3rd of the 4 elements in the array?

```
Names (the stack)
  menu.discounted() on @1002
    result = @1003
    index = 2
    p = 500
  top level
    regular = @1001
    menu = @1002
Heap
  @1001: [2000, 1000, 500, 800]
  @1002: Menu[pricesCents=@1001]
  @1003: [1800, 900, 0, 0]
```

Student: Wait, **in the middle of the loop**, what does that mean?

Prof: Well, Java runs code one step at a time, where “steps” are things like starting a method call, updating a variable, changing an array element, creating an object, and so on. So we can ask questions like “what does memory look like at a particular moment”.

Student: OK, and this picture is right after updating the array with `900`.

Prof: That’s right. We could also talk about the memory diagram at the end of the program

```
Names (the stack)
  menu.discounted() on @1002
    result = @1003
    index = 4
    returns @1003
  top level
    regular = @1001
    menu = @1002
    sale = @1003
Heap
  @1001: [2000, 1000, 500, 800]
  @1002: Menu[pricesCents=@1001]
  @1003: [1800, 900, 450, 720]
```

Prof: Now, Java may or may not actually keep track of the old stack frame like in this picture once the method call returns. But it’s a helpful picture!

Student: So that reference for the new array was made… inside the method?

Prof: That’s right!

Student: And then it gets stored at the top level?

Prof: In this example, that’s right.

#### Practice

Exercise:

Picture memory while `big.area()` is running, just before its `return`. Where is each name stored?

```java
record Pizza(double inches, int costCents) {
  double area() {
    double radius = inches / 2;
    return radius * radius * Math.PI;
  }
}
String shop = "Trash Panda Pizza";
void main() {
  Pizza big = new Pizza(16, 1000);
  double bigArea = big.area();
  System.out.println(shop + ": " + bigArea);
}
```

```java
shop   [a field on the heap / top level / main() / big.area()]
big    [a field on the heap / top level / main() / big.area()]
radius [a field on the heap / top level / main() / big.area()]
inches [a field on the heap / top level / main() / big.area()]
```

## [Methods that Update Arrays](memory/updater-method.html)

Student: So I was thinking about how we just saw a builder example again. My friend told me they never write methods that make new arrays because it’s inefficient, they just write methods that change the arrays.

Prof: Your friend sounds very opinionated.

Student: They know so much stuff! It’s hard to argue with them.

Prof: Well, you can take it on my authority that both kinds are useful; we should study the kind that changes arrays now. We can do the same thing as before, but instead of returning a **new** array, we can change the one stored in the record. Sometimes we call this an update or an in-place update of the array.

Student: OK great now I’ll be able to compare them myself.

Prof: So, we had `discounted` in the last step. Let’s write `discountInPlace`. What do you think the return type should be?

Student: Ummm, `int[]` again?

Prof: So our goal here is to write a method that **changes** the existing array, rather than returning a new one. Do we know a type for methods that have effects and don’t return anything?

Student: Ummm. `void`?

Prof: Right. So let’s set up the method with a `void` return type, and try to change the existing array without making a new one.

```java
record Menu(int[] pricesCents) {
  void discountInPlace() {
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      pricesCents[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
  }
}
int[] regular = { 2000, 1000, 500, 800 };
Menu menu = new Menu(regular);
```

Output:

```text
regular = [2000, 1000, 500, 800]
menu = Menu[pricesCents=[I@7ba]
```

Student: Wait what’s that `I@` thing

Prof: Ah, that’s how **Java** prints arrays. The `I` means `int`, and the `@` followed by the numbers is a reference number made by Java. By default this is what Java shows when you print an array – it prints its reference!

Student: Interesting. OK. Back to the code. So instead of having a new `result` and filling that in, you just… change the `pricesCents`? And that works?

Prof: Let’s see! How do we call it?

Student: I guess… `menu.discountInPlace()`?

Prof: Great idea. It turns out we aren’t allowed to write a method call outside of a definition at the top level! So if we just write `menu.discountInPlace()` we’d get a syntax error. `void`-returning methods have to be called from another method body – `main` works. Have a look at this program; do you notice anything interesting about the output?

```java
record Menu(int[] pricesCents) {
  void discountInPlace() {
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      pricesCents[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
  }
}
int[] regular = { 2000, 1000, 500, 800 };
Menu menu = new Menu(regular);
void main() {
  menu.discountInPlace();
}
```

Output:

```text
regular = [1800, 900, 450, 720]
menu = Menu[pricesCents=[I@924]
```

Student: Whoa, the contents of `regular` changed?

Prof: That’s right. `main` ran and called `discountInPlace`, and that **changed** the contents of the array stored in `regular`. Here’s a memory diagram of what things look like in the middle of the loop for **this** program:

```
Names (the stack)
  menu.discountInPlace() on @1002
    index = 2
    p = 500
  main()
  top level
    regular = @1001
    menu = @1002
Heap
  @1001: [2000 1800, 1000 900, 500, 800]
  @1002: Menu[pricesCents=@1001]
```

Student: Huh so that `@1001` is referred to by… `regular`, and by the `pricesCents` field. And so that reference is being used in the loop?

Prof: That’s right, and that’s why you see the object reference `@1002` in the frame header. That was the receiver for the method call, and so we know that `pricesCents` is referring to the field of **that** object.

Student: That… went a little over my head.

Prof: So when we use `pricesCents` in the body of the loop, it has to refer to **some** value. It isn’t a parameter of the method; it’s a field of the receiver we called it with. The receiver is `@1002`, and **its** `pricesCents` field is `@1001`, so that’s how that lookup occurs.

Student: OK, I think I kind of get it. I definitely understand that there is only one array made in this example, and it’s changing inside the method.

Prof: That’s a good lesson to take from this conversation. This is called an updater method for an array.

#### Practice

```java

    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {

  }
  void discountInPlace() {
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      pricesCents[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
  }
}
int[] regular = { 2000, 1000, 500, 800 };

  menu.discountInPlace();
```

## [Objects, Methods, and Memory](memory/multiple-objects.html)

Student: I think I still don’t get what’s going on with stack frames and method calls. What is the reference in the top of the stack frame for?

Prof: Let’s build up an example with **two** objects whose methods we call.

```java
record Menu(int[] pricesCents) {
  int[] discounted() {
    int[] result = new int[pricesCents.length];
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      result[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
    return result;
  }
  void discountInPlace() {
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      pricesCents[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
  }
}
int[] regular = { 2000, 1000, 500, 800 };
Menu menu = new Menu(regular);
int[] pricy = { 10000, 5000, 9000, 8000 };
Menu pricyMenu = new Menu(pricy);
void main() {
  menu.discountInPlace();
  pricyMenu.discountInPlace();
  menu.discountInPlace();
}
```

Output:

```text
regular = [1620, 810, 405, 648]
menu = Menu[pricesCents=[I@77d]
pricy = [9000, 4500, 8100, 7200]
pricyMenu = Menu[pricesCents=[I@77f]
```

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
    regular = @1001
    menu = @1002
    pricy = @1003
    pricyMenu = @1004
Heap
  @1001: [1620, 810, 405, 648]
  @1002: Menu[pricesCents=@1001]
  @1003: [9000, 4500, 8100, 7200]
  @1004: Menu[pricesCents=@1003]
```

Student: Hmm… so there’s like… three frames? One for each time `discountInPlace` is called?

Prof: Makes sense. So how are they different? The method doesn’t take any arguments, so what makes the frames different from one another?

Student: Oh! So to tell apart the first two calls, it has to know which object is used for each, `menu` or `pricyMenu`.

Prof: Exactly.

Student: That’s cool. So the first call uses `menu`, the second uses `pricyMenu`. Oh and the values in the `menu` one get updated **twice**. Why is that?

Prof: That corresponds to the **two** calls to `discountInPlace` on `menu`. The first time through, it updates all the values once. The second time is **still working with the same array**, so it updates it again.

Student: I see!

#### Practice

This record has a builder and an updater too. Step through the trace to check your answers.

```java
record Section(int[] scores) {
  int[] curved() {
    int[] result = new int[scores.length];
    int index = 0;
    for(int s: scores) {
      result[index] = s + 5;
      index += 1;
    }
    return result;
  }
  void curveInPlace() {
    int index = 0;
    for(int s: scores) {
      scores[index] = s + 5;
      index += 1;
    }
  }
}
int[] morningScores = { 80, 92, 75 };
Section morning = new Section(morningScores);
int[] eveningScores = { 68, 88, 90 };
Section evening = new Section(eveningScores);
void main() {
  int[] curved1 = morning.curved();
  evening.curveInPlace();
  int[] curved2 = morning.curved();
  evening.curveInPlace();
}
```

## [Aliasing](memory/aliasing.html)

Student: Professor I wrote a program and I don’t get why it’s running that way.

Prof: Great! That probably means there’s something good to learn. Let’s see it!

Student: I made two `Menu` instances, but it seems like updating one updates the other:

```java
record Menu(int[] pricesCents) {
  int[] discounted() {
    int[] result = new int[pricesCents.length];
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      result[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
    return result;
  }
  void discountInPlace() {
    int index = 0;
    for(int p: pricesCents) {
      pricesCents[index] = p * 90 / 100;
      index += 1;
    }
  }
}
int[] regular = { 2000, 1000, 500, 800 };
Menu lunch = new Menu(regular);
Menu dinner = new Menu(regular);
int[] lunchPrices = lunch.pricesCents;
int[] dinnerPrices = dinner.pricesCents;
void main() {
  lunch.discountInPlace();
}
```

Output:

```text
regular = [1800, 900, 450, 720]
lunch = Menu[pricesCents=[I@7bf]
dinner = Menu[pricesCents=[I@7bf]
lunchPrices = [1800, 900, 450, 720]
dinnerPrices = [1800, 900, 450, 720]
```

Student: I’m confused because I thought `discountInPlace` would only update the `lunch` menu, not the `dinner` one. But when I show the arrays it seems like all the arrays updated.

Prof: Very interesting! I think what’s happening here is there is only one array.

Student: Only one array?

Prof: That’s right. Let’s look at a memory diagram at the end:

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
    regular = @1001
    lunch = @1002
    dinner = @1003
    lunchPrices = @1001
    dinnerPrices = @1001
Heap
  @1001: [1800, 900, 450, 720]
  @1002: Menu[pricesCents=@1001]
  @1003: Menu[pricesCents=@1001]
```

Prof: So that one array is created and stored in `regular`, and **that same reference** is used to initialize both `lunch` and `dinner`. Look at the two objects – they have different references but both of the `pricesCents` fields store the same array reference!

Student: I see, that one reference is referred to by five different places!

Prof: Right, and the array updates change the elements on the heap, so then if we access those elements through any of the references, we see the updated values. This idea has a name: it is called aliasing, when different names in a program store the same reference. Aliasing makes it so updates through one reference are visible through all the others.

Student: OK, I think I got it!

#### Practice

```java
record Team(String[] players) {
  void replaceFirst(String name) {
    players[0] = name;
  }
}
String[] varsity = { "Ana", "Ben", "Cy" };
String[] jv = { "Dee", "Eli" };
Team red = new Team(varsity);
Team blue = new Team(jv);
Team green = new Team(red.players);
String[] roster = blue.players;
Team gold = new Team(roster);
void main() {
  green.replaceFirst("Zed");
}
```

Exercise:

This program creates two arrays. Which one is stored in each team’s `players` field?

`red.players`: [{ "Ana", "Ben", "Cy" } / { "Dee", "Eli" }]
`blue.players`: [{ "Ana", "Ben", "Cy" } / { "Dee", "Eli" }]
`green.players`: [{ "Ana", "Ben", "Cy" } / { "Dee", "Eli" }]
`gold.players`: [{ "Ana", "Ben", "Cy" } / { "Dee", "Eli" }]

Exercise:

After `main` runs, how many of the four teams have `"Zed"` as their first player?

Answer: ____

## [Nuanced and Nested Structures](memory/arrays-as-fields.html)

Student: We talked about structural vs. reference equality – which one do records use?

Prof: Great question, how would you know?

Student: I guess I’d have to try `.equals()` on an object I created from a record?

Prof: That’s right, or `assertEquals`.

Student: OK let’s try both.

```java
record Car(String make, String model, int year) {}
Car c1 = new Car("Honda", "Civic", 2008);
Car c2 = new Car("Honda", "Civic", 2008);
boolean refEqual = c1 == c2;
boolean structEqual = c1.equals(c2);
void main() {
    assertEquals(c1, c2);
    System.out.println("All tests passed!");
}
```

Output:

```text
All tests passed!
c1 = Car[make=Honda, model=Civic, year=2008]
c2 = Car[make=Honda, model=Civic, year=2008]
refEqual = false
structEqual = true
```

Student: Great! Easy.

Prof: OK, actually, I have some bad news. Let’s say these cars could have an array of ints representing the pressure of the 4 tires (it’ll always be 4 elements long). Just a quick tip, you can use `new int[]{ ... }` to make an int array with specific contents as a value, without defining a new name.

Student: Sure, let’s do it!

```java
record Car(String make, String model, int year, int[] pressures) {}
Car c1 = new Car("Honda", "Civic", 2008, new int[]{ 35, 35, 33, 33 });
Car c2 = new Car("Honda", "Civic", 2008, new int[]{ 35, 35, 33, 33 });
boolean refEqual = c1 == c2;
boolean structEqual = c1.equals(c2);
void main() {
    assertEquals(c1, c2);
    System.out.println("All tests passed!");
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
Exception in thread "Thread-0" org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: expected: <Car[make=Honda, model=Civic, year=2008, pressures=[I@96d]> but was: <Car[make=Honda, model=Civic, year=2008, pressures=[I@97c]>
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals(Unknown Source)
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

Student: Wait, what?

Prof: Right, so that test succeeded before, and now it fails. This is a real gotcha when working with arrays and equality in Java.

Student: What’s going on?

Prof: Well, we need to be precise about what the “structural equality” does on `record` instances in Java. It works by calling `.equals()` on all the pairs of fields that are reference types, and uses `==` on the ones that are primitives. So for `Car` it’s like the method does

```java
boolean equals(Car other) {
    return make.equals(other.make) && model.equals(other.model)
            && year == other.year && pressures.equals(other.pressures);
}
```

Student: But that looks fine?

Prof: What did we learn about the `.equals()` method on arrays?

Student: Ohhhhhh! That does **reference equality** on the two arrays, not structural. It would need to be `Arrays.equals` for that to work.

Prof: That’s right. We’ll have a conversation in the future about how to write **our own** equals method. For now we just need to be careful and conscious of our equality comparisons. Sometimes we might want to use a field lookup to access arrays and compare them directly in a test, for example.

Student: Noted. Wow, Java makes us remember a lot about equality.

Prof: It’s true. Some of this is **necessary** complexity, in that most languages do expose both reference and structural equality (or [even more](https://pyret.org/docs/latest/equality.html)). But some of it is also **incidental** complexity related to arrays in Java, which have pretty specific rules. We’ll see ways to manage both kinds of complexity going forward.

#### Practice

Exercise:

`c1` and `c2` have tire pressures with the same contents. Which line checks that in a test?

```java
void main() {
  [assertArrayEquals(c1.pressures, c2.pressures); / assertEquals(c1.pressures, c2.pressures); / assertEquals(c1, c2); / assertArrayEquals(c1, c2);]
}
```

```java
record Car(String make, String model, int year, int[] pressures) {}
int[] factory = { 35, 35, 33, 33 };
Car car1 = new Car("Honda", "Civic", 2008, factory);
Car car2 = new Car("Honda", "Civic", 2008, factory);
Car car3 = new Car("Honda", "Civic", 2008, new int[]{ 35, 35, 33, 33 });
void main() {
  car1.pressures[0] = 30;
}
```

Exercise:

After `main` runs, what is true of each pair?

`car1.pressures` and `car2.pressures`: [the same array / different arrays, different contents / different arrays, same contents]
`car1.pressures` and `car3.pressures`: [the same array / different arrays, different contents / different arrays, same contents]
`car2.pressures` and `car3.pressures`: [the same array / different arrays, different contents / different arrays, same contents]
`car1.equals(car2)`: [false / true]
`car2.equals(car3)`: [false / true]

## [How Java Runs in Summary](memory/summary.html)

```java
record Bag(int[] counts) {
  int[] doubled() {
    int[] result = new int[counts.length];
    int index = 0;
    for(int n: counts) {
      result[index] = n * 2;
      index += 1;
    }
    return result;
  }
  void addOne() {
    int index = 0;
    for(int n: counts) {
      counts[index] = n + 1;
      index += 1;
    }
  }
}
int[] start = { 1, 2 };
Bag x = new Bag(start);
Bag y = new Bag(x.counts);
int[] more = y.doubled();
void main() {
  x.addOne();
}
```

Exercise:

Java hands out references in the order objects are created, starting at `@1001`. Fill in the memory picture for when `main` finishes.

```java
Names
top level: start = @1001, x = @1002, y = @1003, more = [@1004 / @1001 / @1003]
  y.doubled() on [@1002 / @1003], returns @1004
  main()
    x.addOne() on [@1002 / @1003]

Heap
@1001: [[2, 4] / [2, 3] / [1, 2]]
@1002: Bag[counts=@1001]
@1003: Bag[counts=[@1004 / @1001]]
@1004: [[4, 6] / [2, 4] / [2, 3]]
```

Exercise:

Still at the end of `main`, what does each expression produce?

```java
x == y                     [true / false]
x.equals(y)                [true / false]
start == y.counts          [true / false]
Arrays.equals(start, more) [true / false]
```

Exercise:

This test fails. Why?

```java
record Bag(int[] counts) { }
void main() {
  assertEquals(new Bag(new int[]{ 1, 2 }), new Bag(new int[]{ 1, 2 }));
}
```

Choose one:

- The two arrays have different contents.
- `assertEquals` compares the two `Bag`s with `==`.
- The two `counts` fields hold different arrays, and a record’s `equals` compares an array field with the array’s own `equals`, which checks the reference.
- Records always compare by reference.

# Nested and 2D Structures

## [Rows of Seats](nested-and-2d/2d-arrays.html)

*This example is thanks to Jill Su, contributed in an earlier edition of this book.*

Student: Professor, I have a question. I was getting seats at a movie for me and some friends this weekend. They had assigned seats, and a whole screen that showed the number of empty seats, and also options like “find 3 seats together”. How would I program that?

Prof: Great question. I’m going to lift out a specific, simple version for our discussion – for each seat we will just track a single `boolean` for if it is occupied or not. We can grow it into something more complex later if we want.

Student: I’m OK with that.

Prof: Let’s think about what data we need to store – what types might make sense based on what we’ve seen?

Student: I guess there are a lot of seats, so an array?

Prof: Ah interesting idea; arrays will almost certainly be involved. Let’s look at a picture to help guide our thinking.

[image]

Drawing by Jill Su.

Prof: Let’s first start by making three definitions, one per row. What might that look like?

Student: Hmm there would be three rows. Like `boolean[] topRow = { true, false, true, true, true, true };` and then the second row would be like `{ true, false, false, false, true }`

Prof: Good. So I see you’ve picked `true` for “seat available” and `false` for “not available”. Seems good. So then we need a little new insight if we want to represent the whole theater – we can store all of these array references in another array.

Student: In another array?

Prof: That’s right. We can have types like `boolean[][]` which means “array of array of booleans”. Or, super precisely, “array of references to boolean arrays”. Let’s write the code and look at a memory diagram.

```java
boolean[] top = { true, false, true, true, true, true };
boolean[] middle = { true, false, false, false, true };
boolean[] bottom = { true, true, false, false };
boolean[][] seats = { top, middle, bottom };
```

Output:

```text
top = [true, false, true, true, true, true]
middle = [true, false, false, false, true]
bottom = [true, true, false, false]
seats = [[true, false, true, true, true, true], [true, false, false, false, true], [true, true, false, false]]
```

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
    top = @1001
    middle = @1002
    bottom = @1003
    seats = @1004
Heap
  @1001: [true, false, true, true, true, true]
  @1002: [true, false, false, false, true]
  @1003: [true, true, false, false]
  @1004: [@1001, @1002, @1003]
```

Prof: So if we wanted to represent this as a record, we might have something like this:

```java
record Theater(boolean[][] seats) { }
```

and then we can start to ask questions like “how many empty seats”.

Student: Ah, ok, so you’re thinking like `int emptySeats()` as a method on `Theater`?

Prof: Right, and getting that right will teach us about arrays of arrays. What do you think the loop will look like?

Student: Well, it’s like a counter pattern, right? We learned about those.

Prof: Indeed. If we have a loop that just needs to look at all the elements of a 2d array and count them, we can use a **nested loop** that matches the idea of **nested arrays**:

```java
record Theater(boolean[][] seats) {
  int emptySeats() {
    int howMany = 0;
    for(boolean[] row: seats) {
      for(boolean seat: row) {
        if(seat) { howMany += 1; }
      }
    }
    return howMany;
  }
}
boolean[] top = { true, false, true, true, true, true };
boolean[] middle = { true, false, false, false, true };
boolean[] bottom = { true, true, false, false };
boolean[][] seats = { top, middle, bottom };
Theater theater = new Theater(seats);
int emptySeats = theater.emptySeats();
```

Output:

```text
top = [true, false, true, true, true, true]
middle = [true, false, false, false, true]
bottom = [true, true, false, false]
seats = [[true, false, true, true, true, true], [true, false, false, false, true], [true, true, false, false]]
theater = Theater[seats=[[Z@92b]
emptySeats = 9
```

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
    top = @1001
    middle = @1002
    bottom = @1003
    seats = @1004
    theater = @1005
    emptySeats = 9
Heap
  @1001: [true, false, true, true, true, true]
  @1002: [true, false, false, false, true]
  @1003: [true, true, false, false]
  @1004: [@1001, @1002, @1003]
  @1005: Theater[seats=@1004]
```

Student: OK, I think I get it. So each time through the outer loop, `row` stores one of the array references. Then the inner loop works with that.

Prof: Right!

#### Practice

Exercise:

Trace `theater.emptySeats()`. For each run of the outer loop, how many times does the inner loop’s body run, and what is `howMany` when the inner loop finishes?

`row` is `top`: the inner body runs ____ times, and then `howMany` is ____
`row` is `middle`: the inner body runs ____ times, and then `howMany` is ____
`row` is `bottom`: the inner body runs ____ times, and then `howMany` is ____

## [Sitting with Friends](nested-and-2d/2d-arrays-more.html)

Student: OK, now that we’ve done that, what does the program look like to check if there are enough seats next to each other?

Prof: Ah great question. I think this is a good one to break down into a helper and then answer the overall question. Let’s build it up. Back to the image – say we want 3 seats together. The top row has enough, right?

[image]

Student: Right.

Prof: Did you need to look at any of the other rows to determine that?

Student: I guess not?

Prof: That’s interesting, because **whether or not a row has enough seats** is just a property of one `boolean[]` array, not of the whole theater.

Student: I can see that.

Prof: And then if **any** row has enough seats next to each other, then the theater itself has such a row.

Student: Yeah, I buy that.

Prof: OK, so let’s write the helper first. What do you think it takes as arguments?

Student: I guess just `boolean[] row`?

Prof: Anything else? Will it always check for 3 seats in a row?

Student: Oh right, so I guess also an `int` for how many seats we want.

Prof: And in our simple example for now, what does it return?

Student: A single `boolean` – whether or not the row had enough seats

```java
record Theater(boolean[][] seats) {
  boolean rowHasSeats(boolean[] row, int target) {
    int consecutiveAvailable = 0;
    for(boolean b: row) {
      if(b) { consecutiveAvailable += 1; }
      else { consecutiveAvailable = 0; }
      if(consecutiveAvailable >= target) { return true; }
    }
    return false;
  }
}
boolean[] top = { true, false, true, true, true, true };
boolean[] middle = { true, false, false, false, true };
boolean[] bottom = { true, true, false, false };
boolean[][] seats = { top, middle, bottom };
Theater theater = new Theater(seats);
boolean rowHasSeats = theater.rowHasSeats(top, 3);
```

Output:

```text
top = [true, false, true, true, true, true]
middle = [true, false, false, false, true]
bottom = [true, true, false, false]
seats = [[true, false, true, true, true, true], [true, false, false, false, true], [true, true, false, false]]
theater = Theater[seats=[[Z@75e]
rowHasSeats = true
```

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
    top = @1001
    middle = @1002
    bottom = @1003
    seats = @1004
    theater = @1005
    rowHasSeats = true
Heap
  @1001: [true, false, true, true, true, true]
  @1002: [true, false, false, false, true]
  @1003: [true, true, false, false]
  @1004: [@1001, @1002, @1003]
  @1005: Theater[seats=@1004]
```

Prof: This one is worth tracing from the beginning! It has some interesting ideas. It’s kind of a counter loop, but it also has another pattern – a search that returns as soon as it finds the answer. The `return` in the loop returns from **the whole method**. So if we ever find `target` adjacent seats, we return `true` immediately. We only return `false` if we get through the whole array without finding a sequence like that.

Student: It’s also weird because we don’t use `seats` at all in the method. So we say `theater.rowHasSeats(top, 3)` but we never use any of the fields from `theater`.

Prof: That’s a good observation! Helper methods are often like that; they just work with the data they are given. The methods that call them will look up the right data for them to use.

Student: OK so let’s build the method that uses `seats`?

Prof: Right. I would say this is a search method on the seats array. It returns true as soon as it finds a row with enough seats, using the helper.

```java
record Theater(boolean[][] seats) {
  boolean rowHasSeats(boolean[] row, int target) {
    int consecutiveAvailable = 0;
    for(boolean b: row) {
      if(b) { consecutiveAvailable += 1; }
      else { consecutiveAvailable = 0; }
      if(consecutiveAvailable >= target) { return true; }
    }
    return false;
  }
  boolean hasSeats(int target) {
    for(boolean[] row: seats) {
      if(rowHasSeats(row, target)) { return true; }
    }
    return false;
  }
}
boolean[] top = { true, false, true, true, true, true };
boolean[] middle = { true, false, false, false, true };
boolean[] bottom = { true, true, false, false };
boolean[][] seats = { top, middle, bottom };
Theater theater = new Theater(seats);
boolean rowHasSeats = theater.rowHasSeats(top, 3);
boolean theaterHasSeats = theater.hasSeats(3);
```

Output:

```text
top = [true, false, true, true, true, true]
middle = [true, false, false, false, true]
bottom = [true, true, false, false]
seats = [[true, false, true, true, true, true], [true, false, false, false, true], [true, true, false, false]]
theater = Theater[seats=[[Z@8ca]
rowHasSeats = true
theaterHasSeats = true
```

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
    top = @1001
    middle = @1002
    bottom = @1003
    seats = @1004
    theater = @1005
    rowHasSeats = true
    theaterHasSeats = true
Heap
  @1001: [true, false, true, true, true, true]
  @1002: [true, false, false, false, true]
  @1003: [true, true, false, false]
  @1004: [@1001, @1002, @1003]
  @1005: Theater[seats=@1004]
```

Student: Huh, so it’s kind of like a nested loop, but the inner loop is inside another method.

Prof: That’s right! I think the tricky logic is mostly in the helper – the incremental counter. So I find that I can read this a little easier because each method has its own job.

Student: Could you write it as one bigger nested loop and get the same answers?

Prof: Absolutely. This breakdown is more about how I chose to think about the problem. There are many ways to make it work!

#### Practice

Exercise:

Here is a later showing, where the only three free seats together are in the bottom row:

```java
boolean[] lateTop = { false, true, true, false, true, false };
boolean[] lateMiddle = { true, true, false, true, true };
boolean[] lateBottom = { false, true, true, true };
boolean[][] lateSeats = { lateTop, lateMiddle, lateBottom };
Theater late = new Theater(lateSeats);
```

How many times does each call below call `rowHasSeats`, and what does it produce?

`theater.hasSeats(3)` calls `rowHasSeats` ____ time(s) and produces [true / false]
`late.hasSeats(3)` calls `rowHasSeats` ____ time(s) and produces [true / false]
`late.hasSeats(4)` calls `rowHasSeats` ____ time(s) and produces [true / false]

## [Rasters](nested-and-2d/raster.html)

Student: Prof, my friend took a different CS course and they said we’re representing images all wrong.

Prof: Oh? How so?

Student: The pictures in their class are all represented as arrays of arrays of colors. They call them pixels.

Prof: Ah, they are working with rasterized images!

Student: Huh?

Prof: We can have them, too! It’s a different way of thinking about a picture. Rather than having logical shapes placed on or next to each other, we think about the grid of pixels. Both are valid ways of thinking about an image. And our `Pict` objects can go back and forth to the array representation. Every `Pict` has a `render()` method. Let’s check it out:

```java
Pict rect = new Rect(3, 4, "red");
Raster rastered = rect.render();
```

Output:

```text
rect = Rect[width=3, height=4, color=red]
[image]
rastered = Raster[3x4]
[image]
```

Prof: They show up as the same image, but they have different internal representations. Note the `3x4` in the printed version of the Raster, which matches the size of the `Rect` it came from. We could create the same `Raster` by using its constructor:

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Pict rect = new Rect(3, 4, "red");
Raster rastered = rect.render();
Color[][] colors = {
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED },
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED },
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED },
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED }
};
Raster rastered2 = new Raster(colors);
```

Output:

```text
rect = Rect[width=3, height=4, color=red]
[image]
rastered = Raster[3x4]
[image]
colors = [[java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]], [java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]], [java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]], [java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]]]
rastered2 = Raster[3x4]
[image]
```

Student: Huh, interesting. What’s that `import` line for, and why are we using `Color.RED` instead of `"red"`?

Prof: The way `Raster` is represented uses some of the built-in Java types for doing drawings. The `Pict` constructors like `Rect` and `Circle` have some conveniences for using string names, but once we get to `Raster` we will be talking more about colors as Java sees them. This is part of the [java.awt](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/awt/package-summary.html) library.

Student: OK, I see. When it prints it’s saying `r`, `g`, and `b`. What’s that about?

Prof: Great question, it is called the [RGB](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/what-is-rgb/) model of colors. `R` for red, `G` for green, and `B` for blue. Combining different amounts of red, green, and blue can express a wide array of colors, and its one of the standard ways computers represent them. So a raster is an array of arrays of colors, where each color has these three components. Since we used `Color.RED`, that’s all red. You could create your own colors with different amounts! Here’s the same example with a nice mix of blue and green:

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Pict rect = new Rect(3, 4, "red");
Raster rastered = rect.render();
Color teal = new Color(0, 100, 150);
Color[][] colors = {
  { teal, teal, teal },
  { teal, teal, teal },
  { teal, teal, teal },
  { teal, teal, teal }
};
Raster rastered2 = new Raster(colors);
```

Output:

```text
rect = Rect[width=3, height=4, color=red]
[image]
rastered = Raster[3x4]
[image]
teal = java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150]
colors = [[java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150]], [java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150]], [java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150]], [java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=100,b=150]]]
rastered2 = Raster[3x4]
[image]
```

Student: OK, I think I see. That’s a lot of typing to build a really small image, though, right?

Prof: Indeed! We will need a lot more infrastructure to build up interesting images from this. But there are also things we can do with `Raster` that would be hard to do any other way.

A `Raster` has methods `width()`, `height()`, and `colorAt(x, y)`, where `x` counts across from the left and `y` counts down from the top, both starting at `0`. Here is a small striped flag:

```java
Color[][] stripes = {
  { Color.RED, Color.WHITE, Color.RED, Color.WHITE, Color.RED },
  { Color.RED, Color.WHITE, Color.RED, Color.WHITE, Color.RED }
```

Exercise:

Now go the other way, from a `Pict` to a `Raster`:

```java
Raster dot = new Circle(5, "green").render();
```

A circle is round, but a raster is always a rectangle of pixels, so some pixels are inside the circle and some are not. Pixels outside the circle are transparent.

```java
dot.width()        ____
dot.height()       ____
dot.colorAt(5, 5)  [green / transparent]
dot.colorAt(0, 0)  [green / transparent]
dot.colorAt(2, 7)  [green / transparent]
dot.colorAt(9, 9)  [green / transparent]
```

## [Index Loops with Rasters](nested-and-2d/image-filters.html)

Student: So what’s something we need `Raster` for?

Prof: One of the main things is manipulating images. For example, programs on my computer can crop images, or shrink or grow them, or change their colors.

Student: And it does that with `Raster`?

Prof: More or less. Enough so that we’ll learn something about both arrays and images. First I want to show you that we can load interesting images from files, so that we are transforming something more interesting than rectangles and squares.

```java
Raster r = ImageIO_.load("images/salk.png");
```

Output:

```text
r = Raster[240x189]
[image]
```

Student: Oh that’s useful. So we can load real pictures, not just make shapes.

Prof: Exactly. So, there are a lot of things we can do with this image! For instance, we could ask what the color is at various spots. There is a method on `Raster` called `colorAt` that can tell us the color at a particular place. In a `Raster`, the top row is at index 0 (much like our theater picture). In this picture of the Salk Institute, what color do you think is at 0, 0?

Student: Well, there’s blue sky, so something with a large `b` field?

Prof: Let’s see! The top left is a little dark, so let’s also try something a little more inset into the picture where it gets lighter.

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Raster r = ImageIO_.load("images/salk.png");
Color topLeft = r.colorAt(0, 0);
Color sky = r.colorAt(50, 50);
```

Output:

```text
r = Raster[240x189]
[image]
topLeft = java.awt.Color[r=6,g=9,b=42]
sky = java.awt.Color[r=11,g=41,b=103]
```

Prof: One thing we can do with rasters is calculate interesting image properties. For example, we can get the **average color** of an image.

Student: The average color?

Prof: Right, we can add up all the red, blue, and green channels independently, then divide by the number of pixels. A very blue picture should have a mostly-blue result, a very purple picture would show blue and red, and so on.

Student: OK, I guess that’s interesting.

Prof: It will be a good start for other raster methods. We are going to need something new and useful: an indexing for loop. We’ve seen for-each loops (what we just called a `for` loop before) that work over the elements of an array, but it turns out `Raster` only has `colorAt`, no way to use a for-each loop that goes element by element.

Student: So what does an indexing for loop look like?

Prof: The idea is that the loop variable tracks an index into an array or other structure (like a `Raster`).

```java
for(int index = init; index < maxIndex; index += increment) { ... }
```

The name `index` is your choice, people use `i` and `j` or `counter`, things like that, as well. The value `init` is some starting point; `0` is common for starting at the beginning of an iteration. `maxIndex` is often the length of an array or structure, but some iterations might stop early. Then `increment` is how many indexes to “move ahead” by, which is often `1` but could be different values as well.

Enough talking, let’s see it in action. This will be an **indexed, nested, running-sum loop** that tracks a sum for each of red, blue, and green:

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Color averageColor(Raster raster) {
  int r = 0, g = 0, b = 0;
  int height = raster.height();
  int width = raster.width();
  for(int rowIndex = 0; rowIndex < height; rowIndex += 1) {
    for(int colIndex = 0; colIndex < width; colIndex += 1) {
      r += raster.colorAt(colIndex, rowIndex).getRed();
      g += raster.colorAt(colIndex, rowIndex).getGreen();
      b += raster.colorAt(colIndex, rowIndex).getBlue();
    }
  }
  int totalPix = width * height;
  int rAvg = r / totalPix, gAvg = g / totalPix, bAvg = b / totalPix;
  return new Color(rAvg, gAvg, bAvg);
}
Raster salk = ImageIO_.load("images/salk.png");
Color salkAvg = averageColor(salk);
Color[][] redblue = { { Color.RED, Color.BLUE, Color.BLUE }, { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.BLUE } };
Color redblueAvgs = averageColor(new Raster(redblue)); // should be 127, 0, 127
```

Output:

```text
salk = Raster[240x189]
[image]
salkAvg = java.awt.Color[r=81,g=91,b=109]
redblue = [[java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=0,b=255], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=0,b=255]], [java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=0,g=0,b=255]]]
redblueAvgs = java.awt.Color[r=127,g=0,b=127]
```

Prof: Whew, that was a lot. What questions do you have?

Student: Have we seen `getRed` and `getBlue` before?

Prof: No, I just know those are methods on `Color` that get back those components.

Student: Why is it `colIndex, rowIndex` and not the other way around?

Prof: That’s just the way `Raster.colorAt` is defined; it takes an “x” and then a “y” coordinate.

Student: And unlike picts, the 0 value for y is at the top?

Prof: That’s right, to match Java’s underlying image library more closely.

Student: So the Salk picture is very slightly more blue than anything else?

Prof: Yup.

Student: Could I have nested the loops the other way?

Prof: For this loop, yes. We’re only adding things up, so it doesn’t matter whether we go across each row, one row at a time, or down each column, one column at a time. Either way every pixel gets added in exactly once.

Student: OK! Indexing for loops and rasters. Cool stuff.

#### Practice

Exercise:

Here is a past builder, rewritten with an indexing for loop. The loop variable `i` does the job the separate `index` counter used to do. Pick each part of the loop header so that `halfOff` builds every sale price.

```java
int[] halfOff(int[] pricesCents) {
  int[] result = new int[pricesCents.length];
  for([int i = 1 / int i = 0 / int i = pricesCents.length]; [i <= pricesCents.length / i < pricesCents[i] / i < pricesCents.length]; [i += 1 / i += 2 / i -= 1]) {
    result[i] = pricesCents[i] / 2;
  }
  return result;
}
int[] prices = { 500, 1250, 99 };
int[] half = halfOff(prices);
```

```java
    for(int colIndex = 0; colIndex < raster.width(); colIndex += 1) {
____
    }
  }
  return false;
}
```

## [Negatives](nested-and-2d/more-filters.html)

Prof: Now that we have this loop idea, we can do interesting things like mess with the colors. Have you ever heard of a **negative** of an image?

Student: Maybe? Like where the colors are all weird?

Prof: Right. The negative is the result of “inverting” all the colors. So if `r` was 50 in the original, make it 205 in the negative. The arithmetic is `255 - c` for each color channel `c`. This turns, say, purple (red and blue, no green) into green, just like on a color wheel.

Student: Let’s see what it looks like?

Prof: For now, I’m going to set this up to return a **new** `Raster` to show a builder style for these (we could also use a updater style).

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Color negate(Color c) {
  int negR = 255 - c.getRed();
  int negG = 255 - c.getGreen();
  int negB = 255 - c.getBlue();
  return new Color(negR, negG, negB);
}
Raster negative(Raster raster) {
  Color[][] negativePix = new Color[raster.height()][raster.width()];
  for(int row = 0; row < raster.height(); row += 1) {
    for(int col = 0; col < raster.width(); col += 1) {
      negativePix[row][col] = negate(raster.colorAt(col, row));
    }
  }
  return new Raster(negativePix);
}
Color purple = new Color(255, 0, 255);
Color negPurple = negate(purple);
Color[][] tiny = {
  { Color.RED, Color.WHITE },
  { Color.BLACK, new Color(50, 100, 200) }
};
Raster tinyNeg = negative(new Raster(tiny));
```

Output:

```text
purple = java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=255]
negPurple = java.awt.Color[r=0,g=255,b=0]
tiny = [[java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=255,b=255]], [java.awt.Color[r=0,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=50,g=100,b=200]]]
tinyNeg = Raster[2x2]
[image]
```

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
    purple = magenta
    negPurple = green
    tiny = @1001
    tinyNeg = @1011
Heap
  @1001: [@1002, @1003]
  @1002: [red, white]
  @1003: [black, #3264c8]
  @1004: Raster[pixels=@1005]
  @1005: [@1006, @1007]
  @1006: [red, white]
  @1007: [black, #3264c8]
  @1008: [@1009, @1010]
  @1009: [cyan, black]
  @1010: [white, #cd9b37]
  @1011: Raster[pixels=@1012]
  @1012: [@1013, @1014]
  @1013: [cyan, black]
  @1014: [white, #cd9b37]
```

Student: I see, so it has its own definition of “inverting” and it applies that to every color. And it returns a **new** Raster?

Prof: Right, the original is unchanged. And I just wrote small tests; we can scale it up to larger images:

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Color negate(Color c) {
  int negR = 255 - c.getRed();
  int negG = 255 - c.getGreen();
  int negB = 255 - c.getBlue();
  return new Color(negR, negG, negB);
}
Raster negative(Raster raster) {
  Color[][] negativePix = new Color[raster.height()][raster.width()];
  for(int row = 0; row < raster.height(); row += 1) {
    for(int col = 0; col < raster.width(); col += 1) {
      negativePix[row][col] = negate(raster.colorAt(col, row));
    }
  }
  return new Raster(negativePix);
}
Raster salk = ImageIO_.load("images/salk.png");
Raster salkNeg = negative(salk);
Raster pier = ImageIO_.load("images/pier-under.png");
Raster pierNeg = negative(pier);
```

Output:

```text
salk = Raster[240x189]
[image]
salkNeg = Raster[240x189]
[image]
pier = Raster[180x240]
[image]
pierNeg = Raster[180x240]
[image]
```

Student: Neat!

Prof: In general we call these “image filters” – can you think of any others?

Student: Maybe like making it black and white, or just having one color?

Prof: Yup. And there are lots of others we could try if we wanted to get deep into graphics, like blurring or removing parts of an image. For now we’ll keep it with the kinds of examples you’ve suggested. We could also rotate, crop, flip, and so on.

Student: Cool!


## [Nested and 2D Structures in Summary](nested-and-2d/summary.html)

Exercise:

A `Theater` method `int[] freeSeatsPerRow()` returns one number per row: how many seats in that row are free. Which loop pattern fits each loop?

The outer loop, over `seats`: [best-so-far / running-sum / builder / counter]
The inner loop, over one `row`: [best-so-far / running-sum / builder / counter]

Exercise:

Fill in `freeSeatsPerRow`.

```java
record Theater(boolean[][] seats) {
  int[] freeSeatsPerRow() {
    int[] result = [new int[3] / new int[seats[0].length] / new int[seats.length]];
    int index = 0;
    for(boolean[] row: seats) {
      int free = 0;
      for(boolean seat: row) {
        if(seat) { free += 1; }
      }
      [result[index] = 1; / result[free] = index; / result[index] = free;]
      ____
    }
    return result;
  }
}
boolean[] top = { true, false, true, true, true, true };
boolean[] middle = { true, false, false, false, true };
boolean[] bottom = { true, true, false, false };
boolean[][] seats = { top, middle, bottom };
Theater theater = new Theater(seats);
int[] perRow = theater.freeSeatsPerRow();
```

Exercise:

Someone moves `int free = 0;` up, above the outer loop, so it runs once before either loop starts. With the same `theater`, what does `theater.freeSeatsPerRow()` return now?

Choose one:

- `[9, 9, 9]`
- It doesn’t compile
- `[5, 7, 9]`
- `[5, 2, 2]`

Exercise:

`countWhite` counts the pure white pixels in a raster. Which arguments go to `colorAt`?

```java
import java.awt.Color;
int countWhite(Raster raster) {
  int count = 0;
  for(int row = 0; row < raster.height(); row += 1) {
    for(int col = 0; col < raster.width(); col += 1) {
      if(raster.colorAt([row, col / col, row]).equals(Color.WHITE)) { count += 1; }
    }
  }
  return count;
}
Color[][] stripes = {
  { Color.WHITE, Color.RED, Color.WHITE },
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.BLUE }
};
Raster flag = new Raster(stripes);
int whites = countWhite(flag);
```

# Classes that Share Behavior

## [Searching for Images](sharing-behavior/searching-for-images.html)

*Chapter contributed by Brendan Barber*

Student: I really want to work at Google one day, and I was thinking that the best way for me to get a job there would be to make my own version of Google. Have we covered enough to do that?

Prof: Well, Google, the search engine, is a very large and complex piece of software. Let’s start small and implement a small piece of it. Have you ever used Advanced Image Search on Google? It looks like this:

[image]

Figure 1: Google’s Advanced Image Search ([https://www.google.com/advanced_search?udm=2](https://www.google.com/advanced_search?udm=2))

Student: Hmm, I didn’t know about this. So where would I start with making my own version?

Prof: Here, let’s use what we know about records and methods to start by making a query. We have to describe every image so that we can search specifically for the ones we want. So how about you start out with creating an `ImageData` record that has a `String` with keywords and a `String` for the image file type. Then, create a `boolean` method for checking if a given file extension matches the record’s file type.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }
}
ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png");
boolean pngLiteral = i1.matchesExtension("png");
boolean pngTyped = i1.matchesExtension("PNG".toLowerCase());
boolean jpg = i1.matchesExtension("jpg");
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png]
pngLiteral = true
pngTyped = true
jpg = false
```

Student: Ok, so by defining the keywords and file types of an image, I could now only search for PNG images.

Prof: Exactly. And you can also do the reverse: search for all image types except for PNG images. Now, based on the image from Google, and your own experience searching for images online, what do you think we should add to `ImageData`?

Student: Well, I don’t like when I find low-resolution images. So maybe I should add a width and height?

Prof: Great idea! Add it to the record and also try to make a new method similar to `matchesExtension` but for width instead.

Student: Wait a second, what does `this` mean?

Prof: When we use the `this` keyword, we are referring to “the record that this method was called on.” So if you were to write `i1.matchesExtension("png")`, Java runs the method body with `this` standing for `i1`. So `this.fileType` refers to the `fileType` of `i1`.

Student: Ok, I see. So I need to make sure to use `this` in my `hasWidth` method.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }
  boolean hasWidth(int w) {
    return this.width.equals(w);
  }
}
ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
boolean width640 = i1.hasWidth(640);
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 6: error: Cannot invoke equals(int) on the primitive type int
```

Student: Uhm, what did I do wrong. You taught me that I should be using `.equals()`, like I did when writing the `matchesExtension` method.

Prof: Not quite. Here’s what’s going on: `.equals(...)` is a **method call**, and methods must be called on objects. A primitive value like an `int` **does not have methods**, which is what the compiler means by “primitive type” in that error message. For primitives, `==` already compares the numbers themselves.

Student: So `.equals()` cannot be used in this case, so I should go back to using `==`.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }
  boolean hasWidth(int w) {
    return this.width == w;
  }
}
ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
boolean width640 = i1.hasWidth(640);
boolean width800 = i1.hasWidth(800);
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480]
width640 = true
width800 = false
```

Student: Ok great, but I usually care about the width and the height of the image, and I am not looking for an image that is exactly a certain size.

Prof: Right, so how about you try writing a method that returns `true` if the image is larger than a minimum width AND a minimum height.

Student: Hmm, I only know how to check one thing at a time. I can use `if` statements, one for the width and then inside another one for the height. Can I do that here?

Prof: Try it and see.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }
  boolean hasWidth(int w) {
    return this.width == w;
  }
  boolean largerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) {
    if (this.width >= minWidth) {
      if (this.height >= minHeight) {
        return true;
      }
    }
    return false;
  }
}
ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
boolean bigEnough = i1.largerThan(600, 400);
boolean tooWide = i1.largerThan(700, 400);
boolean tooTall = i1.largerThan(600, 500);
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480]
bigEnough = true
tooWide = false
tooTall = false
```

Student: Nice, it works. `bigEnough` is `true`, and the other two are `false`.

Prof: It does work, and that’s a perfectly good way to write it out.

Student: Hmm, but the answer is `true` when both checks pass, and the order of the width and the height check doesn’t really matter. That feels like it should be shorter.

Prof: It can be. Try taking both of those checks and using `&&` between them. Remember that the return just needs to be an expression that is `true` or `false`, it doesn’t necessarily have to be written out as `return true`.

Student: So I can combine my two checks with `&&` and return the result directly?

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }
  boolean hasWidth(int w) {
    return this.width == w;
  }
  boolean largerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) {
    return this.width >= minWidth && this.height >= minHeight;
  }
}
ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
boolean bigEnough = i1.largerThan(600, 400);
boolean tooWide = i1.largerThan(700, 400);
boolean tooTall = i1.largerThan(600, 500);
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480]
bigEnough = true
tooWide = false
tooTall = false
```

Prof: It’s a good habit to notice when a few nested `if` statements could instead be a single line with `&&`, imagine we had a 3D object and we had width, height, and depth. Then the nesting would be even worse!

Prof: Ok, so let’s review what we have done so far. We wanted a way to search through images, so we defined `ImageData` to have the fields we wanted to sort by and then we added true-or-false questions about the data with `matchesExtension`, `hasWidth`, and `largerThan`.

Student: I don’t think Google is hiring me if this is all I show them, I mean right now all I can do is search by either size or by the file type. I guess I could combine them into one check, but I am gonna get bored if I have to write hundreds of methods in ImageData…

Prof: Hold that thought.

#### Practice

Fill in the blanks so `largerThan` is `true` only when both the width and the height are big enough, and so `matchesExtension("jpg")` is `false` for a PNG.

Exercise:

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }

  ____ largerThan(int ____, int minHeight) {
    ____ this.width >= minWidth [&& / ||] this.height >= ____;
  }
}

void main() {
  ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
  assertEquals(true, i1.matchesExtension("png"));
  assertEquals(____, ____);
  System.out.println("All tests succeeded!");
}
```

## [Combining Queries](sharing-behavior/combining-queries.html)

Student: Ok, so now I want to find images that are both larger than a minimum size and a PNG. So I should write a new method.

Prof: Sure, how would this method work? What arguments would it take, and what would it return?

Student: Well, it should combine `largerThan` and `matchesExtension`, so it needs the arguments of both methods, and it returns a `boolean`. But I’m clever! I’ll just call `largerThan` and `matchesExtension` from inside my new method and join them with `&&`. That way it’s only one line.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }
  boolean largerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) {
    return this.width >= minWidth && this.height >= minHeight;
  }
  boolean largerThanAndMatchesExtension(int minWidth, int minHeight, String ext) {
    return this.largerThan(minWidth, minHeight) && this.matchesExtension(ext);
  }
}
ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
boolean bigPng = i1.largerThanAndMatchesExtension(600, 400, "png");
boolean bigJpg = i1.largerThanAndMatchesExtension(600, 400, "jpg");
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480]
bigPng = true
bigJpg = false
```

Student: There we go, `bigPng` is `true` and `bigJpg` is `false`. Clever, right?

Prof: Nice work. Now, what if you want images that are a PNG *or* a JPG?

Student: Hmm, I’d need another method, `largerThanAndMatchesPngOrJpg`. And then if I wanted images that are larger than a minimum size *or* a WEBP…

Prof: Keep going. Every new way of combining queries needs a new method. And what happens as we add more fields to `ImageData`?

Student: Oh no. Every possible combination of queries needs its own method. I would never finish. I mean, also, there’s no way this is how someone at Google would do this, right? So what am I supposed to do instead?

Prof: What if a query was something you could pass around, like a value?

#### Practice

Fill in the blanks so that `largerThanAndMatchesExtension` is `true` only when the image is big enough *and* has the right extension, by calling the two queries that already exist.

Exercise:

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {
  boolean matchesExtension(String ext) {
    return this.fileType.equals(ext);
  }
  boolean largerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) {
    return this.width >= minWidth && this.height >= minHeight;
  }

  boolean largerThanAndMatchesExtension(int minWidth, int minHeight, String ext) {
    return ____ && ____;
```
