## [Queries as Data](sharing-behavior/queries-as-data.html)

Student: Ok, so how do I “pass around queries like values”? I don’t get that.

Prof: First we have to talk about a new concept called an interface. An interface is a way to describe shared functionality across records. So in our `ImageData` example, what do all of the methods we have been writing share?

Student: Hmm, I guess we are asking a true/false question.

Prof: Correct, but go into more detail. What are we saying is true or false?

Student: Well, in `matchesExtension` we were checking whether the extension matches a certain file type, and in `largerThan` we are checking whether the size is larger than some value… which is a kind of matching as well. So really, it’s all checking for matches.

Prof: Exactly. Here, I will show you an example and we can work through it together. What new keywords do you notice in this code snippet?

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {}

interface ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img);
}

record HasExtension(String ext) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.fileType().equals(this.ext);
  }
}

record LargerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.width() >= this.minWidth && img.height() >= this.minHeight;
  }
}

ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
ImageQuery isPng = new HasExtension("png");
ImageQuery isBig = new LargerThan(600, 400);
boolean pngResult = isPng.matches(i1);
boolean bigResult = isBig.matches(i1);
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480]
isPng = HasExtension[ext=png]
isBig = LargerThan[minWidth=600, minHeight=400]
pngResult = true
bigResult = true
```

Student: Well, there is that `interface` word you mentioned: you created an `ImageQuery`. It looks like a record, but it doesn’t seem to be storing anything. And I think you forgot to write the code for the `matches` method!

Prof: Hmm, you’re right. `ImageQuery` isn’t storing any data, is it? And the `matches` method doesn’t have a return statement… let’s keep going. What is the other detail you notice?

Student: You used a new keyword, `implements`, and you put it outside the record? When I read it out it says “record `LargerThan` implements `ImageQuery`.” And then each of the new records you created has a `matches` method with the same signature as in the interface.

Prof: Good noticing!

Student: But I don’t understand *why*. Why do you have to make `ImageQuery` if you are going to have to write out the method for `matches` every time anyway? In that case we could just make sure each record has the `matches` method and we could call `matches` on whatever we wanted?

Prof: Well, there is one other detail at the end. Notice how we are able to declare both of these records as an `ImageQuery`. How about you try writing out your idea and seeing what happens.

Student: Ok, I bet my way will work.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {}

record HasExtension(String ext) {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.fileType().equals(this.ext);
  }
}

record LargerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.width() >= this.minWidth && img.height() >= this.minHeight;
  }
}

ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
HasExtension isPng = new HasExtension("png");
LargerThan isBig = new LargerThan(600, 400);
boolean pngResult = isPng.matches(i1);
boolean bigResult = isBig.matches(i1);
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480]
isPng = HasExtension[ext=png]
isBig = LargerThan[minWidth=600, minHeight=400]
pngResult = true
bigResult = true
```

Student: See, it works perfectly! And no interface needed.

Prof: You’re right, for now. But, let’s see what happens when we get back to the idea of combining queries: check out what happens when I try to add this new record in. We said we wanted to check for relationships between queries, such as an `Or`.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {}

record HasExtension(String ext) {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.fileType().equals(this.ext);
  }
}

record LargerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.width() >= this.minWidth && img.height() >= this.minHeight;
  }
}

record Or(HasExtension left, HasExtension right) {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return this.left.matches(img) || this.right.matches(img);
  }
}

ImageData i2 = new ImageData("little cat", "jpg", 200, 200);
ImageData i3 = new ImageData("cat waving", "gif", 200, 200);
Or pngOrJpg = new Or(new HasExtension("jpg"), new HasExtension("png"));
boolean jpgResult = pngOrJpg.matches(i2);
boolean gifResult = pngOrJpg.matches(i3);
// Below expected to fail
ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
Or bigOrPng = new Or(new LargerThan(600, 400), new HasExtension("png"));
boolean bigPngResult = bigOrPng.matches(i1);
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 28: error: The constructor Or(LargerThan, HasExtension) is undefined
```

Student: OK, but it has an error.

Prof: Right. What would you do to fix it? How can you change `Or` so that you can construct both `bigOrPng` and `pngOrJpg`?

Student: I guess I can’t. I have to pick either `HasExtension` or `LargerThan` for the fields of `Or`, and neither works for both combinat– OHHH! Wait so the interface helps with this?

Prof: Right! When we have `interface ImageQuery` and records that `implement ImageQuery`, we are allowed to use `ImageQuery` as **the type of any value that implements ImageQuery**. So the implements lines let us replace the field types of `Or` with `ImageQuery`. And **then** we can construct both versions.

Student: That’s so cool! And I bet with that we can do `And` and stuff too.

Prof: Indeed. Give it a try with `And` and `Not` included as well.

Student: Sure, I think I understand the format now.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {}

interface ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img);
}

record HasExtension(String ext) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.fileType().equals(this.ext);
  }
}

record LargerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.width() >= this.minWidth && img.height() >= this.minHeight;
  }
}

record And(ImageQuery left, ImageQuery right) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return this.left.matches(img) && this.right.matches(img);
  }
}

record Or(ImageQuery left, ImageQuery right) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return this.left.matches(img) || this.right.matches(img);
  }
}

record Not(ImageQuery query) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return !this.query.matches(img);
  }
}

ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480);
ImageQuery pngOrJpg = new Or(new HasExtension("png"), new HasExtension("jpg"));
ImageQuery bigPngOrJpg = new And(new LargerThan(600, 400), pngOrJpg);
ImageQuery notPng = new Not(new HasExtension("png"));
boolean r1 = bigPngOrJpg.matches(i1);
boolean r2 = notPng.matches(i1);
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480]
pngOrJpg = Or[left=HasExtension[ext=png], right=HasExtension[ext=jpg]]
bigPngOrJpg = And[left=LargerThan[minWidth=600, minHeight=400], right=Or[left=HasExtension[ext=png], right=HasExtension[ext=jpg]]]
notPng = Not[query=HasExtension[ext=png]]
r1 = true
r2 = false
```

Student: You know, these interfaces are actually kinda nice. But wait a second, you never explained what `public` means? I guess I just started copying your record examples without thinking about it.

Prof: Good catch. `public` is an access modifier. It says who is allowed to use a method. A `public` method can be called by code anywhere.

Student: So why did I have to write it here? We have been calling methods all the time.

Prof: Methods in an interface must be `public`, since the whole point of an interface is that anyone holding an `ImageQuery` can call `matches` on it. A record that implements the interface isn’t allowed to make that method *less* available than the interface promised. Try leaving it off:

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height) {}
  
interface ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img);
}

record HasExtension(String ext) implements ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.fileType().equals(this.ext);
  }
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 8: error: Cannot reduce the visibility of the inherited method from ImageQuery
```

Student: I see, the compiler complains that it “cannot reduce the visibility of the inherited method”.

Prof: Exactly.

Student: Ok, these interfaces are cool and all. But, I wish I didn’t have to type out `new And(new LargerThan(600, 400), new Or(new HasExtension("png"), new HasExtension("jpg")))`. That’s a lot of `new`s to keep track of.

Prof: You’re right. Perhaps you want something in the chaining style we talked about earlier? Something like `isBig.and(isPng)`? We will go over that next.

Student: Yeah, that’d be nice.

#### Practice

Fill in the blanks to write a new query, `Xor`, that matches an image when *exactly one* of its two queries matches (one is true and the other is false).

  boolean matches(ImageData img);

## [Growing ImageData](sharing-behavior/growing-imagedata.html)

Student: Now I want to expand my implementation of `ImageData`. With this new `ImageQuery` interface, that is much easier to do. How about I give each image a file size? I’ll call it `sizeKb` for size in kilobytes. I don’t really know how big a kilobyte is, but I checked my File Explorer on my laptop and it shows a size in KB next to a bunch of images I downloaded from Google.

Prof: Good idea, and nice job looking at real-world examples to base your new fields off of. But, before we add new fields, maybe we should look to see if there is anything we already have that we haven’t added a record for?

Student: Oh, there is that `String keywords` field that we haven’t been using. I’ll add a record for checking keywords as well.

Prof: Good idea. So what two new records are you going to create?

Student: For the file size, I’ll make a `SmallerThanKb` record that takes a kilobyte limit and checks if the file size is smaller than it. For the keywords I’ll make a `HasKeyword` record that takes a `String` word input and checks if it matches the keywords. Strings are compared with `.equals()`, so I’ll use that.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height, int sizeKb) {}

interface ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img);
}

record HasKeyword(String word) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.keywords().equals(this.word);
  }
}

record SmallerThanKb(int limitKb) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.sizeKb() < this.limitKb;
  }
}

void main() {
  ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480, 300);
  ImageQuery catQuery = new HasKeyword("cat");
  assertEquals(true, catQuery.matches(i1));
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
Exception in thread "Thread-0" org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: expected: <true> but was: <false>
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals(Unknown Source)
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

Student: That’s strange. The image’s keywords are `"cat sleeping"`, and I asked for `"cat"`, but the assertion failed. Is `.equals()` broken?

Prof: Nope! `.equals()` did exactly what you told it. It checks whether two Strings are *exactly* the same, and `"cat sleeping"` is not exactly `"cat"`.

Student: Oh, so should I change `String keywords` to be `String[] keywords` instead? Then I could use a loop to check if any of the String values are equivalent.

Prof: You could do that, but there is another option without changing the `ImageData` record. You want to know whether the keywords *contain* the word. Strings have a method for that: `keywords.contains(word)` returns `true` if the word appears anywhere inside the String.

Student: So I swap `.equals()` for `.contains()`. I still think `String[]` would be better… did you purposely make it a `String` so that you could teach me `contains()`?

Prof: Perhaps. Now let’s put the two new records to work. Remember how you didn’t like typing all those `new`s, and wished you could write `isBig.and(isPng)`? Look at the `ImageQuery` interface in the program below. It has three new methods, and each starts with a word you haven’t seen: `default`.

Student: What does `default` mean? The `matches` method had no body in the interface. Every record that implements `ImageQuery` had to have their own method body.

Prof: That’s the difference. A default method (a method with `default`) *does* have a body inside the interface, and every record that implements `ImageQuery` gets it without having to write it themselves. So we write it once, in the interface, instead of in `HasKeyword`, `SmallerThanKb`, `Not` and every other record.

Student: So `this` is whichever query I call `.and()` on? In `cat.and(light)`, `this` is `cat` and `other` is `light`?

Prof: Exactly. Here, try it out yourself.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height, int sizeKb) {}

interface ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img);

  default ImageQuery and(ImageQuery other) {
    return new And(this, other);
  }
  default ImageQuery or(ImageQuery other) {
    return new Or(this, other);
  }
  default ImageQuery not() {
    return new Not(this);
  }
}

record HasKeyword(String word) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.keywords().contains(this.word);
  }
}

record SmallerThanKb(int limitKb) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.sizeKb() < this.limitKb;
  }
}

record HasExtension(String ext) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.fileType().equals(this.ext);
  }
}

record LargerThan(int minWidth, int minHeight) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.width() >= this.minWidth && img.height() >= this.minHeight;
  }
}

record And(ImageQuery left, ImageQuery right) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return this.left.matches(img) && this.right.matches(img);
  }
}

record Or(ImageQuery left, ImageQuery right) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return this.left.matches(img) || this.right.matches(img);
  }
}

record Not(ImageQuery query) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return !this.query.matches(img);
  }
}

ImageData i1 = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480, 300);
ImageQuery cat = new HasKeyword("cat");
ImageQuery light = new SmallerThanKb(500);

boolean r1 = cat.matches(i1);
boolean r2 = cat.and(light).matches(i1);
boolean r3 = cat.and(new LargerThan(1920, 1080)).matches(i1);
boolean r4 = cat.not().or(new HasExtension("png")).matches(i1);
```

Output:

```text
i1 = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480, sizeKb=300]
cat = HasKeyword[word=cat]
light = SmallerThanKb[limitKb=500]
r1 = true
r2 = true
r3 = false
r4 = true
```

Prof: Great job! Now there is still technically a bug with our implementation, but it mostly has to do with the limits of using `contains`. We don’t have to worry about fixing it here, but it’s always important to think about edge cases. Can you think of what some issues with using contains might be?

Student: No not really… It looks like it’s working perfectly fine.

Prof: Imagine that we want to check if the `ImageData` keywords contain `"cat"`, and the image is of a bunch of lecture halls at UC San Diego. Maybe it has `String keywords` set as building names like `"peterson mosaic catalyst"`.

Student: Oh! I see the problem. `contains` would count the `cat` in `catalyst` as a match, so a user looking for cats would get images of buildings instead.

Prof: Yep, these are the kinds of edge cases you have to keep an eye out for. Another one to keep an eye out for is that `contains` is case-sensitive. So `Cat` doesn’t contain `cat`. Think a bit about how you might fix these edge cases, but now we are going to move on to using interfaces in another context.

#### Practice

Exercise:

An image’s keywords are the String `"cat sleeping"`. Which of these is `true`?

Choose one:

- `keywords.contains("cat")`
- `keywords.contains("dog")`
- `keywords.contains("sleeping cat")`
- `keywords.equals("cat")`

The student’s `String[]` idea works too. Let’s build it step by step. Each keyword is now its own String, so `.equals()` asks the right question: is *this one keyword* exactly the word we want?

1. Change `keywords` to hold many Strings instead of one.
2. Loop over every keyword in the image.
3. If a keyword equals the word, we found a match, so we can answer `true` right away.
4. If the loop finishes and nothing matched, the answer is `false`.

Exercise:

```java
record ImageData(____ keywords, String fileType, int width, int height, int sizeKb) {}

interface ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img);
}

record HasKeyword(String word) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    for (____ keyword : img.keywords()) {
      if (keyword.____(this.word)) {
        return ____;
      }
    }
    return ____;
  }
}

void main() {
  System.out.println("All tests succeeded!");
}
```

## [The Pict Library, Revisited](sharing-behavior/the-pict-library.html)

Prof: Are you finding some of this interface stuff a bit familiar? Does it remind you of something we were working with all the way back at the beginning?

Student: Yeah… when I was writing something like `isPng.and(isBig)` it felt very similar to writing `tree.beside(sun)`. The `Pict` library we have been using, that uses interfaces?

Prof: It sure does! You’re right that it is similar, here is an example of using `Pict` like you just mentioned.

```java
Pict dot = new Circle(20, "red");
Pict square = new Rect(40, 40, "blue");

Pict viaRecord = new Beside(dot, square);
Pict viaMethod = dot.beside(square);
Pict stacked = viaMethod.above(new Rect(60, 10, "green"));

void main() {
  assertEquals(viaRecord, viaMethod);
}
```

Output:

```text
dot = Circle[radius=20, color=red]
[image]
square = Rect[width=40, height=40, color=blue]
[image]
viaRecord = Beside[left=Circle[radius=20, color=red], right=Rect[width=40, height=40, color=blue]]
[image]
viaMethod = Beside[left=Circle[radius=20, color=red], right=Rect[width=40, height=40, color=blue]]
[image]
stacked = Above[top=Beside[left=Circle[radius=20, color=red], right=Rect[width=40, height=40, color=blue]], bottom=Rect[width=60, height=10, color=green]]
[image]
```

Student: I see, so when I use `dot.beside(square)`, that is using a `default` method inside of the `Pict` interface?

Prof: Yep.

Student: Ohhh, and there must be a record called `Beside` that implements `Pict`. It’s all coming together now.

Prof: Here, I’ll write out a section of the Pict library so we can talk through it. I trimmed it down a little; the whole thing is in [`Pict.java`](kit/Pict.java).

```java
interface Pict {
    int width();
    int height();

    default Pict beside(Pict other) { return new Beside(this, other); }
    default Pict above(Pict other) { return new Above(this, other); }
    // ... more default methods ...

    void draw(Graphics2D g, int x, int y);
}

record Circle(int radius, Color color) implements Pict {
    // ... plus constructors that accept a color name like "red" ...
    public int width() { return 2 * this.radius; }
    public int height() { return 2 * this.radius; }
    public void draw(Graphics2D g, int x, int y) {
        g.setColor(this.color);
        g.fillOval(x, y, 2 * this.radius, 2 * this.radius);
    }
}

record Beside(Pict left, Pict right) implements Pict {
    public int width() { return this.left.width() + this.right.width(); }
    public int height() { return Math.max(this.left.height(), this.right.height()); }
    public void draw(Graphics2D g, int x, int y) {
        int centerY = this.height() / 2;
        this.left.draw(g, x, y + centerY - this.left.height() / 2);
        this.right.draw(g, x + this.left.width(), y + centerY - this.right.height() / 2);
    }
}
```

Student: Ok, so `Pict` is an interface. And you gave it a `width` and `height` method. So all cases where we implement `Pict` will have a `width` and `height` as well.

Prof: Correct, what else do you notice?

Student: You used `default` just like we did with `ImageQuery`, but instead of using it for `And`, `Not`, `Or`, it’s being used for `beside` and `above`. Although I am a bit confused about the `Graphics2D` part? What is a `Graphics2D`? What are all these lines that say `g` mean?

Prof: For now let’s just treat `Graphics2D` as our way of actually drawing pixels on the screen. `Pict` describes what we want to draw, and `Graphics2D` is part of a library that handles the details of actually drawing it.

Student: So you are hiding things from me again?

Prof: Funnily enough, the creators of `Graphics2D` actually hid all this from me! When I wrote `Pict`, I didn’t have to think too much about how `Graphics2D` works. It abstracted away those details so I could focus on implementing all the shapes and relationships that I wanted `Pict` to have. Programmers rely on the work of others, especially when working on very complicated projects. We have also been using `assertEquals()` the same way, as code someone else wrote that we trust to do its job.

Student: This is a lot to keep track of.

Prof: Let’s just focus on `Pict` a bit more, and just treat the `Graphics2D g` section of the `draw` method as a canvas with a paint brush: when you hand it something, it draws it for you. We only use it inside `draw`, and only the simple records like `Circle` call `Graphics2D` methods directly. The records are what we are focusing on. They hold the data saying “a circle with a given radius and color” or “a circle, then a square beside it”. `Pict` is the type that lets all of them be used interchangeably. Notice that `Beside` holds two `Pict`s, in the same way `And` held two `ImageQuery`s. The drawing part is just what allows us to see and verify the result visually, but all the data is defined by us.

#### Practice

Exercise:

Look at the `draw` method of `Circle` and the `draw` method of `Beside` above. Which statement is true?

Choose one:

- `Beside.draw` paints pixels by calling `g.fillOval` and `g.fillRect` directly.
- A `Circle` stores its own pixels, so `draw` just copies them onto `g`.
- `Circle.draw` calls `Graphics2D` methods to paint itself, while `Beside.draw` hands the same `g` to the `draw` of its two parts, at different positions.
- `Beside` does not need a `draw` method, because the `Pict` interface supplies one.

Exercise:

`Above` is the vertical version of `Beside`. This is the `draw` method of `Above` from the `Pict` library, with one piece missing. The top picture is drawn at the top, so the bottom picture must start just below it. Which expression belongs in place of `/* ??? */`, the `y` argument of the second `draw` call?

```java
record Above(Pict top, Pict bottom) implements Pict {
    public int width() { return Math.max(this.top.width(), this.bottom.width()); }
    public int height() { return this.top.height() + this.bottom.height(); }
    public void draw(Graphics2D g, int x, int y) {
        int centerX = this.width() / 2;
        this.top.draw(g, x + centerX - this.top.width() / 2, y);
        this.bottom.draw(g, x + centerX - this.bottom.width() / 2, /* ??? */);
    }
}
```

Choose one:

- `y + this.top.height()`
- `y + this.bottom.height()`
- `y`
- `this.top.height()`

## [Building Your Own Pict](sharing-behavior/building-your-own-pict.html)

Student: Ok, time to make my own `Pict`! Mine will be called `Art`, so it doesn’t collide with the real one that we have been using so far.

Prof: Good plan. Drawing is the hard part of `Pict`, so let’s skip it. Let’s just focus on the size of your `Art`. Write that as an interface, plus one simple record like the `Rect` from `Pict.java`.

```java
interface Art {
  int width();
  int height();
}

record Block(int width, int height) implements Art {}

void main() {
  Art wall = new Block(3, 2);
  assertEquals(3, wall.width());
  assertEquals(2, wall.height());
}
```

Student: Wait, `Block` doesn’t have a `width` method. Did I need to write it?

Prof: Nope. Every record gets a method for each of its fields, with the same name. `wall.width()` is one of those, and it is what the interface asked for.

Student: Ok. So now I should add something like `Beside`. How about `SideBySide`?

Prof: Go ahead. What is the width of two pictures next to each other? What is the height?

Student: The widths add up, and the height is whichever is taller. And I want a `nextTo` method, like `beside`, so I don’t have to type `new SideBySide(...)`.

```java
interface Art {
  int width();
  int height();

  default Art nextTo(Art other) {
    return new SideBySide(this, other);
  }
}

record Block(int width, int height) implements Art {}

record SideBySide(Art left, Art right) implements Art {
  public int width() {
    return this.left.width() + this.right.width();
  }
  public int height() {
    return Math.max(this.left.height(), this.right.height());
  }
}

void main() {
  Art wall = new Block(3, 2);
  Art tower = new Block(2, 4);
  Art both = wall.nextTo(tower);
  assertEquals(5, both.width());
  assertEquals(4, both.height());
  assertEquals(7, both.nextTo(new Block(2, 1)).width());
}
```

Student: The last line is a `SideBySide` inside another `SideBySide`, and it still works.

Prof: Because `left` and `right` are `Art`s, not `Block`s. It’s the same trick as `And` holding two `ImageQuery`s. Now one that holds a single picture: a `Frame` that adds a border, one unit thick on every side, around another `Art`.

```java
interface Art {
  int width();
  int height();

  default Art nextTo(Art other) {
    return new SideBySide(this, other);
  }
  default Art framed() {
    return new Frame(this);
  }
}

record Block(int width, int height) implements Art {}

record SideBySide(Art left, Art right) implements Art {
  public int width() {
    return this.left.width() + this.right.width();
  }
  public int height() {
    return Math.max(this.left.height(), this.right.height());
  }
}

record Frame(Art inner) implements Art {
  public int width() {
    return this.inner.width() + 2;
  }
  public int height() {
    return this.inner.height() + 2;
  }
}

void main() {
  Art wall = new Block(3, 2);
  assertEquals(5, wall.framed().width());
  assertEquals(7, wall.framed().framed().width());
  assertEquals(7, wall.nextTo(new Block(2, 4)).framed().width());
}
```

Student: A frame of a frame is 4 wider, since each `Frame` asks the picture inside it for its width and adds 2.

Prof: Exactly, and the picture inside might itself be a `Frame` or a `SideBySide`. Each one only has to know about its own parts. That is the same design as `ImageQuery` and as the `Pict` library. It’s an interface that describes what every value can do, simple records, combinator records that hold other values of the interface, and `default` methods that build them.

Prof: Step through this one to watch each part get asked in turn:

```java
interface Art {
  int width();
  int height();

  default Art nextTo(Art other) {
    return new SideBySide(this, other);
  }
  default Art framed() {
    return new Frame(this);
  }
}

record Block(int width, int height) implements Art {}

record SideBySide(Art left, Art right) implements Art {
  public int width() {
    return this.left.width() + this.right.width();
  }
  public int height() {
    return Math.max(this.left.height(), this.right.height());
  }
}

record Frame(Art inner) implements Art {
  public int width() {
    return this.inner.width() + 2;
  }
  public int height() {
    return this.inner.height() + 2;
  }
}

void main() {
  Art wall = new Block(3, 2);
  Art tower = new Block(2, 4);
  Art framed = wall.nextTo(tower).framed();
  int w = framed.width();
}
```

Memory at the end:

```
Names
  top level
Heap
  @1001: Block[width=3, height=2]
  @1002: Block[width=2, height=4]
  @1003: SideBySide[left=@1001, right=@1002]
  @1004: Frame[inner=@1003]
```

# Recursive Data

## [Self-Referential Data](recursive-data/naming-it.html)

Student: Professor, I want to get the hard stuff. The real stuff about programming, the can’t-fake-it, no-nonsense big ideas. Stuff like recursion. My friends in upper division classes are always talking about that.

Prof: Good news! We’ve done recursion already.

Student: What?

Prof: We wrote our first recursive methods the last time we talked. And we’ve been making recursive data since we composed the French flag.

Student: How do you mean? Recursion is the hardest topic in CSE11. That’s what **everyone** says.

Prof: Then you’re doing great, as long as you understood our last conversations!

Student: Which parts?

Prof: Well, let’s bring up an example again and talk through a definition.

```java
record ImageData(String keywords, String fileType, int width, int height, int sizeKb) {}

interface ImageQuery {
  boolean matches(ImageData img);
}

record HasKeyword(String word) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.keywords().contains(this.word);
  }
}

record HasExtension(String ext) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.fileType().equals(this.ext);
  }
}

record SmallerThanKb(int limitKb) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return img.sizeKb() < this.limitKb;
  }
}

record And(ImageQuery left, ImageQuery right) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return left.matches(img) && right.matches(img);
  }
}

record Or(ImageQuery left, ImageQuery right) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData img) {
    return left.matches(img) || right.matches(img);
  }
}

ImageData img = new ImageData("cat sleeping", "png", 640, 480, 300);
ImageQuery cat = new HasKeyword("cat");
ImageQuery png = new HasExtension("png");
ImageQuery jpg = new HasExtension("jpg");
ImageQuery light = new SmallerThanKb(500);
ImageQuery pngOrJpg = new Or(png, jpg);
ImageQuery catPic = new And(cat, pngOrJpg);
ImageQuery query = new And(catPic, light);
boolean found = query.matches(img);
```

Output:

```text
img = ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480, sizeKb=300]
cat = HasKeyword[word=cat]
png = HasExtension[ext=png]
jpg = HasExtension[ext=jpg]
light = SmallerThanKb[limitKb=500]
pngOrJpg = Or[left=HasExtension[ext=png], right=HasExtension[ext=jpg]]
catPic = And[left=HasKeyword[word=cat], right=Or[left=HasExtension[ext=png], right=HasExtension[ext=jpg]]]
query = And[left=And[left=HasKeyword[word=cat], right=Or[left=HasExtension[ext=png], right=HasExtension[ext=jpg]]], right=SmallerThanKb[limitKb=500]]
found = true
```

Prof: So, in terms of definitions:

- The `And` record is a recursive datatype: it both implements `ImageQuery` and it has a field of type `ImageQuery`. That means a field of an `And` record can itself be an instance of `And`.
- The `matches` method is a recursive method: when it calls `matches` on its fields, it may be calling **the exact method it is in**. That is, two stack frames right next to each other, each for the exact same method of the exact same class, just different receivers.

These are the two important definitions of recursion in the object-oriented programs we will write.

Student: Huh. OK. So the memory trace would have multiple stack frames for the `matches` method on `And` at the same time?

Prof: Right, that’s the idea:

```
Names (the stack), over time →
  top level
    img = @1001
    cat = @1002
    png = @1003
    jpg = @1004
    light = @1005
    pngOrJpg = @1006
    catPic = @1007
    query = @1008
    found = true
    query.matches(img) on @1008
      img = @1001
      returns true
      left.matches(img) on @1007
        img = @1001
        returns true
        left.matches(img) on @1002
          img = @1001
          returns true
        right.matches(img) on @1006
          img = @1001
          returns true
          left.matches(img) on @1003
            img = @1001
            returns true
      right.matches(img) on @1005
        img = @1001
        returns true
Heap
  @1001: ImageData[keywords=cat sleeping, fileType=png, width=640, height=480, sizeKb=300]
  @1002: HasKeyword[word=cat]
  @1003: HasExtension[ext=png]
  @1004: HasExtension[ext=jpg]
  @1005: SmallerThanKb[limitKb=500]
  @1006: Or[left=@1003, right=@1004]
  @1007: And[left=@1002, right=@1006]
  @1008: And[left=@1007, right=@1005]
```

Student: Hm, ok so recursive data is when a record could have other instances of the same record in its fields? And recursive methods are when a method can call itself?

Prof: That’s right.

#### Practice

`Beside` from the Pict library is recursive data too: its `left` and `right` are `Pict`s, and its `width` method calls `width` on both of them.

```java
record Beside(Pict left, Pict right) implements Pict {
  public int width() { return left.width() + right.width(); }
  // ...
}

Pict dot = new Circle(10, "red");
Pict box = new Rect(30, 20, "blue");
Pict pair = new Beside(dot, box);
Pict row = new Beside(pair, dot);
int w = row.width();
```

These are the calls of `row.width()` over time, with the receivers left out.

```
Names (the stack), over time →
  top level
    dot = @1001
    box = @1002
    pair = @1003
    row = @1004
    w = 70
    row.width() on @1004
      returns 70
      left.width() on ???
        returns 50
        left.width() on ???
          returns 20
        right.width() on ???
          returns 30
      right.width() on ???
        returns 20
Heap
  @1001: Circle[radius=10, color=red]
  @1002: Rect[width=30, height=20, color=blue]
  @1003: Beside[left=@1001, right=@1002]
  @1004: Beside[left=@1003, right=@1001]
```

Exercise:

Fill in the receiver of each call.

The call that returns `50` runs on ____.
The call that returns `30` runs on ____.
Both calls that return `20` run on ____.

Exercise:

Which two calls are next to each other on the stack, running the same method of the same record?

Choose one:

- the `this.left.width()` that returns `20` and the `this.right.width()` that returns `30`
- the two calls that return `20`
- `row.width()` and the `this.left.width()` that returns `50`

## [Building Up](recursive-data/base-cases.html)

Student: Professor, I was thinking about how social media posts work, and I think I have my own example of recursion! But it doesn’t work right.

Prof: Let’s have a look!

Student: So I was thinking about how you can repost someone’s post but add on your own text. But then someone else can repost your repost. And that seemed like recursive data. Here’s what I tried:

```java
record Post(String message, Post post) { }
```

Prof: Oh super interesting. I totally agree that reposting is an example of recursive data, great observation!

Student: Here’s the issue: I can’t figure out how to create one. I wrote `new Post("check out this cool idea:", new Post(...`. But then I didn’t know what to put in the parentheses. How do I make a `Post` without making a `Post`?

Prof: It’s frustrating right! There’s a good principle to learn here, though. All of the recursive data we’ve seen so far has a key feature: there are some records that have fields that refer back to the type, *and some that don’t*. For example in `ImageQuery`, the `And` and `Or` queries refer back to `ImageQuery`, but the ones that look directly at the image data like `HasExtension` or `HasKeyword` do not.

We call the ones with self-reference the recursive cases and the ones with no self-reference the base cases. What do you think some of the recursive and base cases of data are for `Pict`?

Student: Hmmm so I guess things like `Beside` are recursive cases, because they combine two `Pict`s and `Beside` implements `Pict`.

Prof: Right, and the base cases?

Student: Those must be the simple shapes like `Circle` and `Rect`.

Prof: Right. We don’t need to construct a `Pict` to pass into a `Circle`, and a `Circle` doesn’t store another `Pict`. So this idea of base cases and recursive cases comes up over and over again in representing interesting data.

Student: Really?

Prof: Yeah, I’ll give a few more examples:

- Math expressions like `(4 + 5) - x` → the base cases would be things like numbers and variable names. The recursive cases would be things like add and subtract expressions.
- Files and folders in Google Drive → folders would be the recursive cases (because folders contain files and folders) and files would be base cases (files can’t contain folders).
- Family trees of ancestors → people with known parents are the recursive cases (because they have parent fields that are also people), and the base cases are “unknown” places in the tree where there’s no information about an ancestor

Student: I’ll try one. In a course system, the courses are the recursive cases and the students in the course are the base cases.

Prof: Not quite! There’s no way for a course to contain a course, or a student to contain a student, so there’s no recursion in that example. It’s just nested data. That’s a really good example of the difference between data that is just nested, and data with a **self-reference**.

Student: Can I try another one?

Prof: Sure!

Student: OK so how about course prerequisites. An upper division course is a recursive case, because it has some prerequisites, like CSE12 requires CSE11, so CSE12 must have a field or something that stores CSE11. But CSE11 has no official prerequisites, so it is a base case?

Prof: Great example!

#### Practice

- An email forwarded with the original message inside it
- An employee record that includes an office address
- An email with some attachments
- A folder of playlists, which can also hold other folders
- A repost on social media, with your own text added to someone else’s post
- An org chart, where a manager has a list of the employees who report to them
- A playlist of songs
- A post on social media that mentions a user

Here is a chain of reposts. Each post is either a regular post, or a repost that holds the post it reposts, shown inside it.

┌────────────────────────────────┐

│ │ @ben: "never"              │ │
│ │ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │
│ │ │ @ana: "Does anyone's   │ │ │
│ │ │   code compile on the  │ │ │
│ │ │   first try?"          │ │ │

```

## [Building Up, with Code](recursive-data/base-case-code.html)

Student: So I feel like I get the **idea** of recursion, but I don’t know how to turn your examples into code.

Prof: Let’s get back to your original idea – how would this look for `Post`s, in code?

Student: Do I have to write an interface first?

Prof: That’s how we’ve been doing it; at some point I’ll show you another way, but for this example that’s a good idea.

Student: OK so I need… an interface that represents posts? And then a recursive case and a base case.

Prof: Right – so the recursive case is the one you started with.

Student: A repost?

Prof: Right. And if you think about how posts work, what has to be at the end of a long chain of reposts?

Student: A… regular post?

Prof: Right! OK try turning that into code.

Student: Hmm so something like this?

```java
interface Post {}
record Repost(String message, Post original) { }
record RegularPost(String message) { }
```

Student: OHH so the base case just has the text. Like when you make one Tweet or whatever. I guess real posts have more stuff like images.

Prof: Absolutely, but you’ve captured the recursive structure now: try creating an instance now!

Student: OK…

```java
interface Post {}
record Repost(String message, Post original) { }
record RegularPost(String message) { }
Post r = new Repost("what he said",
          new Repost("what she said",
            new RegularPost("I love to post")));
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 4: error: The constructor Repost(String, Repost) is undefined
line 4: error: Type mismatch: cannot convert from Repost to Post
line 5: error: The constructor Repost(String, RegularPost) is undefined
```

Student: Wait, why didn’t that work?

Prof: This is an important detail: there are two uses of the `Repost` constructor in your program. One of them is taking a `RegularPost`, and the other is taking a `Repost`. But neither of those are `Post` values according to Java!

Student: Huh? I wrote the interface right there!

Prof: Do you remember anything from `ImageQuery` about something we need to add to record definitions?

Student: Oh! I need to say `implements`? Why?

Prof: Well, it’s how we tell Java “I want all `Repost` objects to count as `Post` objects; **and** I want all `RegularPost` objects to count as `Post` objects. It’s also one of the **only** ways to get this kind of sharing of classes with one type in Java.

Student: So without `implements`, there can never be a way to have `Repost` be a `Post`?

Prof: That’s right. Let’s fix it!

```java
interface Post {}
record Repost(String message, Post original) implements Post { }
record RegularPost(String message) implements Post { }
Post r = new Repost("what he said",
          new Repost("what she said",
            new RegularPost("I love to post")));
```

Output:

```text
r = Repost[message=what he said, original=Repost[message=what she said, original=RegularPost[message=I love to post]]]
```

Prof: Nice! Let’s look at the memory diagram.

```
Names (the stack)
  top level
    r = @1003
Heap
  @1001: RegularPost[message=I love to post]
  @1002: Repost[message=what she said, original=@1001]
  @1003: Repost[message=what he said, original=@1002]
```

Student: You know, this does just kind of look like nested data.

Prof: That’s a good observation. There’s a big difference between what you can create with something like your `Post`, `Repost`, and `RegularPost`, though. You can make a chain of `Repost` instances **as long as you want**. With types that describe just nested data, not recursive data, it always has to stop at some point. We’ll explore why that’s special by writing some recursive methods next.

#### Practice

Write an interface `Ancestor`, and two records that implement it: `Known`, with a `String` field `name` and two `Ancestor` fields `parent1` and `parent2`, and `Unknown`, with no fields.

                new Known("Pat", new Unknown(), new Unknown()),
                new Unknown());
```

  new Doc("resume", 40),
  new Folder("photos", new DriveItem[] {
    new Doc("cat", 300),
    new Doc("dog", 280)

Course prerequisites can be written with just one record:

```java

```

There is no separate record for the base case. What plays the part of the base case here?

Choose one:

- A `Course` whose `prereqs` array is empty, like `cse11`

- The `name` field, because it is a `String`

## [Recursive Methods](recursive-data/recursive-methods.html)

Student: How do I know how to make methods for recursive data?

Prof: It can take a little practice! But the split of base case and recursive case helps a lot. The idea is that we implement the method in each class that is part of our recursive data definition – this is called structural recursion specifically, and it matches the examples we’ve seen so far.

Student: So to implement a method I have to implement the same method over and over?

Prof: Kind of! And we’ve seen this a few times. Like for the `matches` method, we had a method body for `HasExtension`, and a method body for `HasKeyword`, and a method body for `Or`, and so on. Each one handled just the behavior specific to its class. In the case of recursive cases like `Or`, it called the same method on its pieces to get its result.

```java
interface ImageQuery { boolean matches(ImageData im); }
record HasExtension(String ext) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData im) { ... ext ... }
}
record HasKeyword(String keyword) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData im) { ... keyword ... }
}
record Or(ImageQuery q1, ImageQuery q2) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData im) { ... q1.matches(im) ... q2.matches(im) ... }
}
record And(ImageQuery q1, ImageQuery q2) implements ImageQuery {
  public boolean matches(ImageData im) { ... q1.matches(im) ... q2.matches(im) ... }
}
```

Prof: The same kind of shape is true of `Pict`

```java
interface Pict { int width(); /* plus many more methods */ }
record Circle(int radius, String color) implements Pict {
  public int width() { ... radius ... }
}
record Rect(int width, int height, String color) implements Pict {
  public int width() { ... width ... }
}
record Beside(Pict left, Pict right) implements Pict {
  public int width() { ... left.width() ... right.width() ... }
}
record Above(Pict top, Pict bottom) implements Pict {
  public int width() { ... top.width() ... bottom.width() ... }
}
```

Student: Hey, you left out a lot of detail in these!

Prof: That’s on purpose – I want to illustrate a **common shape** between these. In all the base cases, the methods worked with just the parameters of the method, and the fields of the class. So `width` for a `Circle` uses the `radius`, `matches` for `HasKeyword` uses the `keyword`, and so on. In contrast the recursive cases make recursive calls using the same-named method on their pieces. It’s a general pattern!

```java
interface RecursiveData { Type recMethod(Param p, ...); }
record BaseCase(Field field, ...) implements RecursiveData {
  public Type recMethod(Param p, ...) { ... field ... }
}
record RecCase(Field field, ... RecursiveData d, ...) implements RecursiveData {
  public Type recMethod(Param p, ...) { ... field ... d.recMethod(p, ...) ... }
}
// Could be several different BaseCase and RecCase classes for a recursive data
// definition, not just base and rec
```

Student: Hmmm I think I’m starting to see. So the recursive case will always have a **field** that refers back to the interface?

Prof: That’s right. Think you can apply it to your `Post` now?

Student: So I already have the outline of my base case and my recursive case. I need to pick a method to try. Maybe like… if a word shows up anywhere in the chain of reposts? Like a search?

Prof: Sounds like a good example. It’s useful to think about the base case first. Actually, before that, let’s think about a few examples. You had the example with two reposts and a regular post. What else should we test?

Student: Probably a regular post on its own?

Prof: Sounds like a good idea. Let’s get that down with placeholder values as answers.

Student: All right.

```java
interface Post {
  boolean hasWord(String word);
}
record Repost(String message, Post original) implements Post {
  public boolean hasWord(String word) { return false; }
}
record RegularPost(String message) implements Post {
  public boolean hasWord(String word) { return false; }
}
Post reg = new RegularPost("Hello world!");
Post r = new Repost("what he said",
          new Repost("what she said",
            new RegularPost("I love to post")));
boolean hasWorld = reg.hasWord("world");
boolean hasPotato = reg.hasWord("potato");
boolean hasPost = r.hasWord("post");
boolean hasSaid = r.hasWord("said");
boolean hasThey = r.hasWord("they");
```

Output:

```text
reg = RegularPost[message=Hello world!]
r = Repost[message=what he said, original=Repost[message=what she said, original=RegularPost[message=I love to post]]]
hasWorld = false
hasPotato = false
hasPost = false
hasSaid = false
hasThey = false
```

Student: Is that what you meant by placeholder values? They return `false`?

Prof: Right. This makes it so we can run it, and we get the check for errors like making sure we spelled the method correctly everywhere. Now we can fill in the cases. Depending on the problem it can be easier to start with the base case or the recursive case, but for me it’s often that the base case is easier. How do we check if a word is in a post chain that’s **just** a regular post? Like what should the answer be for `hasWorld`, and how do we calculate it from `word` and `message`?

Student: Hmm I guess we use `contains` on the string? Like it’d be `return message.contains(word);` or something?

Prof: Awesome. We can fill that in. Then we need to think a little bit about the `Repost` case.

Student: Well it’s like, we check `message.contains` here, too. Then if the `original` field is a `RegularPost`, then we just check that. If the `original` field is a `Repost`, then we need to check its message and its original more.

Prof: Let’s try going from the pattern we had before. What does the pattern tell us should show up in the recursive method?

Student: Hmm well I guess… a recursive call?

Prof: And what would that recursive call look like in this case?

Student: I guess like… hmm.. like `original.hasWord(word)`. So the pattern is like

```java
boolean hasWord(String word) { ... message ... original.hasWord(word) ... }
```

Prof: Right! And what does that recursive call tell you? Describe it.

Student: It’s, I guess a boolean. And it always returns `false` right now.

Prof: Ah, right, so this is important. When we write a recursive method, we need to trust ourselves a little bit. Say we trust ourselves that `hasWord` is going to be implemented perfectly. **Then** what does the return value of `original.hasWord` mean?

Student: It’s whether the word appears in the original’s `message`. Oh wait, no, whether it appears in the whole chain starting at `original`?

Prof: Indeed! And then we need to combine that information with information about this `Repost`. The word appears if it appears in **either** the `message` of this `Repost` **or** in the chain that starts with `original`.

Student: So I combine them with `||` to get the answer?

Prof: Try it!

```java
interface Post {
  boolean hasWord(String word);
}
record Repost(String message, Post original) implements Post {
  public boolean hasWord(String word) {
    return message.contains(word) || original.hasWord(word);
  }
}
record RegularPost(String message) implements Post {
  public boolean hasWord(String word) { return message.contains(word); }
}
Post reg = new RegularPost("Hello world!");
Post r = new Repost("what he said",
          new Repost("what she said",
            new RegularPost("I love to post")));
boolean hasWorld = reg.hasWord("world");
boolean hasPotato = reg.hasWord("potato");
boolean hasPost = r.hasWord("post");
boolean hasSaid = r.hasWord("said");
boolean hasThey = r.hasWord("they");
```

Output:

```text
reg = RegularPost[message=Hello world!]
r = Repost[message=what he said, original=Repost[message=what she said, original=RegularPost[message=I love to post]]]
hasWorld = true
hasPotato = false
hasPost = true
hasSaid = true
hasThey = false
```

Student: Whoa, that worked.

Prof: Pretty cool, right?

## [Tracing Recursive Methods](recursive-data/tracing-recursion.html)

Student: So we wrote this `hasWord` method recursively, that’s great. How would it work on, like, a really big chain of posts? I feel like I’m not totally clear on **how** it runs.

```java
interface Post {
  boolean hasWord(String word);
}
record Repost(String message, Post original) implements Post {
  public boolean hasWord(String word) {
    return message.contains(word) || original.hasWord(word);
  }
}
record RegularPost(String message) implements Post {
  public boolean hasWord(String word) { return message.contains(word); }
}
Post reg = new RegularPost("Hello world!");
Post r = new Repost("what he said",
          new Repost("what she said",
            new RegularPost("I love to post")));
boolean hasWorld = reg.hasWord("world");
boolean hasPotato = reg.hasWord("potato");
boolean hasPost = r.hasWord("post");
boolean hasSaid = r.hasWord("said");
boolean hasThey = r.hasWord("they");
```

Output:

```text
reg = RegularPost[message=Hello world!]
r = Repost[message=what he said, original=Repost[message=what she said, original=RegularPost[message=I love to post]]]
hasWorld = true
hasPotato = false
hasPost = true
hasSaid = true
hasThey = false
```

Prof: That’s a great question. Let’s first look at a memory trace for the call to `r.hasWord("post")` to see a small case, then we can think about generalizing to bigger ones.

```
Names (the stack), over time →
  top level
    reg = @1002
    r = @1008
    hasPost = true
    r.hasWord("post") on @1008
      word = @1009
      returns (false || true) → true
      message.contains(word) on @1003
        s = @1009
        returns false
      original.hasWord(word) on @1007
        word = @1009
        returns (false || true) → true
        message.contains(word) on @1004
          s = @1009
          returns false
        original.hasWord(word) on @1006
          word = @1009
          returns true
          message.contains(word) on @1005
            s = @1009
            returns true
Heap
  @1001: "Hello world!"
  @1002: RegularPost[message=@1001]
  @1003: "what he said"
  @1004: "what she said"
  @1005: "I love to post"
  @1006: RegularPost[message=@1005]
  @1007: Repost[message=@1004, original=@1006]
  @1008: Repost[message=@1003, original=@1007]
  @1009: "post"
```

Prof: So, notice there’s a moment where we have **three** active calls to `hasWord`. Two of them have receivers that are `Repost` instances, and one is a `RegularPost` instance (at the top). The stack “builds up” this computation, and then we’ll get a `true` from the topmost stack frame. We’ll then “unwind” through all the frames, returning `true`, using `||` to combine it with the `false` values that came back from the **other** calls to `message.contains`, and then finally result in `true`. In this example, I drew the strings on the heap, so you can see the receivers given to the `contains` method.

Student: OK, I think I get it. So in `false || true`, the `false` is coming from `message.contains` and the `true` is coming from the recursive call?

Prof: Good observation. That’s right. Do you think that will always be the case, or is that specific to this example?

Student: Hmmm, well the next example looks for `"said"`, which is true on the first of the `Repost` instances. So there would be a true on the left, right?

Prof: Great question, let’s trace that one.

```
Names (the stack), over time →
  top level
    reg = @1002
    r = @1008
    hasSaid = true
    r.hasWord("said") on @1008
      word = @1009
      returns true || original.hasWord(word) → true
      message.contains(word) on @1003
        s = @1009
        returns true
Heap
  @1001: "Hello world!"
  @1002: RegularPost[message=@1001]
  @1003: "what he said"
  @1004: "what she said"
  @1005: "I love to post"
  @1006: RegularPost[message=@1005]
  @1007: Repost[message=@1004, original=@1006]
  @1008: Repost[message=@1003, original=@1007]
  @1009: "said"
```

Student: Wait, where are all the recursive calls?

Prof: In this case, it stops after the first `message.contains`, because if the left value of `||` is `true`, the whole `||` expression stops before evaluating the right hand side. This is called short circuiting.

Student: So even though we wrote a recursive method, it might not actually make recursive calls?

Prof: Right – it’s a search that returns as soon as it finds a match, and might never actually look at `original`. But it will make the recursive call if it needs to. Can you think of an example input that would make **one** recursive call on `r`, but not two?

Student: Hmmm so it would have to match at the second repost but not the first… `"she"`?

Prof: Right! OK now back to your original question. What if there were hundreds of `Repost` instances in a chain, and we searched for a word that **only** appeared in the innermost `RegularPost`. What would the memory diagram look like?

Student: Hmmm so it would have lots and lots of frames at once all with `Repost` receivers, and then one at the very top that is a `RegularPost`? Like our first picture, but way more frames.

```
Names (the stack)
  message.contains(word)
    s = post
    returns true
  original.hasWord(word) on @1001
    word = post
  original.hasWord(word) on @1002
    word = post
  ⋮ 297 more original.hasWord(word) frames, each on a Repost
  original.hasWord(word) on @1300
    word = post
  r.hasWord("post") on @1301
    word = post
  top level
    r = @1301
Heap
  @1001: RegularPost[message=I love to post]
  @1002: Repost[message=lol, original=@1001]
  @1300: Repost[message=lol, original=…]
  @1301: Repost[message=lol, original=@1300]
```

Prof: That’s a great sketch, and it is indeed what the stack looks like for very “deep” recursive calls.

#### Practice

Here is `totalMessageLength` from the last step, called on the chain from before. The lengths of the three messages are in the chart, and the values returned by `totalMessageLength` are left out.

```java

          new Repost("what she said",
            new RegularPost("I love to post")));
int total = r.totalMessageLength();
```

```
Names (the stack), over time →
  top level
    r = @1006
    total = ???
    r.totalMessageLength() on @1006
      returns ???
      message.length() on @1001
        returns 12
      original.totalMessageLength() on @1005
        returns ???
        message.length() on @1002
          returns 13
        original.totalMessageLength() on @1004
          returns ???
          message.length() on @1003
            returns 14
Heap
  @1001: "what he said"
  @1002: "what she said"
  @1003: "I love to post"
  @1004: RegularPost[message=@1003]
  @1005: Repost[message=@1002, original=@1004]

## [A Universal Base Case](recursive-data/null.html)

Student: My friend figured out how to make recursive data without an interface.

Prof: Oh really?

Student: Well, actually it was AI again. But I was trying to figure out some of this recursive data stuff, and it made a program that had `null` in it:

```java
record Person(String name, Person parent1, Person parent2) { }
Person p = new Person("Bob", new Person("Brenda", null, null), null);
```

Output:

```text
p = Person[name=Bob, parent1=Person[name=Brenda, parent1=null, parent2=null], parent2=null]
```

Student: It looks like it uses `null` everywhere we would have had a base case like `Unknown`.

Prof: Ah I see. Yes, you can do this! Java will let you store `null` in a field or variable or parameter of any reference type. So `null` can be stored in a `Person` field.

Student: So why don’t we just use that all the time?

Prof: You can, but it requires using a different style. The main reason is I like having the base case classes to put methods in. For example, if we want to have a `oldestKnownGeneration` method, how do we do that? Try to write it inside `Person`.

Student: Ummm, let’s see, we need to check if either parent is `null` right? And if they are, then we return `1`, because there’s nothing more to visit.

```java
record Person(String name, Person parent1, Person parent2) {
  int oldestKnownGeneration() {
    if(parent1 == null && parent2 == null) { return 1; }
    int oldestParents = Math.max(parent1.oldestKnownGeneration(), parent2.oldestKnownGeneration());
    return 1 + oldestParents;
  }
}
Person p = new Person("Bob", new Person("Brenda", null, null), null);
int oldest = p.oldestKnownGeneration();
```

Output (failed):

```text
Exception in thread "Thread-0" java.lang.NullPointerException
	at Person.oldestKnownGeneration(Unknown Source)
	at <init>(Unknown Source)
```

Student: Wait, why is that an error?

Prof: Let’s look at the trace

```
Names (the stack), over time →
  top level
    p = @1002
    p.oldestKnownGeneration() on @1002
      throws NullPointerException: parent2 is null
      parent1.oldestKnownGeneration() on @1001
        returns 1
Heap
  @1001: Person[name=Brenda, parent1=null, parent2=null]
  @1002: Person[name=Bob, parent1=@1001, parent2=null]
```

Prof: On the person with name `"Bob"`, there’s one parent that’s null and another that isn’t. So we try to call `parent2.oldestKnownGeneration()`, but `parent2` is `null`. That is exactly what `NullPointerException` means: trying to use a field or call a method on the value `null`.

So we’d actually need two checks – one for each parent. Those would be some number, or 0 if null. In my opinion, the code for this gets pretty complex:

```java
record Person(String name, Person parent1, Person parent2) {
  int oldestKnownGeneration() {
    int oldest = 0;
    if(parent1 != null) { oldest = parent1.oldestKnownGeneration(); }
    if(parent2 != null) { oldest = Math.max(oldest, parent2.oldestKnownGeneration()); }
    return 1 + oldest;
  }
}
Person p = new Person("Bob", new Person("Brenda", null, null), null);
int oldest = p.oldestKnownGeneration();
```

Output:

```text
p = Person[name=Bob, parent1=Person[name=Brenda, parent1=null, parent2=null], parent2=null]
oldest = 2
```

Student: Huh. How did you know to do both of those checks?

Prof: Lots of experience. It’s not clear to me in all cases how to structure this code. I find the structural definition works better. Plus, this example had a clear “empty” case – when the ancestor is unknown. In other cases, like your `Post`, the base case actually has information in it, like the message of a `RegularPost`.

Student: Hmm, OK. So sometimes we can use `null` for base cases?

Prof: I think you **can**, but it’s not clear how often you **should**. And `NullPointerException` is not a fun one to get. My advice is to try to write `null`-free programs! And if you see `null` come up in a recursive program you’re reading, try to think of it like a base case class.

Student: Huh. I’ll think about that.

#### Practice

Here is another method on the same `Person` record, which counts the known people in a family tree. It checks `parent1` for `null`, but not `parent2`.

```java
record Person(String name, Person parent1, Person parent2) {
  int countKnown() {
    int count = 1;
    if(parent1 != null) { count += parent1.countKnown(); }
    count += parent2.countKnown();
    return count;
  }
}
Person ana = new Person("Ana", new Person("Ben", null, null), new Person("Cy", null, null));
int known = ana.countKnown();
```

Choose one:

- At `parent1.countKnown()`, in the call on Ana
- At `parent1.countKnown()`, in the call on Ben
- At `parent2.countKnown()`, in the call on Ben

# Java Details

## [Sweet Little Lies](java-details/things-you-havent-told-me.html)

Student: Professor, I’ve been reading `Pict.java`, and there’s a lot you haven’t been telling me.

Prof: Oh?

Student: Just look at like, the `rotate` method. Sometimes the method header says `rotate(int)` and sometimes it says `rotate(double)`, but both seem to work. I remember `default` from earlier, but how can there be two defaults of the same method?

```java
default Pict rotate(int degrees) { return new Rotate(this, degrees); }
default Pict rotate(double degrees) { return new Rotate(this, degrees); }
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 71–72](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L71-L72)

Prof: Ah, I see what you mean. Yeah, there are a number of conveniences in `Pict.java` that we haven’t talked through. We can address some!

Student: OK, so let’s do this one first. How are there two rotates?

Prof: This is called overloading. We can write the same method name, in the same class, with different parameters. Java will use the arguments and types in the call to figure out which one to call. Here’s a very simple example:

```java
String whatType(int n) { return "Got int " + n; }
String whatType(double d) { return "Got double " + d; }
String whatType(int[][] arr) { return "Got int[][] " + Arrays.deepToString(arr); }

String t1 = whatType(5);
String t2 = whatType(5.0);
String t3 = whatType(new int[][]{ { 4, 5 } });
```

Output:

```text
t1 = Got int 5
t2 = Got double 5.0
t3 = Got int[][] [[4, 5]]
```

Prof: It will work with most types, and a lot of built-in libraries use it in another way: for the same method taking different **numbers** of arguments. For example, `substring` can take just one argument, and then it takes the rest of the string starting from that index, or it can take an explicit end index:

```java
String s = "trash panda";
String rest = s.substring(6);
String front = s.substring(0, 5);
```

Output:

```text
s = trash panda
rest = panda
front = trash
```

Student: Oh that explains why sometimes documentation for Java lists the same method twice.

Prof: That’s just it! So it is an incredibly handy convenience. I use it for both of these cases.

Student: Wait, are there other cases?

Prof: Yeah, so there are a ton of complex rules for what happens with overloading, mostly I don’t try to remember them all and look them up when needed.

Student: You don’t remember them all?

Prof: Honestly, yeah. Well, OK here’s a complex example:

```java
interface Region {}
record RectRegion() implements Region {}
record CircleRegion() implements Region {}

String whatType(Region r) { return "Got Region " + r; }
String whatType(RectRegion rr) { return "Got RectRegion " + rr; }

RectRegion rr = new RectRegion();
Region r = rr;
Region c = new CircleRegion();

String t1 = whatType(r);
String t2 = whatType(rr);
String t3 = whatType(new RectRegion());
String t4 = whatType(c);
```

Output:

```text
rr = RectRegion[]
r = RectRegion[]
c = CircleRegion[]
t1 = Got Region RectRegion[]
t2 = Got RectRegion RectRegion[]
t3 = Got RectRegion RectRegion[]
t4 = Got Region CircleRegion[]
```

Student: What the heck? It’s the *same object* stored in `r` and `rr`, right?

Prof: Yup, good noticing. `r` and `rr` would store the same reference, but **different code** is called for `whatType` on `r` and `rr`!

Student: That’s so weird because I thought when you call methods the receiver decides it.

Prof: Right, the receiver decides which class to look in. Here these are top-level methods so that detail isn’t involved. But once we figure out which class to find the methods in, Java does another round of selection based on the arguments. And here’s the tricky part – it does it based on the *types of the arguments*, not based on the *argument values*. So this is one place in Java where the type you use for a variable can change what code runs! If you change the type of `r` to `RectRegion` instead of `Region`, it will call the other method.

Student: Hm. I’m not sure I like that.

Prof: Frankly, me either. I definitely like overloading for simple cases, like taking a number or a string, or for different **lengths** of argument lists. But I find the interaction of overloading with interfaces and implements to be really tricky to think through. It has uses, so you should be aware it’s possible. But I mostly just use it for convenience. If you want to read more you can see both [tutorials](https://dev.java/learn/language/oop/classes-objects/defining-methods/#overloading) and [somewhat more dense references](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-8.html#jls-8.4.9).

Student: Oh interesting. So it just makes it so you can rotate with either an int or a double? But the body is exactly the same for both! How can that work?

Prof: Well, it turns out the `Rotate` constructor is **also** overloaded.

Student: You can overload a constructor?

Prof: Hold that thought :-)

#### Practice

`slice` builds a new array out of part of another one, from index `start` up to (but not including) index `end`, just like `substring` does for a `String`. Write an overload of `slice` that takes only `arr` and `start`, and slices all the way to the end of the array. It can call the `slice` that’s already there.

Exercise:

```java
int[] slice(int[] arr, int start, int end) {
  int[] result = new int[end - start];
  int index = 0;
  for (int i = start; i < end; i += 1) {
    result[index] = arr[i];
    index += 1;
  }
  return result;
}

____ {
  ____
}

int[] nums = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 };
int[] middle = slice(nums, 1, 3);
int[] rest = slice(nums, 1);
```

## [Records Under (or Over) Construction](java-details/under-construction.html)

Student: I noticed that both `new Circle(5, "red")` and `new Circle(5, Color.RED)` work. Does that mean you can overload constructors, and how does that work?

Prof: Yes, you can! Imagine we wanted a helpful constructor for a `RectangleRegion`, which has a corner point, a width and a height. The constructor just takes a width and a height, and always puts the corner at 0, 0:

```java
record Point(double x, double y) { }
record RectangleRegion(Point p, double w, double h) {
  RectangleRegion(double w, double h) {
    this(new Point(0, 0), w, h);
  }
}
RectangleRegion r = new RectangleRegion(new Point(1, 2), 4.0, 5.0);
RectangleRegion r2 = new RectangleRegion(4.0, 5.0);
```

Output:

```text
r = RectangleRegion[p=Point[x=1.0, y=2.0], w=4.0, h=5.0]
r2 = RectangleRegion[p=Point[x=0.0, y=0.0], w=4.0, h=5.0]
```

Prof: You can see that `r2` has the `Point[x=0.0, y=0.0]` – that was created in the constructor. What else do you notice about the syntax here?

Student: Well, it uses `this` with parentheses after it.

Prof: Right! So inside a constructor, `this(...)` means to call another constructor. In this case we’re calling the one Java wrote for the record (the one that takes a `Point` and two `double` values) from the one that takes just the two `double` arguments.

Student: Interesting! So does `this` with the parentheses work everywhere?

Prof: No it’s super specific – `this(...)` is actually only allowed inside constructors, and it always means to call another constructor!

Student: Huh. Oh and so what **is** a constructor?

Prof: Great question. A constructor is code that gets called when you use `new` on a record (or class) name. The constructor definition looks like a method definition, but instead of a separate return type and method name, it **just** has the class or record name.

Student: Oh so that’s why it looks weird – `RectangleRegion` on its own looks like a return type of a method, but there’s no name for it.

Prof: Exactly right – that’s the special syntax of a constructor definition. It is kind of like a method – it gets called on a new object and helps create it. In a `record` definition, there’s one that Java writes for the record (also called the canonical constructor) that sets the field values.

Student: And that’s how `Circle` works?

Prof: That’s right. There are several constructors in `Circle`:

```java
record Circle(int radius, Color color) implements Pict {
    // ...
    Circle(int radius, String color) { this(radius, Colors.named(color)); }
    Circle(double radius, String color) { this(Px.of(radius), Colors.named(color)); }
    // ...
}
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 142–152](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L142-L152)

Student: Huh, so that’s what’s been running all along? Wait whats `Px.of` and `Colors.named`?

Prof: Great questions, we’ll get there! I’ll give a short answer now: `Px.of` is a method to turn `double` values in to specific pixel sizes – the `Pict` library assumes all sizes are in round pixel amounts. And `Colors.named` is a method that takes a friendly string name like `"red"` and produces `Color.RED`. They are more conveniences!

Student: OK, I can sort of see it. I’ll wait for more.

#### Practice

Here `RectangleRegion` has two more constructors. Each one calls another with `this(...)`.

```java
record RectangleRegion(Point p, double w, double h) {
  RectangleRegion(double w, double h) { this(new Point(0, 0), w, h); }
  RectangleRegion(double side) { this(new Point(0, 0), side, side); }
  RectangleRegion(Point p, double side) { this(p, side, side); }
}
```

Exercise:

What does each one make?

`new RectangleRegion(3.0)` makes [a square at (0, 0) / a square at (1, 1) / a rectangle at (1, 1) that isn't square / a rectangle at (0, 0) that isn't square]
`new RectangleRegion(3.0, 4.0)` makes [a square at (0, 0) / a square at (1, 1) / a rectangle at (1, 1) that isn't square / a rectangle at (0, 0) that isn't square]
`new RectangleRegion(new Point(1, 1), 2.0)` makes [a square at (0, 0) / a square at (1, 1) / a rectangle at (1, 1) that isn't square / a rectangle at (0, 0) that isn't square]
`new RectangleRegion(new Point(1, 1), 2.0, 3.0)` makes [a square at (0, 0) / a square at (1, 1) / a rectangle at (1, 1) that isn't square / a rectangle at (0, 0) that isn't square]
`new RectangleRegion(3)` makes [a square at (0, 0) / a square at (1, 1) / a rectangle at (1, 1) that isn't square / a rectangle at (0, 0) that isn't square]

## [Programming, with Class](java-details/programming-with-class.html)

Student: OK professor we really need to talk about something. You keep accidentally saying `class` when you mean `record`, or saying “class or record”, and you won’t tell me what a `class` is. Can we please get that defined?

Prof: Hah! It’s time, you’re right. So a `class` is the same thing as a `record`, but missing some stuff that we need to write ourselves if we want to program like we have with records.

Student: What stuff?

Prof: Kind of a lot of things, actually. I’ll take some of them piece by piece, and it might take a few conversations to fill it all in. But we will be telling very few lies by the end.

Student: Very few, eh?

Prof: Let’s dive in. So, let’s take a record we know and love, the `Point`. We’re going to slowly change it into a class. First we’ll just change the keyword from `record` to `class`

```java
record Point(double x, double y) { }
```

```java
class Point(double x, double y) { }
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 1: error: Syntax error on token "class", char expected
```

Student: Ummm that’s just an error.

Prof: Indeed. In `class` declarations, we don’t put the field definitions in parentheses like that. We put them in the class body:

```java
class Point {
  double x;
  double y;
}
```

Student: Why? That seems longer.

Prof: It’s just how classes work! Now let’s try to create a `Point`:

```java
class Point {
  double x;
  double y;
}
Point p = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 5: error: The constructor Point(double, double) is undefined
```

Student: Huh? Why an error? You made it correctly.

Prof: Actually, I didn’t! The default constructor for a `class` takes no arguments, and all the fields are left as the placeholder or default value for their type:

```java
class Point {
  double x;
  double y;
}
Point p = new Point();
```

Output:

```text
p = Point@b62
```

Student: Wait… so are you going to say we have to write a constructor?

Prof: That’s right! We have to write our own constructors in a class definition:

```java
class Point {
  double x;
  double y;
  Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
}
Point p = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
```

Output:

```text
p = Point@cc0
```

Student: That’s weird-looking. It uses `this`? What’s the difference between `this.x` and `x`?

Prof: Great question. Let’s look at a memory diagram **during the call to the constructor**:

```
Names (the stack)
  new Point(4.0, 5.0) on @1001
    x = 4.0
    y = 5.0
  top level
Heap
  @1001: Point[x=0.0 4.0, y=0.0]
```

Prof: So we’ve got a freshly-created object, `@1001`. It has `x` and `y` fields, they started as the placeholder values `0.0`. The arguments to the constructor were `4.0` and `5.0` – that’s the parameters `x` and `y`. Then the body of the constructor **changes** the field values to hold the values of the parameters.

Student: So `this.x = x` changes a value on the heap?

Prof: That’s right, this is a new operation we haven’t seen called field update. It lets us change the value of a field of an object stored on the heap, just as you said. So the constructor does two field updates, and then the object is in the state we are used to after using a `record` canonical constructor. You can think of it as the record filling in this code for you, just based on the fields you put in parentheses after the record name.

Student: Cool! Wait, so why bother using a class? Records just save typing, right?

Prof: Well, there’s more to learn here, this is just the first of the things records do for us, but also we will need to talk more to explore their restrictions.

    this.y = y;

    System.out.println("nothing");
  }
}

What does each one print?

`new Point(3.0)` prints [nothing / one double, then two doubles / two doubles, then one double / two doubles / one double]
`new Point()` prints [nothing / one double, then two doubles / two doubles, then one double / two doubles / one double]
`new Point(3)` prints [nothing / one double, then two doubles / two doubles, then one double / two doubles / one double]
