## [Classes and Equality](java-details/class-equality.html)

Student: So what else is different between records and classes? You said there was more.

Prof: One other big difference is equality.

Student: Equality?

Prof: Like `==` vs `.equals()`, and what those mean.

Student: Oh, so objects with classes don’t have `.equals()` or something?

Prof: Well… they kind of do.

Student: Kind of?

Prof: There **is** a default `.equals()` that every class gets, but it’s different from the one on records, and it just checks `==`:

```java
class PointC {
  double x;
  double y;
  PointC(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
}
record PointR(double x, double y) { }

PointC c1 = new PointC(4.0, 5.0);
PointC c2 = new PointC(4.0, 5.0);
boolean c1Equalsc2 = c1.equals(c2);
PointR r1 = new PointR(4.0, 5.0);
PointR r2 = new PointR(4.0, 5.0);
boolean r1Equalse2 = r1.equals(r2);
```

Output:

```text
c1 = PointC@777
c2 = PointC@782
c1Equalsc2 = false
r1 = PointR[x=4.0, y=5.0]
r2 = PointR[x=4.0, y=5.0]
r1Equalse2 = true
```

Student: So the `.equals` acts more like arrays’ equals method?

Prof: That’s right, it’s the default. If you want, you can **define your own**.

Student: You mean like, write my own equals method?

Prof: That’s right:

```java
class PointC {
  double x;
  double y;
  PointC(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  boolean equals(PointC other) {
    return this.x == other.x && this.y == other.y;
  }
}
record PointR(double x, double y) { }

PointC c1 = new PointC(4.0, 5.0);
PointC c2 = new PointC(4.0, 5.0);
boolean c1Equalsc2 = c1.equals(c2);
PointR r1 = new PointR(4.0, 5.0);
PointR r2 = new PointR(4.0, 5.0);
boolean r1Equalse2 = r1.equals(r2);
```

Output:

```text
c1 = PointC@8f0
c2 = PointC@8fb
c1Equalsc2 = true
r1 = PointR[x=4.0, y=5.0]
r2 = PointR[x=4.0, y=5.0]
r1Equalse2 = true
```

Student: Huh, that’s interesting. But why would you ever want that? Won’t it always just compare the fields with either `==` or `.equals`?

Prof: **Great** question. Consider this program:

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Pict rect = new Rect(3, 2, "red");
Raster r1 = rect.render();
Color[][] colors = {
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED },
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED }
};
Raster r2 = new Raster(colors);
```

Output:

```text
rect = Rect[width=3, height=2, color=red]
[image]
r1 = Raster[3x2]
[image]
colors = [[java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]], [java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]]]
r2 = Raster[3x2]
[image]
```

Prof: Now, are `r1` and `r2` the same image?

Student: Yeah, obviously.

Prof: And should they be `.equals()`?

Student: Well obviously they should be… Oh right but the fields are arrays. So the `record` version won’t work.

Prof: Indeed! So `Raster` actually defines a `.equals` that provides this:

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object other) {
    if (this == other) return true;
    if (!(other instanceof Raster r)) return false;
    if (this.width() != r.width() || this.height() != r.height()) return false;
    for (int y = 0; y < this.height(); y++) {
        if (!Arrays.equals(this.pixels[y], r.pixels[y])) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 476–485](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L476-L485)

Prof: And that code is what compares the arrays in this example:

```java
import java.awt.Color;
Pict rect = new Rect(3, 2, "red");
Raster r1 = rect.render();
Color[][] colors = {
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED },
  { Color.RED, Color.RED, Color.RED }
};
Raster r2 = new Raster(colors);
boolean sameImage = r1.equals(r2);
boolean sameObject = r1 == r2;
```

Output:

```text
rect = Rect[width=3, height=2, color=red]
[image]
r1 = Raster[3x2]
[image]
colors = [[java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]], [java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0], java.awt.Color[r=255,g=0,b=0]]]
r2 = Raster[3x2]
[image]
sameImage = true
sameObject = false
```

Student: I see. I feel like you’ve just brought up more questions though – what’s `Object`, and what’s `instanceof` and whats the `Raster` in parentheses doing?

Prof: Yeah, it’s a lot. Trust me, we’ll get there. For now, I just want you to see that we compare the pixels of the rasters in this equals method, and there wouldn’t be a way to define equals this way with a `class` **or** a `record` without writing `equals` ourselves.

Student: So we **need** `.equals()` for any comparisons between classes to be more than `==`, and sometimes we need it to check something more than just comparing field by field.

Prof: Nice summary. It’s worth saying that our `.equals()` is cheating a little bit by not using `Object`, but that’s a lie I’ll make you live with a little longer.

## [A Static Shock](java-details/static.html)

Student: I went and looked up the `Px` and `Colors` classes, because you wouldn’t tell me about them. What’s going on with the word `static` in them? I can kind of read them but I don’t know what that part means. And also what’s going on with `throw`?

```java
    /** A width, height, or radius: zero is fine (an empty picture), negative is not. */
    static int size(String what, int v) {
        if (v < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(what + " is negative: " + v);
        return v;
    }
}
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 88–93](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L88-L93)

Prof: Great questions. Let’s take them one at a time. First `throw` – this is Java’s built in way of reporting errors. When `throw ...` evaluates, it stops the current methods **and all methods on the stack**. It will report the error you created, and also the stack trace. This is called throwing an exception.

Student: I’ve seen stack traces before! So you’re telling me if I give a negative number I’ll get an error from `size`?

Prof: That’s right.

Student: What is `IllegalArgumentException`?

Prof: Java has many built in exceptions – they are descriptions of errors that can happen. In this case, the `size` method is just used to check if a number is non-negative. It’s used where we want to make sure a `radius` or a `width` is zero or more.

Student: Huh, OK. Wait what’s `what`?

Prof: What?

Student: The parameter, it’s called `what`, but it’s only used in the error message?

Prof: That’s right – reporting errors is important! So important that sometimes we have information included **just in case** an error occurs.

Student: OK, so in this use in `Raster` it’s just to say whether width or height was wrong?

```java
    Raster(int width, int height) {
        this.width = Px.size("width", width);
        this.height = Px.size("height", height);
        // ...
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 412–414](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L412-L414)

Prof: That’s it – it assigns `width` or height to the value after checking it.

Student: And I’m seeing something now that I look at this code. Can I make a guess about `static`?

Prof: By all means!

Student: Well, I see that `size` was declared `static`. And then we did one of those calls like we do on `Math` where it’s a capital thing before the dot, which ought to be a class. So is that how we call `size` because it’s static?

Prof: Nice analysis! You got it. A `static` method has no receiver. We usually use it for library methods that aren’t associated with any object instance. So a lot of `Math` and `Arrays` are like that, because they work directly on numbers or arrays without constructing an object first. And in the Pict library, that’s what `Px` is doing.

Student: OK now I want to see what it does.

Prof: Try doing a call from another method, called from `main`, to see the trace.

```java
void anotherMethod() {
  System.out.println("Should be just 4 " + Px.size("test", 4));
  System.out.println("Throw an error" + Px.size("test", -3));
}
void main() {
  anotherMethod();
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
Should be just 4 4
Exception in thread "Thread-0" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: test is negative: -3
	at Px.size(Unknown Source)
	at anotherMethod(Unknown Source)
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

*In the book, the version of Java that runs cannot show line numbers. When running in a full-fledged programming environment, you’d see something like this:*

```text
$ javac Throw.java Pict.java
$ java Throw
Should be just 4 4
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: test is negative: -3
	at Px.size(Pict.java:90)
	at Throw.anotherMethod(Throw.java:3)
	at Throw.main(Throw.java:6)
```

Student: Neat! So I can see that the stack has `Px.size`, then `anotherMethod`, then `main`. Wait! That’s the same order as the stack in a memory diagram!

Prof: Indeed – the stack trace captures exactly the stack we draw. To draw it the way we usually do:

```
Names (the stack)
  Px.size("test", -3)
    what = test
    v = -3
    throws IllegalArgumentException
  anotherMethod()
  main()
  top level
Heap
```

Student: Interesting. So those diagrams really are what’s happening.

Prof: They are pretty accurate!

Exercise:

Each of these is a call we have made somewhere in the book. Is it a `static` method, or an instance method?

`"trash".length()` is [instance: called on an object / static: called on a class]
`Integer.parseInt("42")` is [instance: called on an object / static: called on a class]
`dot.beside(square)` is [instance: called on an object / static: called on a class]
`Arrays.equals(a, b)` is [instance: called on an object / static: called on a class]
`raster.colorAt(0, 0)` is [instance: called on an object / static: called on a class]
`Colors.named("red")` is [instance: called on an object / static: called on a class]
`query.matches(img)` is [instance: called on an object / static: called on a class]

```java
record Point(double x, double y) {
  double distanceTo(Point other) {
    return Math.sqrt((x - other.x) * (x - other.x) + (y - other.y) * (y - other.y));
  }
  Point flipped() { return new Point(y, x); }
  Point origin() { return new Point(0, 0); }
  double average(double a, double b) { return (a + b) / 2; }

}
```

## [Primitives: The Full `cast`](java-details/casting.html)

Student: I’m looking at some other methods now. What’s going on in `Px.of`? Two weird things – what’s `isNaN`/`isInfinite`, and what’s the `(int)` at the bottom?

```java
  static int of(double v) {
      if (Double.isNaN(v) || Double.isInfinite(v)) {
          throw new IllegalArgumentException("measurement must be a number, got " + v);
      }
      return (int) Math.round(v);
  }
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 82–87](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L82-L87)

Prof: Great questions both. When `double` arithmetic was designed, a decision was made to have no **errors** be reported from it. So unlike `1 / 0` on ints, which reports an error, `1 / 0` evaluates to `Infinity`, which is a valid `double` value. Similarly, things like `Math.sqrt(-1)` don’t have a mathematical answer in terms of a `double`. These produce a special `NaN` (stands for “Not a Number”) value. The check here is making sure that the value is not one of those special nonsense values before converting it to an `int`.

Student: Hmm OK. That’s a lot but I kind of see. And then what about `(int)` – you said that’s converting to an int?

Prof: Right, `(int)v` is called a cast, which turns one primitive type into another. (There are other types of casts, but this is the one on primitives). Casting is actually super complex and fraught. The simple explanation is that it drops the decimal part of the double to make an int. It’s very useful because it allows us to go back and forth between the primitive types.

Student: What’s so hard about that?

Prof: The problem is that `int` can only represent numbers up to about 2^31, while double can reprsent much bigger numbers than that. So consider this weird example:

```java
int x = (int)1234567890123.0;
int y = (int)9999999999999.0;
```

Output:

```text
x = 2147483647
y = 2147483647
```

Student: Huh? They’re clearly not the same.

Prof: Right, so casting “clamps” for the double to int conversion. That number is the biggest int, and it’s returned for any cast of a double larger than that.

Student: Weird. Do I have to care?

Prof: Kind of! In the Pict library these casts are used for pixels meant to be displayed on screen, so having a width of billions of them doesn’t make much sense. But in many applications we **do** have billions of things, like cents. So this can matter a lot, so it’s a choice to convert. There’s no easy answer either, you have to think about your data and what operations happen on it.

Student: Hmmm, that seems important and also very hard.

Prof: It leads to a lot of mistakes in real code. Keep it in mind. OK so while we are on the topic I want to mention **all** the primitive types:

- `byte`: whole numbers from −128 to 127
- `short`: whole numbers from −32,768 to 32,767
- `int`: whole numbers from −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (about ±2 billion)
- `long`: whole numbers up to about ±9.2 × 1018
- `float`: decimal numbers up to about ±3.4 × 1038
- `double`: decimal numbers up to about ±1.8 × 10308
- `char`: a single character, like `'a'`
- `boolean`: `true` or `false`

It’s good to know all of these for reading code.

Student: So can I cast between any of them?

Prof: In general casting from a smaller type to a bigger type works pretty well – `int` to `double` for example, because double is bigger. Casting from bigger to smaller, or between same-sized values, can lose information. So it’s important to look up the real rules, test, and so on when doing it.

`(int) -3.99` is ____
`(double) 7 / 2` is ____
`(double) (7 / 2)` is ____
`(int) 1e10` is ____
`(int) Math.round(2.5)` is ____

- `long` to `int`

## [Visibility Modifiers](java-details/access.html)

Student: I have another confusion here. When I make a record, I can access its fields with dot, and you’ve shown that.

Prof: Absolutely!

Student: But I can’t do that with fields on stuff like `Circle`:

```java
Circle c = new Circle(4, "red");
int radius = c.radius;
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 2: error: The field Circle.radius is not visible
```

Student: Why won’t it let me access that?

Prof: Great question! This has to do with visibility modifiers.

Student: Visibility modifiers?

Prof: Yeah. So we haven’t really bothered to write them except one – `public`. We had to add that when we implemented methods from an interface, remember?

Student: Yeah I remember that. You told me to just write it and not question it.

Prof: So all fields and methods can have one of several visibilities, which affect which other classes can use them directly. The ones we’ve been encountering implicitly are:

- `private` – the field or method can be accessed only within the class or within classes declared in the same file, for the kind of programs we write (ones with a `void main()`)
- No modifier given (called “package private”) – the field or method can be accessed only within the class or other classes in files in the same “package” (roughly a folder)
- `public` – any context can access the field or method

Student: But I don’t see any code where `radius` is made `private`:

```java
record Circle(int radius, Color color) implements Pict {
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 142–142](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L142-L142)

Prof: That’s true. What’s happening is `record` fields have `private` access. It’s by default and it can’t be changed.

Student: Really? So how have we been able to… oh because the other classes, or main or whatever, are in the same file. But wait, I can access it if I add parentheses:

```java
Circle c = new Circle(4, "red");
int radius = c.radius();
```

Output:

```text
c = Circle[radius=4, color=red]
[image]
radius = 4
```

Prof: Correct. This is a trick `record`s pull off – it’s helpful to be able to see the private fields’ values. So records **also** add a public accessor method or getter with exactly the name of the field. So going back to our `Point` class that corresponds to a `record`, it would actually look like:

```java
// record Point(double x, double y) {} expands to...
class Point {
  private double x;
  private double y;
  public Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  public boolean equals(Point other) {
    return other.x == this.x && other.y == this.y;
  }
  public double x() { return this.x; }
  public double y() { return this.y; }
}
```

Prof: For a record, making the constructor `public` makes sense because the job of a record is to construct data. So the defaults all make sense. And records are actually doing quite a bit of **typing** for us (and saving us tedious reading), because we want these patterns over and over.

Student: And why would you want things to be private? It seems like it just adds errors to your program. Things should just be visible.

Prof: You know, I partially agree with you. But there’s a good argument for keeping fields private, and it’s what most people actually recommend! The idea is that it limits where you have to look to see what happens to a particular field. If you want to ask a question like “does this `int` field only ever increase” that’s a very complicated question to answer if any code in a big program could change it. But if you have **all** the uses of the field in one place, you can audit that quickly.

Especially these days with agents adding code all the time, things like `private` help set up some boundaries so you can still check a guarantee like “my field only increases” even if thousands of lines of code are added outside that class.

Student: Huh, that’s actually pretty cool. So that’s it then, that’s how records and classes correspond? No more lies?

Prof: Um, well, the `equals` method is a little weird. And I left out something called `hashCode` that is not relevant for what we’re doing right now. We will have to directly address updating `equals` when we talk about the `Object` class, but that’ll be another day. There’s one more detail of `record` that I want to share now, though.

Record fields are what’s called `final`, which means you can’t do field **update** on them.

Student: OK, why not?

Prof: The idea with records is that they create fixed data for representing something that doesn’t change. This is super common in programming, and it’s something Java makes easy. In general, fields on `class` declarations **can** have field updates applied to those fields. So one step more honest would be to put `final` in:

```java
// record Point(double x, double y) {} expands to...
class Point {
  private final double x;
  private final double y;
  public Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  public boolean equals(Point other) {
    return other.x == this.x && other.y == this.y;
  }
  public double x() { return this.x; }
  public double y() { return this.y; }
}
```

Prof: And **that** is as far as we will go for now.

Student: So I can read all of Pict now?

Prof: A lot more of it, for sure. There’s more to learn still, but I think that gives a good picture of a lot of what I was hiding or sliding past.

# Extending Classes

## [Overriding Methods](extending-classes/tostring-override.html)

Student: Professor, I’m seeing something I don’t quite understand with classes.

Prof: What is it?

Student: Well, when the book or my programs print out records, they print the field names and values. But that doesn’t happen for my `Point` class.

Prof: Oh, interesting! Let’s have a look at your code.

```java
record PointR(double x, double y) { }
class PointC {
  double x;
  double y;
  PointC(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
}
void main() {
  PointR p1 = new PointR(4.0, 5.0);
  PointC p2 = new PointC(4.0, 5.0);
  System.out.println("p1: " + p1);
  System.out.println("p2: " + p2);
}
```

Output:

```text
p1: PointR[x=4.0, y=5.0]
p2: PointC@730
```

Student: See, they print very differently! The second one just prints `PointC@` and then a number that has nothing to do with `x` or `y`.

Prof: Right! That’s a great point. So one thing to make clear up front – when an object is added to a string with `+`, Java calls the `toString()` method on that object to get the `String` to concatenate. So here we are seeing that objects created from `record` constructors have a different `toString()` than those created with classes.

Student: OK, that sounds reasonable. How do I make `PointC` print like `PointR`? Do I write a `toString`?

Prof: That’s right.

Student: So it’s like how we needed to write our own `equals()`? And by default `record` puts in a good `toString`?

Prof: Yup, right again.

Student: So wait a minute. Where are the “bad” default `equals()` and `toString()` coming from?

Prof: Excellent question! And this leads perfectly into our next topic. You’re getting good at asking questions like that.

Student: Thanks, I guess. Sort of feels inevitable.

Prof: Here’s what’s going on. There is a built-in class in Java called `Object` (with a capital `O`). It has the “default” implementations of `toString` and `equals` that all classes use if they don’t define their own. If they **do** define their own, it is called overriding that method.

Student: That sounds kind of like an interface with default methods.

Prof: It is quite like that. Most of what `Object` does **is** effectively default methods. But it’s actually using a slightly different mechanism than `implements` – it is using inheritance, which has some of its own tradeoffs. I’ll give a small example where I make up my own class called `Objekt` with a `stringify()` method. The idea is to show the structure that Java has with its own built-in `Object`, but writing it all out ourselves:

```java
class Objekt {
  public String stringify() { return "Objekt"; }
}
class SubClass1 extends Objekt {
  int x;
  @Override
  public String stringify() { return "SubClass1[x=" + x + "]"; }
}
class SubClass2 extends Objekt {
  int y;
}
Objekt b1 = new Objekt();
SubClass1 sc1 = new SubClass1();
SubClass2 sc2 = new SubClass2();
String b1A = b1.stringify();
String sc1A = sc1.stringify();
String sc2A = sc2.stringify();
```

Output:

```text
b1 = Objekt@8c1
sc1 = SubClass1@8c9
sc2 = SubClass2@8ca
b1A = Objekt
sc1A = SubClass1[x=0]
sc2A = Objekt
```

Prof: What do you notice?

Student: Hm… I notice that we can call `stringify` on `sc2` without having it defined at all. I guess that means it is using the one on `Objekt`?

Prof: That’s right.

Student: And I notice that the `SubClass1` definition says `@Override`. What’s that? I tried deleting the whole `@Override` line and the program behaved the same.

Prof: Great question. `@Override` says “I mean to override this method!” Java will only give an error if that method **isn’t** defined on a class or interface being extended or implemented.

Student: Oh right, and `extends` is another word here, what does that mean?

Prof: When a class `Child` extends another class `Parent`, it tells Java that `Child` is a subclass of `Parent` (we call `Parent` the superclass). This means a few things happen:

- Method calls and field lookups on `Child` objects will look for methods and fields in `Parent` if they aren’t found on `Child`
- `Child` objects “count” as having the `Parent` type, so they can be stored in `Parent` variables and parameters, in elements of `Parent` arrays, and so on

This is **a lot** like interfaces, except for the fields piece, which we haven’t explored, but we can get to that soon.

Student: Wait, but how are our classes like `PointC` getting the defaults from `Object`?

Prof: Another great question – if you don’t write `extends` on a class definition in Java, it **implicitly** extends `Object`. It’s like Java adds that in for you. So the default `toString` and `equals` really are coming from there!

Also there’s one more definition worth sharing now: Java says subtyping is what’s happening when one type can be stored in a variable of a different type. So in Java’s terms, `SubClass1` in the example above is a **subtype** of `Objekt` because it can be stored in an `Objekt`-typed variable. Subtyping also applies to interfaces: `Circle` is a **subtype** of `Pict` because of the `implements` relationship.

## [Sharing Fields](extending-classes/abstracting-shared-fields.html)

Student: When do I use inheritance?

Prof: There are a few different cases people talk about. One I think is important is **sharing fields** across classes.

Student: Sharing fields?

Prof: Let’s think about representing locations on a service like Google Maps. They might want to have a bunch of different classes for them, and an interface that ties them together. A heads up, we’re getting into some longer examples:

```java
interface Place {
  String pinLabel();
  boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east);
}
class Restaurant implements Place {
  String name;
  double lat;
  double lng;
  double stars;
  Restaurant(String name, double lat, double lng, double stars) {
    this.name = name;
    this.lat = lat;
    this.lng = lng;
    this.stars = stars;
  }
  public String pinLabel() { return name + " (" + stars + " stars)"; }
  public boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east) {
    return lat >= south && lat <= north && lng >= west && lng <= east;
  }
}
class Park implements Place {
  String name;
  double lat;
  double lng;
  int acres;
  Park(String name, double lat, double lng, int acres) {
    this.name = name;
    this.lat = lat;
    this.lng = lng;
    this.acres = acres;
  }
  public String pinLabel() { return name + " (" + acres + " acres)"; }
  public boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east) {
    return lat >= south && lat <= north && lng >= west && lng <= east;
  }
}
class BusStop implements Place {
  int route;
  double lat;
  double lng;
  BusStop(int route, double lat, double lng) {
    this.route = route;
    this.lat = lat;
    this.lng = lng;
  }
  public String pinLabel() { return "Bus " + route; }
  public boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east) {
    return lat >= south && lat <= north && lng >= west && lng <= east;
  }
}
void main() {
  Place[] places = {
    new Restaurant("Taco Shop", 32.8795, -117.2359, 4.5),
    new Park("Balboa Park", 32.7341, -117.1446, 1200),
    new BusStop(30, 32.8790, -117.2368),
  };
  double south = 32.86;
  double north = 32.90;
  double west = -117.25;
  double east = -117.22;
  for (Place p : places) {
    if (p.onScreen(south, north, west, east)) {
      System.out.println(p.pinLabel());
    }
  }
}
```

Output:

```text
Taco Shop (4.5 stars)
Bus 30
```

Student: Wow you weren’t kidding that it’s longer.

Prof: Well, we’re talking about some more substantial design questions, so our programs do need to grow a bit! What do you notice and wonder?

Student: Well, I notice that each of these classes `implements Place` – there is no inheritance yet, because I don’t see `extends`.

Prof: Good, good. Other things?

Student: I wonder what a Pin is.

Prof: Oh good question. That’s a word for a point on a virtual map. So like a little icon or shape that shows up. The example is meant to capture different kinds of places and the information they might show. For example, the restaurant has a star rating but the bus stop just names its bus route.

Student: I see. And I notice that classes are being used instead of records.

Prof: Right, `extends` only works with classes, and we’ll see how it does help us a bit here. There is something shared across all the classes: do you see it?

Student: Hmmm… I guess lat and lng are shared across all of them.

Prof: Right. And with what we have, can we do anything to avoid having all those copies of `lat` and `lng`?

Student: Can we put `lat` and `lng` in one class, and then extend it from all of these?

Prof: That’s right! So the base class might be like this, though we’d have one problem:

```java
class Location implements Place {
  double lat;
  double lng;
  Location(double lat, double lng) { this.lat = lat; this.lng = lng; }
  public boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east) {
    return lat >= south && lat <= north && lng >= west && lng <= east;
  }
}
// Then BusStop, Restaurant, etc can extend Location
```

Student: It says it implements `Place`, but has no `pinLabel`?

Prof: Yup. So we have to fill in some `pinLabel` if we want this to compile.

Student: What should it return?

Prof: It’s hard to say. At some point I’ll show you how to avoid having to choose, for now I’ll just fill something in:

```java
class Location implements Place {
  // ...
  public String pinLabel() { return "Unknown Location"; }
}
```

Student: OK, so then what do the other classes look like?

Prof: Well, they gain `extends` and lose their `lat`/`lng` fields. But we have to decide what to do in the constructor. There is a special keyword, `super(...)` that we’ll need to use. In a constructor it calls the **parent class constructor** with the given arguments. It lets us re-use the constructor from the class we inherited.

```java
interface Place {
  String pinLabel();
  boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east);
}
class Location implements Place {
  double lat;
  double lng;
  Location(double lat, double lng) {
    this.lat = lat;
    this.lng = lng;
  }
  public String pinLabel() { return "Unknown Location"; }
  public boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east) {
    return lat >= south && lat <= north && lng >= west && lng <= east;
  }
}
class Restaurant extends Location {
  String name;
  double stars;
  Restaurant(String name, double lat, double lng, double stars) {
    super(lat, lng);
    this.name = name;
    this.stars = stars;
  }
  @Override
  public String pinLabel() { return name + " (" + stars + " stars)"; }
}
class Park extends Location {
  String name;
  int acres;
  Park(String name, double lat, double lng, int acres) {
    super(lat, lng);
    this.name = name;
    this.acres = acres;
  }
  @Override
  public String pinLabel() { return name + " (" + acres + " acres)"; }
}
class BusStop extends Location {
  int route;
  BusStop(int route, double lat, double lng) {
    super(lat, lng);
    this.route = route;
  }
  @Override
  public String pinLabel() { return "Bus " + route; }
}
void main() {
  Place[] places = {
    new Restaurant("Taco Shop", 32.8795, -117.2359, 4.5),
    new Park("Balboa Park", 32.7341, -117.1446, 1200),
    new BusStop(30, 32.8790, -117.2368),
  };
  double south = 32.86;
  double north = 32.90;
  double west = -117.25;
  double east = -117.22;
  for (Place p : places) {
    if (p.onScreen(south, north, west, east)) {
      System.out.println(p.pinLabel());
    }
  }
}
```

Output:

```text
Taco Shop (4.5 stars)
Bus 30
```

Prof: So we’ve moved the idea of a location out of all these places, and made that be the job of `Location`, which can also have the correct implementation of `onScreen` shared by all the subclasses. Now each of the subclasses is solely responsible for the implementation of `pinLabel`.

Student: Interesting!

#### Practice

Exercise:

Here is a social media feed, already refactored so `Message` holds the `message` field that every post shares. `TextPost` and `Repost` are done. Fill in `VideoPost` the same way.

```java
interface Post {
  String preview();
  boolean mentions(String word);
}
class Message implements Post {
  String message;
  Message(String message) {
    this.message = message;
  }
  public String preview() { return message; }
  public boolean mentions(String word) { return message.contains(word); }
}
class TextPost extends Message {
  boolean edited;
  TextPost(String message, boolean edited) {
    super(message);
    this.edited = edited;
  }
  @Override
  public String preview() {
    if (edited) { return message + " (edited)"; }
    return message;
  }
}
class Repost extends Message {
  String from;
  Repost(String message, String from) {
    super(message);
    this.from = from;
  }
  @Override
  public String preview() { return "Reposted from " + from + ": " + message; }
}
class VideoPost ____ {
  int seconds;
  VideoPost(String message, int seconds) {
    ____
    this.seconds = seconds;
  }
  @Override
  public String preview() { return message + " [video, " + seconds + "s]"; }
}

Post[] feed = {
  new TextPost("Exam moved to Friday", true),
  new Repost("Free pizza in the CSE lobby", "tritons"),
  new VideoPost("My cat learns Java", 42),
};
String third = feed[2].preview();
boolean aboutCats = feed[2].mentions("cat");
```

## [Navigating Class Hierarchies](extending-classes/the-class-hierarchy.html)

Student: So can a class extend a class that extends another class?

Prof: Indeed.

Student: And can two classes extend the same class?

Prof: Yup.

Student: And can one class extend two other classes?

Prof: No! That’s actually an interesting case called **multiple inheritance**, which Java doesn’t support. I welcome you to look it up on your own, though.

Student: Hm. OK. How do you keep it all straight?

Prof: Class diagrams can help. We draw classes and interfaces with arrows between them. An arrow between two classes points from the subclass to the superclass. A dashed arrow points from a class to an implemented interface. We try to lay out the picture so `Object` goes on top, and all the arrows point up. Here’s an example using `Location`:

```java
interface Place { ... }
class Location implements Place { ... }
class Park extends Location { ... }
class BusStop extends Location { ... }
class Restaurant extends Location { ... }
```

```
Object
  toString()
  equals(Object o)
Location under Object, Place
  double lat
  double lng
  pinLabel()
  onScreen()
BusStop under Location
  int route
  ↑ pinLabel()
Restaurant under Location
  double stars
  ↑ pinLabel()
Park under Location
  int acres
  ↑ pinLabel()
Place (interface)
  pinLabel()
  onScreen()
```

Student: What’s the ↑?

Prof: That’s a marker for a method that is **overriding** a method on a superclass.

Student: Ah. Why isn’t `onScreen()` in the classes like `BusStop`?

Prof: They don’t have their own implementation: they inherit it from `Location`. So if you have an object of type `BusStop`, Java needs to look around in the class hierarchy to find the method for it.

Student: Oh interesting, so does the hierarchy go in a memory diagram?

Prof: Kind of. It’s fixed when we write the program, because we can’t change where an arrow points when the program is running. It sort of sits off to the side and helps us figure out method and field lookups.

## [Navigating the Class Hierarchy 2](extending-classes/instanceof.html)

Student: One thing I find really confusing is when we store a subclass object in a superclass variable. Is there any way to tell which type the object actually is?

Prof: There is in fact! Check it out, we can use it on our old friend, `Pict`:

```java
Pict c = new Circle(20, "red");
boolean isCircle = c instanceof Circle;
boolean isRectangle = c instanceof Rect;
```

Output:

```text
c = Circle[radius=20, color=red]
[image]
isCircle = true
isRectangle = false
```

Prof: So it tells us that `c` is in fact a `Circle`, and is **not** a `Rect`, from our program.

Student: Huh, that’s interesting. What would `c instanceof Pict` say?

Prof: Let’s try a few more:

```java
Pict r = new Rect(20, 40, "red");
boolean isCircle = r instanceof Circle;
boolean isRectangle = r instanceof Rect;
boolean isPict = r instanceof Pict;
```

Output:

```text
r = Rect[width=20, height=40, color=red]
[image]
isCircle = false
isRectangle = true
isPict = true
```

Student: Huh, interesting. So does it work for `extends`, too?

Prof: Indeed!

```java
interface Place {}
class Location implements Place {}
class BusStop extends Location {}
class Restaurant extends Location {}
Place b = new BusStop();
boolean isPlace = b instanceof Place;
boolean isLocation = b instanceof Location;
```

Output:

```text
b = BusStop@aef
isPlace = true
isLocation = true
```

Student: OK, so how does that work? Does it like… search the class diagram?

Prof: Exactly. `a instanceof C` starts at the class of the object in `a`. If that isn’t `C`, it checks that class’s superclass and anything it implements, all the way up the diagram, looking for `C`. If `a instanceof C`, then the value stored in `a` could be stored in a variable of type `C`.

Student: Cool, where do I use that?

Prof: Honestly? Mostly you don’t.

Student: Mostly I don’t? What do you mean?

Prof: Well, most of the time we try to make our programs work out using the general interface types, like `Pict` or `Place`, for most variables. Then we just rely on the methods defined on them being present. Field lookups and class-specific work happen inside the class, and calling a method will select the class for the right object. So `instanceof` is honestly not needed much in well-written code.

Student: Hm… then why’d you show me?

Prof: Well, you’ll still see it in some places. And we need it to wrap up some of our discussion of `Object` and `equals`.

#### Practice

Location loc = new DogPark();
```

```

`p instanceof DogPark` is [false / true]
`p instanceof BusStop` is [false / true]
`loc instanceof Park` is [false / true]

## [Overriding equals and Casting to a Class](extending-classes/class-cast.html)

Student: Professor, the thing you showed me about `equals()` doesn’t work.

Prof: How do you mean?

Student: Well, I wanted to write some tests, like you suggested, and I tried using `assertEquals` with the class definition for `Point`.

```java
class Point {
  double x, y;
  Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  boolean equals(Point other) {
    return this.x == other.x && this.y == other.y;
  }
}

void main() {
  Point p1 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  Point p2 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  assertEquals(p1, p2);
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
Exception in thread "Thread-0" org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: expected: <Point@6ef> but was: <Point@6f0>
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.failNotEqual(Unknown Source)
	at org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals(Unknown Source)
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

Student: See, it fails! But if I make `Point` a record and get rid of `equals`, the assert passes.

Prof: Ah I see. Yeah this is a pretty subtle point! Here’s what’s going on. The default `equals()` on `Object` looks like this:

```java
public boolean equals(Object other)
```

See the issue?

Student: No…

Prof: Let’s try two things. First, add an `@Override` on your `equals` method for `Point`.

Student: OK…

```java
class Point {
  double x, y;
  Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  @Override
  boolean equals(Point other) {
    return this.x == other.x && this.y == other.y;
  }
}

void main() {
  Point p1 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  Point p2 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  assertEquals(p1, p2);
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 8: error: The method equals(Point) of type Point must override or implement a supertype method
```

Student: Huh. It fails now. But I **am** overriding `equals`.

Prof: So this is where it’s a little tricky, and we need to be precise. We override a method not just by name, but by **type**. So let’s put the two methods right next to each other:

```java
public boolean equals(Object other) // the one in Java's Object
public boolean equals(Point other)  // the one in your Point class
```

Student: So… how do I fix it? Do I have to write the `Object` version? OK, I can change the signature…

```java
class Point {
  double x, y;
  Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  @Override
  public boolean equals(Object other) {
    return this.x == other.x && this.y == other.y;
  }
}

void main() {
  Point p1 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  Point p2 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  assertEquals(p1, p2);
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 9: error: x cannot be resolved or is not a field
line 9: error: y cannot be resolved or is not a field
```

Student: Huh? It doesn’t work now

Prof: Right – since that parameter is type `Object`, Java can’t prove that it has `x` and `y` fields. You could call `new Point(4.0, 5.0).equals("a string")`, for example, and the string certainly doesn’t have those fields.

Student: Ugh, OK. Oh wait! I can use `instanceof`! Because I just want to do the x and y checks if I know it’s a `Point`!

```java
class Point {
  double x, y;
  Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  @Override
  public boolean equals(Object other) {
    if(!(other instanceof Point)) { return false; }
    return this.x == other.x && this.y == other.y;
  }
}

void main() {
  Point p1 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  Point p2 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  assertEquals(p1, p2);
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 10: error: x cannot be resolved or is not a field
line 10: error: y cannot be resolved or is not a field
```

Student: Ugh what’s wrong?

Prof: Wow, nice job. I just need to give you one more step. This is something that comes up in programming a lot – even though something is obvious to **us**, the programmer, it is not obvious to the **programming language**. Here **you** know that `other` must be a `Point` after the `if`. But Java doesn’t!

Student: Well that’s silly.

Prof: I know. But it’s actually a pretty common scenario. Here we need to tell Java “trust me, it’s a `Point`”. We can do that with a class cast. We write `(C)o` for some class `C` and value `o`. Java will make sure `o instanceof C`, and if it is, it will let us treat `o` as a `C`. If it’s not, that’s an error (a `ClassCastException`). So you could do that with `other` and `Point`.

Student: So like… where? Like after the if?

Prof: That’s the right spot, because it’s where you **know** you have a `Point`, and not some other subclass of `Object` like `String` or `Location`.

Student: Here goes…

```java
class Point {
  double x, y;
  Point(double x, double y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  @Override
  public boolean equals(Object other) {
    if(!(other instanceof Point)) { return false; }
    Point p = (Point)other;
    return this.x == p.x && this.y == p.y;
  }
}

void main() {
  Point p1 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  Point p2 = new Point(4.0, 5.0);
  assertEquals(p1, p2);
}
```

Student: Hey, that works!

Prof: Right – this also helps fully explain what was going on in the `equals` for `Raster`. This is a super common pattern: do the `instanceof` check, do the cast, and then do the checks.

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object other) {
    if (this == other) return true;
    if (!(other instanceof Raster r)) return false;
    if (this.width() != r.width() || this.height() != r.height()) return false;
    for (int y = 0; y < this.height(); y++) {
        if (!Arrays.equals(this.pixels[y], r.pixels[y])) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 476–485](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L476-L485)

Student: But that has one more line, with `==` at the top.

Prof: Right, so if two objects are reference equal, they are certainly `.equals()`, so that check is also at the top of most `equals()` methods. You could add it to yours!

Student: Thanks, I will

}

# Abstract Classes and Mutation

## [Default Implementations vs. Abstract Methods](abstract-classes-and-mutation/abstract-classes.html)

Student: There’s something bothering me. In the `Location` example we talked about before, the location class had that method that returned `Unknown Location`, and then all the other classes overrode it. It looked like this:

```java
  public String pinLabel() { return "Unknown Location"; }
```

Prof: Right. All the subclasses had a `pinLabel` method with `@Override` to give their own behavior.

Student: Well, isn’t it weird that we have this code, but it’s not going to be used ever?

Prof: Well, what if we made a `Location` directly?

Student: I guess, but in all the examples we only made subclasses. Like we never used `new Location` as a constructor. So it seems just silly that it even **has** this method.

Prof: That’s an interesting observation! So you are wondering if we could just leave it out, because it gets implemented on all the subclasses? What happens if we do? That’s pretty testable. Here was the setup:

```java
interface Place {
  String pinLabel();
  boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east);
}
class Location implements Place {
  double lat;
  double lng;
  Location(double lat, double lng) {
    this.lat = lat;
    this.lng = lng;
  }
  // REMOVED: public String pinLabel() { return "Unknown Location"; }
  public boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east) {
    return lat >= south && lat <= north && lng >= west && lng <= east;
  }
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 5: error: The type Location must implement the inherited abstract method Place.pinLabel()
```

Student: Yeah, so it says it has to be there, because `Location` implements `Place`.

Prof: This is a great observation. What would help here is a special kind of class – a class that is not meant for **creating on its own**, but is meant for describing some fields and methods shared across many classes, and then some methods that need to be implemented by subclasses. Does that sound right?

Student: Yeah, that’s right

Prof: This is called an abstract class or an abstract base class. Here’s what it looks like:

```java
interface Place {
  String pinLabel();
  boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east);
}
abstract class Location implements Place {
  double lat;
  double lng;
  Location(double lat, double lng) {
    this.lat = lat;
    this.lng = lng;
  }
  public abstract String pinLabel();
  public boolean onScreen(double south, double north, double west, double east) {
    return lat >= south && lat <= north && lng >= west && lng <= east;
  }
}
```

Prof: There are a few interesting consequences of this. First, `Location` being `abstract` means it’s a compile error to use `new Location`.

Student: Really? A compile error? Then why have the constructor at all?

Prof: You can still call the constructor using `super` from a subclass, so the code there is still relevant.

Student: Hmm OK I get it. And so then the `abstract` method doesn’t have a body?

Prof: Yes, in that way it’s very similar to an interface. Actually, in this case since `Location` declares that it implements `Place`, you could leave off the `abstract` method definition entirely, and it’d still compile and mean the same thing.

Student: How does that work?

Prof: Java figures it out – since `pinLabel` is part of the interface, that means any class that `extends Location` must implement it as well. So it counts the same as an `abstract` method.

Student: Huh, interesting.

#### Practice

Exercise:

Here are social media posts with an abstract base class. `Message` holds the fields every post shares and a `snippet` method they all use; each subclass gives its own `preview`. Write the body of each subclass constructor.

```java
interface Post {
  String preview();
  String snippet();
}
abstract class Message implements Post {
  String username;
  String message;
  int likes;
  Message(String username, String message, int likes) {
    this.username = username;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = likes;
  }
  public abstract String preview();
  public String snippet() {
    if (message.length() <= 10) { return "@" + username + ": " + message; }
    return "@" + username + ": " + message.substring(0, 10) + "...";
  }
}
class TextPost extends Message {
  boolean edited;
  TextPost(String username, String message, int likes, boolean edited) {
    ____
  }
  public String preview() {
    String text = "@" + username + ": " + message;
    if (edited) { text = text + " (edited)"; }
    return text + " | " + likes + " likes";
  }
}
class Repost extends Message {
  String from;
  Repost(String username, String message, int likes, String from) {
    ____
  }
  public String preview() {
    return "@" + username + " reposted @" + from + ": " + message + " | " + likes + " likes";
  }
}
class VideoPost extends Message {
  int seconds;
  VideoPost(String username, String message, int likes, int seconds) {
    ____
  }
  public String preview() {
    return "@" + username + ": " + message + " [video, " + seconds + "s] | " + likes + " likes";
  }
}

Post[] feed = {
  new TextPost("cse11", "Exam moved to Friday", 12, true),
  new Repost("ana", "Free pizza in the CSE lobby", 40, "tritons"),
  new VideoPost("ben", "My cat learns Java", 7, 42),

String[] previews = { feed[0].preview(), feed[1].preview(), feed[2].preview() };

```

## [Dynamic Dispatch](abstract-classes-and-mutation/dynamic-dispatch.html)

Student: I’m starting to kind of understand something that’s happening here, but I want to talk through it.

Prof: Go for it.

Student: So in Pict.java, there’s this part of the `render` method that calls `draw`:

```java
interface Pict {
    // ...
    default Raster render() {
        // ...
        var g = img.createGraphics();
        // ...
        draw(g, 0, 0);
        // ...
    }
```

[`Pict.java`, lines 30–45](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/blob/fa26/Pict.java#L30-L45)

Student: And I’m trying to figure out how Java knows which `draw` method to call. Because `render` is written inside the `Pict` interface, so how does Java know whether it is calling `draw` on a `Circle` or a `Rectangle` or a `Beside` or whatever? There’s nothing in the `Pict` interface that can know.

Prof: Oh that’s a terrific question. We can answer it with a pretty small memory diagram.

```java
Pict r = new Rect(10, 20, "blue");
Pict c = new Circle(50, "green");
Raster rPix = r.render();
Raster cPix = c.render();
```

Output:

```text
r = Rect[width=10, height=20, color=blue]
[image]
c = Circle[radius=50, color=green]
[image]
rPix = Raster[10x20]
[image]
cPix = Raster[100x100]
[image]
```

Prof: Let’s think about the memory diagram at the moment `draw` is called from the first `render` call:

```
Names (the stack)
  draw(g, 0, 0) on @1001
    g = @1004
    x = 0
    y = 0
  r.render() on @1001
    img = @1003
    g = @1004
  top level
    r = @1001
    c = @1002
Heap
  @1001: Rect[width=10, height=20, color=blue]
  @1002: Circle[radius=50, color=green]
  @1003: BufferedImage
  @1004: Graphics2D
```

Prof: The key thing here is the instance referred to by `this`, which is the receiver of `render`. What class is that instance from?

Student: `Rect`, right? But the type of the variable `r` was `Pict`.

Prof: And that’s the key point – Java uses **the class of the instance** to find the method. Not the type you wrote down in the program. The name of the class used with `new` to construct the object is where Java starts its search for the method.

Student: So then the second time, the receiver (or `this`) would be referring to `@1002`, so it would find the `Circle` one?

Prof: Correct.

Student: Wait so how does it find `render()`? That’s not on the `Circle` or `Rectangle` class.

Prof: Java stores the class and interface hierarchy. If it can’t find the method on the class, it looks at its parent class or `implements` arrows to search for the implementation. There **must** be an implementation if the program compiled; that’s what all the compile checks are for.

```
Rect under Pict
  int width
  int height
  Color color
  width()
  height()
  draw(Graphics2D g, int x, int y)
Circle under Pict
  int radius
  Color color
  width()
  height()
  draw(Graphics2D g, int x, int y)
Pict (interface)
  width()
  height()
  render()
  draw(Graphics2D g, int x, int y)
```

Student: OK, so if we had a `render` in `Circle` it would have used that one instead?

Prof: That’s exactly right, and you’ve just reconstructed overriding!

Student: Oh, I guess so.

Prof: There’s a name for this: dynamic dispatch. This is a defining feature of object-oriented programming. The class of the object, not the type of the variable, is used to determine which method to call. That makes it so one line in the program, like the call to `draw()` in `render()`, can actually call many **different** methods in one run of a program, depending on the receiver’s class.

Student: So that’s object-oriented programming?

Prof: Yes, I’d say a program that relies on dynamic dispatch is very much written in an object-oriented style.

#### Practice

Exercise:

Using these classes, whose method body runs for each call?

```java
interface Post {
  String preview();
  default String badge() { return ""; }
  default String share() { return "Check this out: " + preview(); }
}
class TextPost implements Post {
  String message;
  TextPost(String message) { this.message = message; }
  public String preview() { return message + badge(); }
}
class PinnedPost extends TextPost {
  PinnedPost(String message) { super(message); }
  @Override
  public String badge() { return " [pinned]"; }
}

Post t = new TextPost("Free pizza in the CSE lobby");
Post p = new PinnedPost("Exam moved to Friday");
```

`t.badge()` runs the one in [Post / TextPost / PinnedPost]
`p.badge()` runs the one in [Post / TextPost / PinnedPost]
`p.preview()` runs the one in [Post / TextPost / PinnedPost]
`p.share()` runs the one in [Post / TextPost / PinnedPost]
`t.share()` returns ____
`p.share()` returns ____

## [Liking a Post](abstract-classes-and-mutation/likes.html)

Student: I tried something, and I’m not sure I get what happened.

Prof: I’m all ears.

Student: I was thinking about how to represent an Instagram post. It has a user, and text, and images, but also you can like it. And that makes a counter go up that everyone can see. So I tried writing a class for a post like that

```java
class Post {
  String user;
  String message;
  int likes;
  Post(String user, String message, int likes) {
    this.user = user;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = likes;
  }
  String summary() {
    return "@" + user + ": " + message + " | ❤️" + likes;
  }
  void like() {
    this.likes = likes + 1;
  }
}
void main() {
  Post p1 = new Post("joe", "CSE-PACE next Tuesday!", 22);
  System.out.println(p1.summary());
  p1.like();
  System.out.println(p1.summary());
}
```

Output:

```text
@joe: CSE-PACE next Tuesday! | ❤️22
@joe: CSE-PACE next Tuesday! | ❤️23
```

Student: Did I do that right? Am I allowed to write that?

Prof: For sure! Why were you worried you might not have?

Student: Well, we haven’t written the `this.likes =` lines outside of a constructor before. And a record won’t let us do it.

Prof: What do you mean a record won’t let you?

Student: Well, look:

```java
record Post(String user, String message, int likes) {
  String summary() {
    return "@" + user + ": " + message + " | ❤️" + likes;
  }
  void like() {
    this.likes = likes + 1;
  }
}
void main() {
  Post p1 = new Post("joe", "CSE-PACE next Tuesday!", 22);
  System.out.println(p1.summary());
  p1.like();
  System.out.println(p1.summary());
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 6: error: The final field Post.likes cannot be assigned
```

Student: It says the `final` field cannot be assigned?

Prof: Right, so that’s one more modifier to learn about. `final` on a field says that it cannot be updated **outside of the constructor**. All the fields of a `record` are implicitly `final`. But you can get the same error message with a class:

```java
class C {
  final int x;
  C() {
    this.x = 10;
  }
  void tryToChangeMe() {
    this.x = 1;
  }
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 7: error: The final field C.x cannot be assigned
```

Prof: What you’re seeing in your program is actually the **default** for classes: fields are mutable unless we ask them to be immutable with `final`. The field update statement `this.x = v;` will only work on non-final fields.

Student: Is there any way to do field update on a record field, then?

Prof: No. You could say that’s a reason to not… `like()` records.

Student: …

Prof: Get it?

Student: … Yes.

Prof: Anyway, I think your program is great. It captures the idea of using a field update to model the likes of a post, and that’s something that can **only** be done with a `class`, not with a `record`.

Student: And you can still assign `final` fields inside the constructor, though?

Prof: Correct. Otherwise there would be no way to initialize those values. So Java simply will error if you write field updates in other places, but allows it in constructors.

#### Practice

This `Post` keeps its hashtags in an array, and `retag` swaps in a new one:

```java
class Post {
  String user;
  String message;
  String[] tags;
  Post(String user, String message, String[] tags) {
    this.user = user;
    this.message = message;
    this.tags = tags;
  }
  void retag(String[] newTags) {
    this.tags = newTags;
  }
}
String[] a = {"cse11", "java"};
String[] b = {"pizza"};
Post p = new Post("joe", "Free pizza in the CSE lobby", a);
void main() {
  p.retag(b);
}
```

Here is memory just as `retag` starts, before its field update runs:

```
Names (the stack)
  p.retag(b) on @1003
    newTags = @1002
  main()
  top level
    a = @1001
    b = @1002
    p = @1003
Heap
  @1001: [cse11, java]
  @1002: [pizza]
  @1003: Post[user=joe, message=Free pizza in the CSE lobby, tags=@1001]
```

the `tags` field of `@1003` holds [@1002 / @1003 / @1001]

## [Sharing vs. Copying](abstract-classes-and-mutation/sharing-vs-copying.html)

Student: I have a question – when I make a repost on Instagram, does it make a copy of the post or does it store something more like a reference?

Prof: More like a reference. It probably stores something like a “post id number” of the original post. Why do you ask?

Student: Well I was thinking about how that would look in Java.

Prof: Oh that’s a good question. They’d look pretty different, here’s how I’d think of them:

```java
class Post {
  String user;
  String message;
  int likes;
  Post(String user, String message, int likes) {
    this.user = user;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = likes;
  }
  String summary() {
    return "@" + user + ": " + message + " | ❤️" + likes;
  }
  void like() {
    this.likes = likes + 1;
  }
  RepostCopy repostCopy(String reposter) {
    return new RepostCopy(reposter, user, message, likes);
  }
  RepostRef repostRef(String reposter) {
    return new RepostRef(reposter, this);
  }
}

class RepostCopy {
  String user;
  String originalUser;
  String message;
  int likes;
  RepostCopy(String user, String originalUser, String message, int likes) {
    this.user = user;
    this.originalUser = originalUser;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = likes;
  }
}
class RepostRef {
  String user;
  Post original;
  RepostRef(String user, Post original) {
    this.user = user;
    this.original = original;
  }
  void like() {
    original.like();
  }
}
void main() {
  Post p = new Post("joe", "CSE-PACE next Tuesday!", 22);
  RepostCopy copy = p.repostCopy("ana");
  RepostRef ref = p.repostRef("ben");
  p.like();
  p.like();
  System.out.println(p.summary());
  System.out.println("copy has " + copy.likes + " likes");
  System.out.println("ref has " + ref.original.likes + " likes");
}
```

Output:

```text
@joe: CSE-PACE next Tuesday! | ❤️24
copy has 22 likes
ref has 24 likes
```

Prof: What are some things you notice and wonder about here?

Student: Well, the printed out likes are different for the last three lines.

Prof: Which one **didn’t** change, the copy or the reference?

Student: Um, the copy didn’t change. Oh, interesting. Because it made a new object with its own `likes` field?

Prof: Right. If we look at the memory diagram when we call `p.like()`, we can see that we’re updating a reference that is **aliased** with the `RepostRef` object but not with the `RepostCopy` object. So the change doesn’t show up when we look at the `RepostCopy`

```
Names (the stack)
  p.like() on @1001
  main()
    p = @1001
    copy = @1002
    ref = @1003
  top level
Heap
  @1001: Post[user=joe, message=CSE-PACE next Tuesday!, likes=22 23]
  @1002: RepostCopy[user=ana, originalUser=joe, message=CSE-PACE next Tuesday!, likes=22]
  @1003: RepostRef[user=ben, original=@1001]
```

Student: I see! So that really is like there is **one** orginal post, if we use the ref. And when you like a repost, it likes the original.

Prof: Right, and that’s why resharing ought to have a reference to the original, not a copy of its contents.

    return new RepostCopy(reposter, user, message, tags);
  }
  RepostRef repostRef(String reposter) {
    return new RepostRef(reposter, this);
  }
}
class RepostCopy {
  String user;
  String originalUser;
  String message;
  String[] tags;
  RepostCopy(String user, String originalUser, String message, String[] tags) {
    this.user = user;
    this.originalUser = originalUser;
    this.message = message;
    this.tags = tags;
  }
}
class RepostRef {
  String user;
  Post original;
  RepostRef(String user, Post original) {
    this.user = user;
    this.original = original;
  }
}
String[] a = {"cse11", "java"};
String[] b = {"pizza"};

# Collections and Generics

## [ArrayList Intro](collections-and-generics/arraylist-intro.html)

Student: Professor, something has been annoying me about arrays. Sometimes when making an array, I don’t yet know how many elements I would like to store in it. Should I just make the array be really long? That seems like it would be a waste of space.

Prof: You’re right, creating a really long empty array is a bad idea in many cases. That is a limit of arrays: whenever we want to make an array longer, we have to make a whole new array and copy all the data over. That is pretty annoying. Here, let me introduce you to a class that Java provides to us to help with this issue. Java provides us with collections, data structures for storing a collection of objects. One of these collections is `ArrayList`.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();
void main() {
  names.add("Ada");
  names.add("Grace");
  names.add("Alan");
}
```

Output:

```text
names = [Ada, Grace, Alan]
```

Prof: What do you notice from this code?

Student: You are creating a new `ArrayList` object.

Prof: Correct. Based on the definition, what type of data is this ArrayList called `names` storing?

Student: It looks like `String`, but it’s using notation we haven’t talked about before, it has `String` inside of arrows?

Prof: We will go over the specifics of that notation later, for now you are correct that it is storing elements of type `String`.

Student: Ok, and then after that we are adding names to the `ArrayList names`.

Prof: Notice that `add()` is a method. We can’t use `names[index] = "Ada"`, that isn’t valid code. When we use `add()`, it appends the element to the end of our `ArrayList`.

Student: And whenever we append a new element, that means that the `ArrayList` is now one element longer. So can I use `names.length` like I do with arrays?

Prof: It’s different with `ArrayList`, you instead check using a method called `size()`. You also access elements with a method as well: `get()`, which allows you to fetch an element at a specific index, similar to an array.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();
String first;
int count;
void main() {
  names.add("Ada");
  names.add("Grace");
  names.add("Alan");

  first = names.get(0);
  count = names.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
names = [Ada, Grace, Alan]
first = Ada
count = 3
```

Student: But what if I don’t want to add an element at the end? Or what if I want to replace one of the names in the list?

Prof: There are other methods you can use, such as `add(index, value)` and `set(index, value)`. And you can use `remove(index)` to get rid of elements as well.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();
String removed;
int count;
String all;
void main() {
  names.add("Ada");
  names.add("Grace");
  names.add("Alan");

  names.add(1, "Edsger");
  removed = names.remove(0);
  names.set(0, "Margaret");
  count = names.size();
  all = names.toString();
}
```

Output:

```text
names = [Margaret, Grace, Alan]
removed = Ada
count = 3
all = [Margaret, Grace, Alan]
```

Prof: When you remove an element at index 0, and don’t replace it, what would you get if you tried to use `get(0)`?

Student: Well that index would be empty, so it wouldn’t contain a `String` object. In that case it must be `null`!

Prof: That’s a good guess if this were an array, but an `ArrayList` never leaves a gap. When you `remove` an element, everything after it shifts down one index to close the gap, and `size()` goes down by one. So `get(0)` gives you the element that used to be at index 1. Likewise, `add(index, value)` shifts the later elements up to make room.

Prof: Now `ArrayList` also comes with some other helpful methods. One of the most useful is `contains()`, which tells you whether or not the `ArrayList` contains a certain element. Since duplicate values are allowed in an `ArrayList`, all it tells you is that the element is in the ArrayList at least once.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();
boolean hasAda;
boolean hasLinus;
int count;
void main() {
  names.add("Ada");
  names.add("Ada");

  hasAda = names.contains("Ada");
  hasLinus = names.contains("Linus");
  count = names.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
names = [Ada, Ada]
hasAda = true
hasLinus = false
count = 2
```

Student: Hey Professor? I just tried to make an ArrayList of type int, but it doesn’t seem to be working.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<int> nums = new ArrayList<int>();
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 3: error: Syntax error, insert "Dimensions" to complete ReferenceType
line 3: error: Syntax error, insert "Dimensions" to complete ReferenceType
```

Prof: Collections in Java, such as an ArrayList, can only store objects. You can’t put primitives in a collection.

Student: But what if I want to store a list of whole numbers?

Prof: You can still do that, Java has a version for each primitive that is an object instead. For `int` you can instead use `Integer`, and Java turns an `int` like `3` into an `Integer` for you when you `add` it. Try re-writing your code with that instead.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>();
int total;
void main() {
  nums.add(3);
  nums.add(10);
  nums.add(3);
  total = nums.get(0) + nums.get(1);
}
```

Output:

```text
nums = [3, 10, 3]
total = 13
```

Prof: There you go. Remember that `ArrayList` is ordered like standard arrays, and that the first element is index 0. But unlike an array their size can be changed when using `add()` and `remove()`. From here, we will talk about some other types of collections in Java that are less like arrays.

  names.add("Ada");
  names.add("Alan");
  ____
  ____
  int count = ____;
  System.out.println(names);
  System.out.println(count);
}
```

## [HashSet Introduction](collections-and-generics/hashset-intro.html)

Prof: Can you think of any situation where you wouldn’t want duplicates in a collection? Where you only care whether an element is present at least once?

Student: Maybe a list of all the CSE courses at UC San Diego? A course can’t be in the catalog twice.

Prof: Good example. Let’s use that to introduce another type of collection in Java, the `HashSet`.

```java
import java.util.HashSet;

HashSet<String> courses = new HashSet<String>();
int count;
String all;
void main() {
  courses.add("CSE 11");
  courses.add("CSE 12");
  courses.add("CSE 11");
  count = courses.size();
  all = courses.toString();
}
```

Output:

```text
courses = [CSE 12, CSE 11]
count = 2
all = [CSE 12, CSE 11]
```

Prof: What do you notice about the `count` and output from `toString`?

Student: Even though we added CSE 11 twice, it only shows up in the `HashSet` once.

Prof: Exactly. Unlike an `ArrayList`, `HashSet` can’t contain duplicate elements. Also, the `add()` method for `HashSet` returns whether or not the element could be added.

```java
import java.util.HashSet;

HashSet<String> courses = new HashSet<String>();
boolean first = courses.add("CSE 11");
boolean second = courses.add("CSE 11");
```

Output:

```text
courses = [CSE 11]
first = true
second = false
```

Student: So, when `courses` was empty, the first `add()` appended “CSE 11”, but the second time nothing changed and it returned false.

Prof: Almost, but I notice you said appended, but that isn’t really the right word. `HashSet` is unordered, so when an element is added it doesn’t necessarily get appended to the end.

Student: Am I able to use `contains()` like we did with `ArrayList`?

Prof: Yep. And `contains()` is usually why programmers choose to use a `HashSet`, since determining whether or not a `HashSet` contains a given value can be much faster than checking an array or `ArrayList`. We won’t go over the specifics in this class, but it is good to remember that the advantage of a `HashSet` is faster `contains()` and `remove()`.

Student: For `ArrayList`, `remove()` took an index as the argument. But you said that `HashSet` doesn’t have indexes?

Prof: Right, so for `remove()` the argument is instead the element you would like to remove.

```java
import java.util.HashSet;

HashSet<String> courses = new HashSet<String>();
boolean hasCse11;
boolean removed;
boolean removedAgain;
boolean stillHasCse11;
int count;
void main() {
  courses.add("CSE 11");
  courses.add("CSE 12");

  hasCse11 = courses.contains("CSE 11");
  removed = courses.remove("CSE 11");
  removedAgain = courses.remove("CSE 11");
  stillHasCse11 = courses.contains("CSE 11");
  count = courses.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
courses = [CSE 12]
hasCse11 = true
removed = true
removedAgain = false
stillHasCse11 = false
count = 1
```

Prof: How about you try creating a set of `Integer`, and then writing a for-each loop to sum all of the values in the `HashSet`. For-each loops work on `ArrayList` as well.

```java
import java.util.HashSet;

HashSet<Integer> scores = new HashSet<Integer>();
int total;
void main() {
  scores.add(90);
  scores.add(75);
  scores.add(90);
  scores.add(60);

  total = 0;
  for (int score : scores) {
    total += score;
  }
}
```

Output:

```text
scores = [90, 75, 60]
total = 225
```

Prof: Now here’s a question: What order did you sum the scores in?

Student: Well I assume it did 90 + 75 + 60, since that was the order I put them into the `HashSet`, and second time I tried to add 90 it was already in the set.

Prof: Not necessarily, because the set is unordered, we don’t know what order it did the summation. But in this case, addition doesn’t result in a different value when you change the order.

Prof: Here, look at this example. Now we are going to create a set of `Point`, what do you think the `size()` for points will return?

```java
import java.util.HashSet;

record Point(int x, int y) { }

HashSet<Point> points = new HashSet<Point>();
int count;
void main() {
  points.add(new Point(1, 2));
  points.add(new Point(1, 2));
  points.add(new Point(2, 1));
  count = points.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
points = [Point[x=1, y=2], Point[x=2, y=1]]
count = 2
```

Student: So `count` is 2. The two `new Point(1, 2)` are different objects, but the set only kept one of them.

Prof: Right. Two records with the same fields count as the same element, and so do two `String`s with the same text. That works for `String` and for records. For a class you write yourself, it takes more work to make a set treat two objects as the same, and we won’t get into that here.

Prof: Now that we have learned about both `ArrayList` and `HashSet`, here is a nice trick that uses both of them. If we create an `ArrayList`, we can add duplicate elements to it. Normally with an array, if I asked you to give me a new array with all the duplicates removed what would you have to do?

Student: I would probably create an empty array, then loop through the old one and add any that aren’t already in the new array. But then I would have to write another for-loop that checks if the new array already has that element…

Prof: Well, here’s the helpful trick: You can create a `HashSet` from an `ArrayList` like this.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashSet;

ArrayList<String> requests = new ArrayList<String>();
HashSet<String> distinct;
int total;
int offered;
void main() {
  requests.add("CSE 11");
  requests.add("CSE 12");
  requests.add("CSE 11");
  requests.add("MATH 18");
  requests.add("CSE 12");

  distinct = new HashSet<String>(requests);
  total = requests.size();
  offered = distinct.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
requests = [CSE 11, CSE 12, CSE 11, MATH 18, CSE 12]
distinct = [MATH 18, CSE 12, CSE 11]
total = 5
offered = 3
```

Student: Ok I see.

Prof: `HashSet` is an important tool to keep in your Java toolbox. Remember that while `ArrayList` is needed when the position in your list matters, `HashSet` is better for questions about whether or not an element is present.

#### Practice

Exercise:

The list below has repeats. Fill in the code that builds a `HashSet` from it, and then sets `offered` to the number of distinct names.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
