```java
  List.of("Ada", "Grace", "Ada", "Alan", "Grace", "Ada"));

HashSet<String> distinct = new HashSet<String>(____);
int total = names.size();
int offered = ____;
```

Exercise:

Once that program has run, what are the values of `total` and `offered`?

```java
total = ____
offered = ____
```

## [HashMap Introduction](collections-and-generics/hashmap-intro.html)

Student: So `ArrayList` lets me put things at specific positions, and `HashSet` ensures that there are no duplicates. But what if I wanted something different? Let’s say I was storing a bunch of students in a class, and some of them have the same first name. I can’t use a `HashSet` because then there would be no way to have two students with the same name, and an `ArrayList` would have no way to distinguish between the students.

Prof: Hmm, that is a real problem. In practice, when you turn in an assignment what do you put on your submission so that we can tell students with the same name apart?

Student: My student ID number? That’s unique. But if I created a `HashSet` of student ID numbers, how would I be able to know which name corresponds to which ID?

Prof: Java has a data structure that is perfect for this: `HashMap`. It stores data as key-value pairs. Here is your student example written out as a `HashMap`. What do you notice?

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<Integer, String> directory = new HashMap<Integer, String>();
String name;
int count;
String all;
void main() {
  directory.put(12345, "Ricardo");
  directory.put(67890, "Navya");
  directory.put(13579, "Sofia");

  name = directory.get(67890);
  count = directory.size();
  all = directory.toString();
}
```

Output:

```text
directory = {67890=Navya, 12345=Ricardo, 13579=Sofia}
name = Navya
count = 3
all = {67890=Navya, 12345=Ricardo, 13579=Sofia}
```

Student: So when we define a HashMap, we give two different types inside the angle brackets. And then instead of using `add()`, we use `put()` and are passing in two values for each element?

Prof: Yes, in this example the `Integer` student ID is the key, while the `String` student name is the value.

Student: What would happen if I put the same student ID number twice? Would it be ignored, like adding a duplicate to a `HashSet`?

Prof: Not quite. The keys are unique, just like the elements of a `HashSet`, but a second `put` with the same key replaces the old value instead of being ignored. The values are not unique, though. This is important for our student directory example, as we want to be able to support multiple students with the same name.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<Integer, String> directory = new HashMap<Integer, String>();
String before;
String fresh;
String current;
int count;
void main() {
  directory.put(12345, "Ricardo");
  directory.put(67890, "Navya");

  before = directory.put(12345, "Maitrayee");
  fresh = directory.put(24680, "Maitrayee");
  current = directory.get(12345);
  count = directory.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
directory = {67890=Navya, 24680=Maitrayee, 12345=Maitrayee}
before = Ricardo
fresh = null
current = Maitrayee
count = 3
```

Prof: Notice what `put()` returns when you already have a value at that key?

Student: It returns the old value, and replaces it in the `HashMap` with the new one. But when there wasn’t a value there yet, it returns `null`. And you also used a method we have seen before, `get()`. You passed in the key and it returned the value.

Prof: Yep, `HashMap` is designed for you to fetch a value using a key.

Student: What if you try to fetch a value from a key that doesn’t exist? Will it give you an error?

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<Integer, String> directory = new HashMap<Integer, String>();
String missing;
void main() {
  directory.put(12345, "Ricardo");
  directory.put(67890, "Navya");

  missing = directory.get(11111);
}
```

Output:

```text
directory = {67890=Navya, 12345=Ricardo}
missing = null
```

Student: Ah so it’s `null`.

Prof: A `null` value can be problematic for your program, so it’s a good idea to check if a key exists before attempting to fetch and use a value. `HashMap` provides a method for this called `containsKey()`. And just like `ArrayList` and `HashSet` you can remove elements. `remove()` takes the key and removes both the key and the value.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<Integer, String> directory = new HashMap<Integer, String>();
boolean hasRicardo;
boolean hasNobody;
String removed;
String removedAgain;
int count;
void main() {
  directory.put(12345, "Ricardo");
  directory.put(67890, "Navya");

  hasRicardo = directory.containsKey(12345);
  hasNobody = directory.containsKey(11111);

  removed = directory.remove(12345);
  removedAgain = directory.remove(12345);
  count = directory.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
directory = {67890=Navya}
hasRicardo = true
hasNobody = false
removed = Ricardo
removedAgain = null
count = 1
```

Student: Hey Professor, I made a `HashMap` of how many points each student has, and asked for a student I haven’t added yet. But, my program crashed! Do I need to use the `containsKey` here? Or is there a better way to deal with this problem?

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<String, Integer> points = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
int adaPoints;
int linusPoints;
void main() {
  points.put("Ada", 90);

  adaPoints = points.get("Ada");
  linusPoints = points.get("Linus");
}
```

Output (failed):

```text
Exception in thread "Thread-0" java.lang.NullPointerException
	at main(Unknown Source)
```

Prof: For situations like this, there is a special kind of get method. You can use `getOrDefault()` which takes a second argument representing the default value to use if the `HashMap` doesn’t contain that key.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<String, Integer> points = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
int adaPoints;
int linusPoints;
void main() {
  points.put("Ada", 90);

  adaPoints = points.getOrDefault("Ada", 0);
  linusPoints = points.getOrDefault("Linus", 0);
}
```

Output:

```text
points = {Ada=90}
adaPoints = 90
linusPoints = 0
```

Student: What if I want to use a for-each loop? If I try to write it like this there is an error.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<String, Integer> points = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
int total;
void main() {
  points.put("Ada", 90);
  points.put("Grace", 75);

  total = 0;
  for (int p : points) {
    total += p;
  }
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 10: error: Can only iterate over an array or an instance of java.lang.Iterable
```

Prof: Think about this: when you are looping through `points`, and setting `int p` to be each element, how are we supposed to know whether you want `int p` to be the key or the value?

Student: Well obviously I want it to be the value. The value is the one that is an `Integer`.

Prof: We need to specify whether you are trying to loop through the keys or the values. Let’s start with an example of the keys. We can use `points.keySet()` to tell Java that we want to loop through the set of all keys in the `HashMap`.

Student: Ok, but what if I want to loop through all the point values?

Prof: You can use `points.values()`. Remember that just like `HashSet`, there isn’t a set order. This is fine in this case for summation.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<String, Integer> points = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
int total;
int sameTotal;
void main() {
  points.put("Ada", 90);
  points.put("Grace", 75);
  points.put("Alan", 60);

  total = 0;
  for (String student : points.keySet()) {
    total += points.get(student);
  }

  sameTotal = 0;
  for (int p : points.values()) {
    sameTotal += p;
  }
}
```

Output:

```text
points = {Grace=75, Alan=60, Ada=90}
total = 225
sameTotal = 225
```

Prof: Based on what we have talked about, try writing code that checks how many times each word appears in an array. I’ll give you a `String[]` array to start off with, try to use a `HashMap`.

Student: Ok, to count the number of times a word appears, I would need to loop through the list and add 1 to the total for each appearance. So the keys should be the word, because that is unique, and the values should be the count. At the beginning the `HashMap` is empty, and whenever a word appears, I either add it to the `HashMap` if it is new, or increment the value by 1.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

String[] words = {"to", "be", "or", "not", "to", "be"};

HashMap<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
int toCount;
int distinct;
void main() {
  for (String w : words) {
    counts.put(w, counts.getOrDefault(w, 0) + 1);
  }

  toCount = counts.get("to");
  distinct = counts.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
words = [to, be, or, not, to, be]
counts = {not=1, be=2, or=1, to=2}
toCount = 2
distinct = 4
```

Prof: There you go. Now that we have seen all three, here is how to choose between them. Use an `ArrayList` when the position of your elements matters, or when you need to allow duplicates. Use a `HashSet` when you only care whether or not an element is present, and you don’t want duplicates. Use a `HashMap` when you want to look up a value using a key, like finding a student’s name from their ID. Keys are unique, but the values can be duplicates. Both `HashSet` and `HashMap` are unordered, and their advantage is fast lookups, so ask yourself what question your program is really asking.

Student: So how would I use one of these in a real program, like with the `Post` class from before?

Prof: Let’s look at that next.

#### Practice

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
void main() {
  stock.put("apple", 3);
  stock.put("pear", 5);
  ____
  ____
  int apples = ____;
  System.out.println(apples);
  System.out.println(stock.size());
}
```

## [Using ArrayList with Post](collections-and-generics/arraylist-use-case.html)

Student: Ok Professor, I think I’m ready to use an `ArrayList` in my own programs.

Prof: Sure, let’s go back to an example we have gone over before. We made a `Post` class.

```java
class Post {
  String user;
  String message;
  int likes;

  Post(String user, String message) {
    this.user = user;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = 0;
  }

  void like() {
    this.likes = this.likes + 1;
  }
}

Post original = new Post("joe", "CSE-PACE next Tuesday!");
int likes;
void main() {
  original.like();
  likes = original.likes;
}
```

Output:

```text
original = Post@737
likes = 1
```

Prof: Imagine we wanted to support replies on our posts. How would you go about implementing replies to a post using an `ArrayList`?

Student: I should have every `Post` contain an `ArrayList` of replies, and the type should be other posts, so I’ll use an `ArrayList<Post>`.

Prof: Good idea. You should also include a reference to the `Post` it’s replying to, since each reply is also a `Post`.

Student: Ok, I understand.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

class Post {
  String user;
  String message;
  int likes;
  ArrayList<Post> replies;
  Post replyTo;

  Post(String user, String message) {
    this.user = user;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = 0;
    this.replies = new ArrayList<Post>();
    this.replyTo = null;
  }

  void like() {
    this.likes = this.likes + 1;
  }
}

Post original = new Post("joe", "CSE-PACE next Tuesday!");
int count;
void main() {
  count = original.replies.size();
}
```

Output:

```text
original = Post@8ca
count = 0
```

Student: Ok now I am going to add a `reply()` method. It needs to make a `new Post()` and set `replyTo` to be the original `Post`. And then add this new reply to the `ArrayList`.

Prof: Implement that method. After you run it, let’s take a moment to think through what it actually builds in memory.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

class Post {
  String user;
  String message;
  int likes;
  ArrayList<Post> replies;
  Post replyTo;

  Post(String user, String message) {
    this.user = user;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = 0;
    this.replies = new ArrayList<Post>();
    this.replyTo = null;
  }

  void like() {
    this.likes = this.likes + 1;
  }

  Post reply(String user, String message) {
    Post r = new Post(user, message);
    r.replyTo = this;
    this.replies.add(r);
    return r;
  }
}

Post original = new Post("joe", "CSE-PACE next Tuesday!");
int count;
String backUser;
void main() {
  Post r = original.reply("ada", "I'll be there");
  original.reply("grace", "Is there pizza?");
  count = original.replies.size();
  backUser = r.replyTo.user;
}
```

Output:

```text
original = Post@a5d
count = 2
backUser = joe
```

Prof: Here’s the picture just after both `reply` calls, but before we read `count` and `backUser`:

```
Names (the stack)
  main()
    r = @1003
  top level
    original = @1001
    count = 0
    backUser = null
Heap
  @1001: Post[user=joe, message=CSE-PACE next Tuesday!, likes=0, replies=@1002, replyTo=null]
  @1002: [@1003, @1005]
  @1003: Post[user=ada, message=I'll be there, likes=0, replies=@1004, replyTo=@1001]
  @1004: []
  @1005: Post[user=grace, message=Is there pizza?, likes=0, replies=@1006, replyTo=@1001]
  @1006: []
```

Prof: Each `reply` did two things at once: it made a new `Post` and pointed that post’s `replyTo` back at the one it was replying to. That leaves a link from the original to the reply through the list, and from the reply back to the original through `replyTo`.

Student: Now for the likes. Since we are using references, whenever we like a `Post` it shouldn’t matter whether I reach it through the variable `r` or through `original.replies.get(0)`. They both point at the same object, so liking one should show up on the other.

Prof: Exactly, the posts are mutable. They can be changed without making a copy.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

class Post {
  String user;
  String message;
  int likes;
  ArrayList<Post> replies;
  Post replyTo;

  Post(String user, String message) {
    this.user = user;
    this.message = message;
    this.likes = 0;
    this.replies = new ArrayList<Post>();
    this.replyTo = null;
  }

  void like() {
    this.likes = this.likes + 1;
  }

  Post reply(String user, String message) {
    Post r = new Post(user, message);
    r.replyTo = this;
    this.replies.add(r);
    return r;
  }
}

Post original = new Post("joe", "CSE-PACE next Tuesday!");
int viaVariable;
int viaList;
void main() {
  Post r = original.reply("ada", "I'll be there");
  original.replies.get(0).like();
  viaVariable = r.likes;
  viaList = original.replies.get(0).likes;
}
```

Output:

```text
original = Post@bee
viaVariable = 1
viaList = 1
```

Student: So we’ve been using `ArrayList`, `HashSet`, and `HashMap`. They have a lot of similarities — are they connected in any way?

Prof: They sure are. Each one of these classes **implements** an interface. `ArrayList` is one kind of `List`, and a `List` is a kind of `Collection`. `HashSet` is a `Set`, which is also a `Collection`. `HashMap` is a bit different as a `Map` holds key/value pairs rather than single elements. Here’s the class hierarchy for that.

```
Collection (interface)
  add(E e)
  contains(Object o)
  remove(Object o)
  size()
List (interface) under Collection
  get(int index)
  add(int index, E e)
  set(int index, E e)
  remove(int index)
Set (interface) under Collection
Map (interface)
  put(K key, V value)
  get(Object key)
  containsKey(Object key)
  getOrDefault(Object key, V d)
ArrayList under List
HashSet under Set
HashMap under Map
```

Prof: Because `ArrayList` is a `List`, you will sometimes see the field written as `List<Post> replies` instead of `ArrayList<Post>`. We only covered one type of list, but you will learn about others in future classes. The full set of methods each one offers is in the [Java documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/List.html).

- `p.replies` is unchanged until `like()` is called
- `p.replies` contains `r` and `r.replyTo` is `p`
- `r.replies` contains `p` and `p.replyTo` is `r`

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

  ArrayList<Post> replies = new ArrayList<Post>();
```

## [Generics Overview](collections-and-generics/generics-overview.html)

Student: Ok Professor, you said you’d teach me what the angle brackets in `ArrayList<String>` mean.

Prof: Those are generics. `ArrayList` is one class that can hold any kind of object, so it needs to be told which kind you want for this particular list. The thing in the angle brackets is called the type argument. `ArrayList<String>` is a list of `String`s, and `ArrayList<Integer>` is a list of `Integer`s.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> words = new ArrayList<String>();
ArrayList<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>();
String w;
int n;
void main() {
  words.add("hello");
  nums.add(42);
  w = words.get(0);
  n = nums.get(0);
}
```

Output:

```text
words = [hello]
nums = [42]
w = hello
n = 42
```

Prof: Look at the types of what comes out. `words.get(0)` is a `String`, and `nums.get(0)` is an `Integer`. The type argument decides what `get` gives back and what `add` accepts.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

record Point(int x, int y) { }

ArrayList<Point> points = new ArrayList<Point>();
int x;
void main() {
  points.add(new Point(3, 4));
  x = points.get(0).x();
}
```

Output:

```text
points = [Point[x=3, y=4]]
x = 3
```

Student: What stops me from putting the wrong thing in? Like using `add(3)` to an `ArrayList<String>`?

Prof: The compiler would stop you. Before your program runs, Java checks every use of `words` against the type argument. If you try to add something that isn’t a `String`, you get a compile error.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> words = new ArrayList<String>();
void main() {
  words.add(3);
}
```

Output (compile error):

```text
line 5: error: The method add(int, String) in the type ArrayList<String> is not applicable for the arguments (int)
```

Prof: This is the same reason `ArrayList<int>` didn’t work earlier. A type argument has to be a reference type, like a class or record, not a primitive, so for whole numbers we use `Integer`. It’s also why you can call `words.get(0).length()`: the compiler already knows the element is a `String`.

Student: `HashMap` had two things in its brackets. Does that work the same way?

Prof: Yes, you just give one type argument for each blank, in order. Remember that for a `HashMap<Integer, String>` the first is the type of the **keys** and the second is the type of the **values**.

```java
import java.util.HashMap;

HashMap<Integer, String> directory = new HashMap<Integer, String>();
String name;
void main() {
  directory.put(12345, "Ricardo");
  name = directory.get(12345);
}
```

Output:

```text
directory = {12345=Ricardo}
name = Ricardo
```

Prof: When you read the Java documentation, you’ll see these written as `ArrayList<E>` and `HashMap<K, V>`. The letters are placeholders that your type arguments fill in. The `E` stands for the **element** type, and `K` and `V` for the **key** and **value** types. So when the documentation says that `get` returns an `E`, for your `ArrayList<String>` that means a `String`. You’ll learn how to write classes with placeholders like these in later courses.

# Appendix: The Pict Library

## [Pict Library Reference](pict-library/pict-library.html)

### Shapes

- `Circle(int radius, String color)`
- `CircleOutline(int radius, String color)`
- `Rect(int width, int height, String color)`
- `RectOutline(int width, int height, String color)`
- `Triangle(int width, int height, String color)`
- `TriangleOutline(int width, int height, String color)`
- `Text(String content, int size, String color)`

A size of `0` makes an empty picture, such as `new Rect(0, 0, "white")`: it takes up no room, so it is a handy starting point for building a picture up piece by piece. A negative size is an error.

### Colors

`"red"`, `"green"`, `"blue"`, `"yellow"`, `"orange"`, `"pink"`, `"magenta"`, `"cyan"`, `"purple"`, `"brown"`, `"black"`, `"white"`, `"gray"`, `"grey"`, `"lightgray"`, `"darkgray"`

`"transparent"` paints nothing, but takes up its size like any other picture.

### Combinations

- `Beside(Pict left, Pict right)`
- `Above(Pict top, Pict bottom)`
- `Below(Pict bottom, Pict top)`
- `Overlay(Pict front, Pict back)`
- `OverlayAt(Pict front, int x, int y, Pict back)`
- `OverlayAtAlign(Pict front, int x, int y, String align, Pict back)` — `align` is `"center"`, `"bottom-left"`, `"bottom-right"`, `"top-left"` or `"top-right"`
- `AddLine(Pict base, int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, String color)`
- `AddLine(Pict base, int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, int thickness, String color)`

### Transformations

- `Rotate(Pict pict, int degrees)`

### Pict Methods

- `int width()`
- `int height()`
- `Pict beside(Pict other)` – this picture on the left, `other` on the right
- `Pict above(Pict other)` – this picture on top, `other` under it
- `Pict below(Pict other)` – this picture on the bottom, `other` on top of it
- `Pict overlay(Pict other)` – this picture in front, `other` behind it
- `Pict overlayAt(int x, int y, Pict other)`
- `Pict overlayAtAlign(int x, int y, String align, Pict other)`
- `Pict addLine(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, String color)`
- `Pict addLine(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, int thickness, String color)`
- `Raster render()`
- `Pict rotate(int degrees)`

### Fractional Sizes and Angles

Every size, position, thickness, and angle above also accepts a `double`, rounded to the nearest whole pixel or degree. A picture stores and prints whole numbers either way. A measurement of `NaN` or infinity is an error.

- `Circle(double radius, String color)`
- `CircleOutline(double radius, String color)`
- `Rect(double width, double height, String color)`
- `RectOutline(double width, double height, String color)`
- `Triangle(double width, double height, String color)`
- `TriangleOutline(double width, double height, String color)`
- `Text(String content, double size, String color)`
- `OverlayAt(Pict front, double x, double y, Pict back)`
- `OverlayAtAlign(Pict front, double x, double y, String align, Pict back)`
- `AddLine(Pict base, double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2, String color)`
- `AddLine(Pict base, double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2, double thickness, String color)`
- `Rotate(Pict pict, double degrees)`
- `Pict overlayAt(double x, double y, Pict other)`
- `Pict overlayAtAlign(double x, double y, String align, Pict other)`
- `Pict addLine(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2, String color)`
- `Pict addLine(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2, double thickness, String color)`
- `Pict rotate(double degrees)`

### Rasters

A `Raster` is a rectangle of pixels, each a `Color` from `java.awt` (start the file with `import java.awt.Color;`). `x` counts across from the left and `y` counts down from the top, both starting at `0`.

- `Raster(Color[][] pixels)` – one inner array per row, top row first; every row must have the same length, and no pixel may be `null`. The raster copies the array, so changing `pixels` afterward does not change it.
- `Raster(int width, int height)` – every pixel transparent
- `int width()` – the length of each row
- `int height()` – the number of rows
- `Color colorAt(int x, int y)` – the pixel in row `y`, column `x`
- `void setColorAt(int x, int y, Color color)`
- `FromRaster(Raster raster)` – a `Pict` that shows the raster’s pixels

Two rasters are `equals` when they have the same size and the same color at every pixel, however they were made. `Pict.render()` turns any picture into a raster.

### Java Colors

- `Color.RED`, `Color.GREEN`, `Color.BLUE`, `Color.WHITE`, `Color.BLACK`, and the other names in `java.awt.Color`
- `new Color(int r, int g, int b)` – red, green, and blue amounts from `0` to `255`
- `new Color(int r, int g, int b, int alpha)` – `alpha` `0` is fully transparent, `255` fully solid

A `Color` prints as `java.awt.Color[r=…,g=…,b=…]`, without its alpha, so a transparent pixel prints the same as black.

### Showing and Saving

- `ImageIO_.show(Pict p)`
- `ImageIO_.show(Raster r)`
- `ImageIO_.save(Pict p, String filename)`
- `ImageIO_.save(Raster r, String filename)`
- `ImageIO_.save(Pict[] frames, String filename)` — an animated GIF, 100 ms per frame, looping
- `ImageIO_.save(Pict[] frames, int delayMs, String filename)`
- `ImageIO_.save(Pict[] frames, int delayMs, boolean loop, String filename)`
- `ImageIO_.load(String filename)` – a `Raster`; a file you saved wins over one of the book’s images with the same name
- `ImageIO_.render(Pict p)`

Showing an empty picture puts up a small gray dotted circle, so you can see that something was shown. Saving one is an error, because PNG and GIF files need at least one pixel.

The book’s images: `images/geisel.png`, `images/salk.png`, `images/cove.png`, `images/blacks-beach.png`, `images/torrey-cliffs.png`, `images/pier.png`, `images/pier-under.png`

### Credits

The Pict library is based on the image library from How to Design Programs and Racket, and on work by Ben Lerner at Northeastern University. It is re-implemented here to make it run well in the book and suit the needs of this course.

# Appendix: Working on Your Own Computer

This page was written by Opus 5.5 (an AI model) on 2026-10-06 and has not yet been edited by the authors.

## [The Kit](your-own-computer/the-kit.html)

Everything in this book runs in the page. When you want your programs in files of your own, start from the *kit*: the book’s `Pict` library, JUnit for testing, and a small example of each. There are two ways to get it.

### In a Codespace

[Open the kit in a GitHub Codespace](https://codespaces.new/ucsd-cse11/kit?ref=fa26). A Codespace is VS Code running in your browser on a computer GitHub provides, with Java 25 and the Java extensions already installed; the first start takes a minute or two. You need a GitHub account, and a Codespace you leave alone for a few weeks is deleted, so download anything you want to keep.

### On your own computer

[Download the kit](kit/cse11-kit.zip) (a zip; it is also on GitHub as [the kit repository](https://github.com/ucsd-cse11/kit/tree/fa26)). You will need Java 25 or newer: install a JDK from [adoptium.net](https://adoptium.net), then check with

```
java -version
```

### What is in it

- [`Pict.java`](kit/Pict.java) — the library this book uses, the same file the book’s pages run. On your computer `ImageIO_.show` opens a window instead of drawing below the code (a Codespace has no display, so there it saves `shown-0.png`), and file names are relative to the folder you run `java` in.
- [`Example.java`](kit/Example.java) — a program that uses it.
- [`ExampleTest.java`](kit/ExampleTest.java) — JUnit tests.
- [`lib/junit.jar`](kit/lib/junit.jar) — JUnit itself, under [its license](kit/lib/LICENSE-junit.md).
- [`README.md`](kit/README.md) — these instructions, short.

### Running a program

In the kit’s folder:

```
java -ea Example.java
```

Java compiles `Example.java`, and the `Pict.java` next to it, as it starts; `-ea` turns on `assert`, as the book’s widgets do. This one saves `example.png`.

### Running the tests

```
javac -d out -cp lib/junit.jar *.java
java -jar lib/junit.jar execute --class-path out --scan-class-path
```

The first line compiles everything into `out/`; the second finds every `@Test` there and runs it. In VS Code, the Testing panel does the same.

The general idea of the recipe and a build through structurally recursive data is of course from [How to Design Programs](https://htdp.org).

It is re-implemented here to make it run well in the book and suit the needs of this course.

# Glossary

## argument

A value given to a constructor or method call. One of the things in the parentheses when making a call. Can be an expression that evaluates to a value; the argument expressions are evaluated first to values, then the method is called.

## `boolean`

A primitive value that is either `true` or `false`, for use in conditional checks.

## composition

Taking the results of one or more methods or values and combining them together with new methods or constructors to create new results.

## constructor

A special kind of method that works with `new`. Constructors are created along with each `record` or `class` definition.

## constructor use

An expression of the form `new Name(arguments...)`. `Name` must be the name of a `class` or `record`. The arguments are given to the constructor, usually to initialize field values.

## definition

A statement of the form `Type name = value;`

Can appear at the toplevel, in a method body, or as a class member.

## `double`

One of the types of “floating-point” numbers, which can represent non-integer numbers in a wide range. Arithmetic on `double` often has unavoidable error, so programs that use `double`s need to consider arithmetic error.

## field

A part of a record or class definition. Consists of a name, a type, and optional modifiers. Defines a storage slot for instances of that class or record.

## instance

Synonym for object.

## `int`

A primitive type, describing exact integers in the range −231 to 231 - 1, inclusive.

## integer division

Division that truncates towards 0, applied when using `/` on integer values.

## method body

The statements that compute a return value (or have effects, in the case of a `void` returning method) in a method definition.

## nested data

When an instance of one compound data type is stored inside another.

## object

A value created via constructor use. Has fields and stores the name of the constructor used to create it (known as the object’s `class`).

## operator

Operators are symbols like `+` and `<` and `&&` that go in between two expressions. They have specific meaning on number types and `boolean`s and `String`s.

## parameter

The names in a method definition that get their values at method call time from the arguments that are passed. Written with a type and a name (but no value; that is supplied at the call). Java checks that method calls use the right types.

## `Pict`

A datatype specific to the library that comes with this book for representing images.

## primitive type

A set of fixed-size, base values part of the Java language. They have keyword, lowercase types (`int`, `double`, `boolean`, and so on). They are stored directly in variables, fields, and array elements, and never have a reference created for them.

## `record`

A definition of a new datatype, with specific fields and methods. Java defines a canonical constructor for the record that takes all the listed fields, an `equals` method, a `toString` method, accessor methods, and other defaults.

## reference type

Types of values that are stored on the heap — objects and arrays. A reference type is either an array type, the name of a class, or the name of an interface. By convention these are usually written in uppercase. A reference-typed field, variable, or array element stores the reference, with the contents of the object or array stored in a dedicated address on the heap.

## return type

A type that describes what a method definition is guaranteed to return. Java will check that the method body in fact returns a value of that type.

## `String`

A built-in class in Java for representing text data. Stores a sequence of characters. Every string literal turns into one.

## string literal

Text between double quotes. Turns into a `String` when the program runs.

## type

A name for a set of values. Can be an **object type**, typically written in uppercase as the name of a class, record, or interface, an **array type** which has an object or array type followed by brackets `[]`, or a primitive type like `int`, `double`, or `boolean`

## value

Things that can be stored in variables, fields, and array elements, passed as arguments, or returned from methods are values. All the primitives are values, and references are values. Technically, arrays and objects are not values in Java, only references to them are values, but sometimes we conflate the two when talking about code.
